all.title: Insider threat detection: a socio-technical analysis of behavioural pathways in malicious insider fraud
all.abstract: Purpose Cybersecurity is inherently interdisciplinary, yet insider threats are often examined through technical or behavioural lenses in isolation. This paper aims to focus on fraud committed by malicious insiders and aims to improve the understanding of how such attacks develop, thereby enhancing detection and prevention. Design/methodology/approach A novel methodological approach is adopted, integrating grounded theory (GT) with behaviour sequence analysis (BSA) to examine socio-technical events. This enables identification of key indicators and the temporal pathways leading to insider fraud. Findings The findings caution against assuming a single, distinct fraudster profile. Within the cases examined, individuals involved in fraud sometimes engaged in other forms of insider misconduct, including intellectual property theft. The results question established frameworks, such as the fraud triangle, by demonstrating the complexity and dynamic nature of insider fraud. In several cases, information concerning offending or intent was communicated through online or face-to-face interactions. The pattern warrants further investigation, as a potential source of detection using natural language processing methods. Practical implications Drawing on situational prevention theory, the paper offers recommendations for organisations, including strengthening access controls and promoting transparency regarding insider incidents to improve detection and prevention. Originality/value This study advances insider threat research by combining GT with behaviour sequence analysis to examine socio-technical behaviour sequences. It identifies preliminary pathways and warning signals within the cases examined, offering an alternative to static profiling approaches.

all.title: Evaluating Ongoing Access Attacks on the Web
all.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
all.abstract: In ongoing access attacks, an adversary reconfigures security features on a compromised account to maintain access, despite victim attempts to remove them. Such attacks are particularly common in interpersonal violence where abusers often use them for continuous monitoring, surveillance, and stalking of their victims. Despite the severity and prevalence of these attacks in practice, we are aware of only one prior study that considers them, and only in the context of authentication via passkeys. We provide the first study of ongoing access attacks that holistically considers all available authentication mechanisms. First, we survey modern account security features to characterize 11 types of access routes: different ways in which a user can configure the account to obtain authenticated access. Many web services now offer a multitude of access routes, including single-sign on, passkeys, recovery mechanisms, and more, resulting in a rich attack surface even for adversaries that only use service-provided user interfaces. Using these access routes, we experimentally simulate ongoing access attacks for 20 popular services, showing that 14 of these offer an access route that is irrevocable or not properly remediated by service-provided guidance, leaving adversarial access intact.

all.title: Meme Coin Factories: Uncovering Large-Scale Manipulations on pump.fun
all.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
all.abstract: Once complex, creating and deploying a new cryptocurrency has become trivial. Coin launchpads now allow users to generate a new coin with merely a few clicks, at a minimal cost. Launchpad popularity has grown in tandem with the rise of "meme coins," which usually do not offer any novel technological properties and are purely created for fun. The most prominent coin launchpad, pump.fun, has gained significant traction, grossing over 100 million USD in daily trading volume. The mass adoption of coin launchpads, however, also enables strategic actors to easily manipulate trading signals, unbeknownst to inexperienced traders who then buy certain coins, and enable these strategic actors to profit from rapid and unsustainable price increases ("pumps"). To identify such manipulations at scale, we conduct a large-scale study of pump.fun, collecting information on all 15 million coins launched in the last two years, and performing analysis on large, random samples of transaction data. We identify five classes of manipulation strategies: 1) wash trading, 2) creator address obfuscation, 3) coordinated sell, 4) copycat coins, and 5) social media manipulation. We find that strategic actors often bypass the platform interface and implement these strategies in a highly automated and low-latency fashion, by interacting directly with the blockchain. We further uncover the existence of "Market-Manipulation-as-a-service (MMaaS)," third-party tools that enable users to perform these manipulations without any technical expertise. We conclude by devising mitigations and proposing recommendations for traders, pump.fun, wallets or chain scanners, software development platforms, and regulators.

all.title: SAR-related sanction publications under article 60 of directive (EU) 2015/849: a comparison of banking and insurance supervision in Germany and France against the background of responsive regulation
institutions: FOM University of Applied Sciences for Economics and Management
all.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how the publication of sanctions under Article 60 of Directive (EU) 2015/849 functions as an enforcement instrument and whether it meets the requirements of responsive regulation, comparing the banking and insurance supervisors of Germany (BaFin) and France (ACPR) for breaches of suspicious activity reporting (SAR) obligations. Design/methodology/approach The study combines a comparative legal analysis, translating the statutory escalation instruments into the enforcement pyramid with a content analysis of published sanction decisions from the BaFin and ACPR registers, filtered to anti-money-laundering (AML) reporting breaches. Findings Both regimes equip supervisors with instruments capable of responsive enforcement, yet practice diverges sharply. BaFin publications remain abstract and largely restate the statute, whereas ACPR publications disclose detailed facts. German publications therefore convey considerably less of the information on which the learning and shaming mechanisms of responsive regulation depend. Article 60, being minimum harmonising, leaves this to national legislators. Research limitations/implications The study analyses supervisory communication, not real-world effectiveness. It relies on government and audit data, is confined to two jurisdictions and to SAR-related breaches and cannot establish behavioural or causal effects. Practical implications The union legislator should concretise the mandatory content of sanction publications, including under the 2024 AML package. Originality/value This paper is the first to analyse Article 60 sanction publications through the lens of responsive regulation and to compare German and French supervisory practice. It further provides a permanently archived comparative data set of the analysed publications for future research.

all.title: The Opacity Penalty in Digital Banking: How Technology Distributes SME Credit Constraints
all.abstract: This paper investigates how bank digitalization affects credit supply within established SME lending relationships using panel data linking 179,921 European SMEs to 54 relationship banks across 15 countries (2009–2019) and a novel index of bank technology adoption. We find that bank digitalization increases average long-term debt growth by approximately 0.10% points, offsetting around 12% of sample-period deleveraging, with effects concentrated in long-term credit and substantially weaker for short-term credit. The aggregate effect masks a strong distributional effect, documenting that long-term credit growth declines for the smallest existing customers, and increases for the largest, generating a 0.18%-point gap between the two. These findings persist across various institutional environments and are robust to a difference-in-differences design that exploits the EU’s Payment Services Directive and to instrumental-variables estimation using Google Trends index. This evidence implies that bank digitalization systematically redistributes credit growth toward more transparent borrowers within existing banking relationships, rather than democratizing credit access across the SME population, thereby challenging optimism about banking sector digitalization.

all.title: Money laundering, terrorist financing, and smuggling: emerging threats to Pakistan’s national security
institutions: Shaheed Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto Institute of Science and Technology
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the institutional and regulatory factors shaping the implementation of Pakistan’s anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT) framework, with specific attention to security risks allied with smuggling-related illicit financial flows. It develops a sequential-mechanism framework linking regulatory compliance, institutional weaknesses, interagency coordination and enforcement effectiveness to the potential intersection between smuggling, money laundering and terrorist financing. Design/methodology/approach This research uses legal document analysis as a risk-assessment method. It examines the legislative frameworks, policy instruments and official government reports to evaluate the effectiveness of Pakistan’s anti-money laundering (AML) and countering the financing of terrorism (CFT) regimes. Findings The analysis indicates that, although Pakistan has made improvements driven in part by Financial Action Task Force compliance requirements, significant deficiencies remain. These include weak institutional capacity, insufficient interagency coordination and inadequate oversight of high-risk sectors, particularly non-profit organizations and real estate. The study also underscores how emerging digital technologies create new vulnerabilities by enabling porous financial boundaries and facilitating illicit financial transactions. Originality/value By articulating the security implications of financial crime and mapping the systemic vulnerabilities within Pakistan’s AML/CFT architecture, this paper offers context-specific reforms aimed at strengthening intelligence capabilities, regulatory compliance and regional cooperation. This integrated perspective contributes to a deeper understanding of how illicit finance directly undermines national security.

all.title: FEDS Paper: Where's The Bank? Banking Access in the Era of Branch Consolidation(Revised)
all.abstract: Robert M. Adams and Shane M. Sherlund The number of U.S. bank branches fell more than 19 log points between 2014 and 2024, prompting concerns about eroding access to banking services. We study this contraction using a free-entry, two-dimensional spatial competition model in the tradition of Lösch and Hotelling. The model predicts that equilibrium branch density scales linearly with local customer density and that the elasticity of mean nearest-branch distance with respect to the number of branches is -1/2 . Using branch locations and census-block-level data on households and employment, we estimate elasticities between -0.37 and -0.52. These lie near the two-dimensional prediction and reject the -1 implied by one-dimensional models. Differences in branch access across demographic groups are economically small, and they did not widen over the decade. The branch contraction is consistent with the equilibrium response of a competitive spatial system to an industry-wide profitability shock, rather than a localized withdrawal of service.

all.title: FEDS Paper: The Welfare Effects of Bank Liquidity and Capital Requirements(Revised)
all.abstract: Skander J. Van den Heuvel and Sergio Villalvazo The stringency of bank liquidity and capital requirements should depend on their social costs and benefits. Equilibrium asset returns yield two simple formulas that express the welfare cost of each requirement as a function of observable variables only. Based on U.S. data, the welfare cost of a 10% liquidity requirement is equivalent to a permanent loss in consumption of about 0.02%, a modest impact. Even using conservative measurements, the cost of a similarly sized increase in the capital requirement is roughly tenfold. Still, optimal policy relies on both requirements to mitigate moral hazard from deposit insurance and is close to Basel III levels.

all.title: VRLLM: Turning LLMs into Powerful Tabular Classifiers
all.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on text, but whether pretrained LLMs are effective for large-scale tabular classification remains unclear, as many previous works demonstrate that LLMs' tabular data classification performance falls behind tree-based models or neural architectures designed for tabular data. At Visa Research, we managed to fine-tune a pretrained Llama 3.2 1B LLM on billions of rows of labeled tabular data and make it outperform a wide array of tabular classifiers and even our competitive production deep learning model. For ease of reference, we refer to the model as the Visa Research LLM (VRLLM). In this paper, we share how we achieved this exciting result, covering data preparation, training recipe, ablation studies of design choices and deployment validation. We also benchmark frontier LLMs on the same task and analyze their prediction behavior across model families and generations. Our interpretability experiments suggest that VRLLM learns feature-specific predictive associations, while component ablations indicate that the earliest two FFN layers contribute to the emergence of linearly decodable task information. Our paper provides an engineering recipe and a focused empirical case study on adapting compact LLMs to industrial tabular prediction tasks.

all.title: The Struggle to "Do Life Right" in an Always-Online World: Teens, Mobile Phones, and the Limits of Individual Responsibility
all.abstract: Today’s teens have grown up with mobile phones and social media mediating daily routines, social relationships, and schooling, yet their experiences are often reduced to narratives of distraction, mental health risks, and addiction. In this paper we present a qualitative study including a questionnaire (n = 47) and focus groups (n = 34) with upper-level high school students to examine how they experience mobile phone and social media use and how they believe they are perceived by adult figures and media. Our findings show that teens encounter phones as infrastructural rather than optional, with use shaped by expectations of availability and participation. Teens described situational strategies for managing phone use around studying and sleep, alongside ambivalent social media experiences. Teens reflected on limits of self-regulation within environments demanding connectivity, pointing to a need for redistributed responsibility between teens, adults, school leadership and platform design.

all.title: Cell-TRICC: A Model-Based Approach to Cellwise-Trimmed Co-Clustering
all.abstract: Co-clustering consists of simultaneously partitioning the rows and columns of a data matrix. It is an unsupervised technique well suited to explore and extract patterns from high-dimensional data. It is often the case that real data contain outliers: such anomalous values could impair standard statistical methods, while being interesting pieces of information. Despite this fact and the wide applicability of co-clustering, very little literature is concerned with outlier-robust co-clustering approaches. Building on the well-known framework of Latent Block Models, we propose a novel co-clustering method that can deal with cellwise contaminated matrices. We focus on count data modeled by Poisson distributions, but the main ideas are general. Robustness is sought through cellwise trimming, implemented as an additional step in a stochastic EM-like algorithm. Model selection is performed by using novel Bayesian criteria to select the number of groups and the trimming level simultaneously. Finally, our approach is tested and compared to existing methods through extensive simulations, and showcased on a fully fledged application to a trade monitoring problem. The real-data analysis shows the potential of the proposed methodology both as a data exploration and anomaly detection tool, and is further enriched by insights drawn from original visualizations and diagnostic plots.

all.title: Financial stability implications of AI adoption in the financial industry and the real economy
all.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the financial industry as well as the broader economy, creating both opportunities and risks. Banks and asset managers, which represent key channels of financial intermediation in the euro area, are increasingly using AI for tasks such as credit scoring, fraud detection and portfolio management. While AI adoption can support innovation and enhance operational efficiency, it may also introduce new risks and amplify existing vulnerabilities, including a reliance on a small number of technology providers that creates concentration and third-party dependencies across the financial system. At the same time, financial institutions are also increasingly exposed to AI-driven developments in the real economy. A novel firm-level indicator suggests that a sizeable share of firms, concentrated mainly in the IT and financial sectors, is significantly exposed to AI-related opportunities and risks. Policies should focus on improving the quality of data that monitor the use of AI, strengthening the oversight of critical AI providers and adapting market safeguards and supervisory capabilities to emerging risks.

all.title: Developing A Conceptual Framework For AI-Assisted Compliance Monitoring and Anomaly Detection in High-Volume Transaction Environments
all.venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
all.abstract: Financial institutions and payment platforms now process transaction volumes that routinely exceed the practical capacity of rule-based compliance monitoring. This paper develops a conceptual framework for embedding artificial intelligence into compliance monitoring and anomaly detection within high-volume transaction environments. Drawing on literature spanning anti-money laundering supervision, fraud detection, graph-based machine learning, federated learning, concept drift adaptation, and financial model risk governance, the framework organizes the compliance monitoring function into six interdependent layers: data ingestion and integration, feature engineering and entity resolution, a hybrid detection engine, explainability and risk scoring, human-in-the-loop review, and governance with continuous feedback. The framework treats detection accuracy and regulatory defensibility as joint design objectives rather than competing priorities, positioning explainability and human oversight as structural components rather than after-the-fact controls. The paper situates the framework against existing regulatory expectations, including the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk guidance and the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act, discusses sector-specific extensions to digital assets, insurance, and cross-institutional consortia, illustrates the framework through a hypothetical high-volume payments scenario, and compares it against alternative approaches. It concludes by identifying the limitations of a purely conceptual contribution and outlining directions for empirical validation.

all.title: Vision language model (VLM)-enabled counterfactual reasoning for illegal dumping profiling in metropolitan cities
all.abstract: Street view analytics (SVA) has gained increasing value in environmental criminology. However, most of the analyses are based only on limited factual information, which could lead to potential bias and limit opportunities to investigate the effect of a specific factor of interest while holding others constant. Generating counterfactual street views using vision language models (VLMs) provides a promising avenue for counterfactual reasoning and allows for the controlled study of individual factors. This study presents a novel approach that generates diverse counterfactual street views and compares them with their factual counterparts, using illegal dumping sites in urban environments as a case study. The baseline is a dataset of 757 Google Street Views (GSVs), of which 506 are illegal dumping sites and 251 are controls. Seven VLMs were benchmarked, and Nano Banana Pro was chosen to generate 1000 more counterfactual views with different featured factors. Of these, 921 passed quality screening and were retained for the main analysis. The data was analyzed by two high-powered VLMs namely GPT-5.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.6. In both evaluator graphs, visible litter and surface defects were associated with higher model scores for identifying illegal dumping sites, and well-maintained pavement with lower scores. The resulting graphs describe responses to controlled visual edits and provide hypotheses about environmental influences for future field validation. This approach can be scaled to broader studies of location-based environmental crime.

all.title: Generative AI and the restructuring of criminal opportunity
institutions: London School of Economics and Political Science
all.abstract: Fifty years after Crime as Opportunity (Mayhew et al., 1976 ), the opportunity paradigm remains criminology’s most productive account of how and where crime happens. This theoretical article asks what generative artificial intelligence (hereafter AI) does to the opportunity structure that the paradigm describes. It argues that AI is not merely another item in the long list of technologies that create new targets; it is a change in the supply of offender capability itself. Distinguishing three criminal uses of AI—expert on demand, producer of synthetic artefacts and autonomous agent—and placing them beside the crime harvests of earlier technologies, the article works through the constitutive dimensions of a criminal opportunity—effort, risk and reward—and the guardianship that bears on them. AI lowers the effort required to offend, weakens the perceived risk of detection and raises the expected yield per attempt, moving previously unprofitable targets across the threshold of viability. These claims are illustrated with recent evidence on AI-assisted phishing, no-code malware, agent-executed extortion and insurgent use of frontier models. The article maps AI mechanisms onto the five families of situational prevention and analyses where guardianship is most efficiently located—at the target, in the channel or in the tool—in a contest in which defenders also hold AI. It contends that the paradigm’s explanatory core survives intact, but that its preventive centre of gravity must move upstream, to the model and platform layer, and closes with a research agenda.

all.title: CMN e BC aprimoram medidas para prevenir riscos associados ao endividamento
all.abstract: O Conselho Monetário Nacional (CMN) e o Banco Central (BC) aprovaram um conjunto de medidas para aprimorar a conduta e o tratamento prudencial dos riscos associados à concessão de crédito e ao endividamento, especialmente de pessoas físicas. As iniciativas buscam favorecer a concessão sustentável de crédito, fortalecer a disciplina de mercado e aprimorar o acompanhamento de indicadores relevantes para avaliações sobre o endividamento, os padrões de concessão e a solidez das instituições e de suas carteiras de crédito. As medidas também atuam no reforço dos critérios de originação de crédito, gerenciamento de riscos, mensuração do comprometimento financeiro das pessoas físicas e ampliação da transparência sobre o endividamento. all.title: TeleGapper: On the (un)reliability of privacy policies in Telegram Mini Apps
institutions: IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca
all.abstract: Telegram Mini Apps are Web applications embedded within the Telegram client, forming an ecosystem of third-party services within a major messaging platform. Despite their growing adoption and access to Telegram-provided context, their privacy properties remain largely unexplored. Unlike ecosystems such as WeChat, which rely on tightly controlled, proprietary execution frameworks, Telegram adopts a different model: Mini Apps run inside a WebView, combining platform-provided context with standard Web capabilities and unrestricted outbound networking. This enables applications to transmit user-related information to analytics, advertising, tracking, or other third parties through ordinary Web requests, potentially without adequate disclosure. Privacy disclosures are critical for transparency. Telegram allows Mini Apps either to define an application-specific privacy policy or to rely on a platform-provided default policy. While the latter reduces the developer’s disclosure burden, it may lead to generic statements that do not accurately capture data practices of individual Mini Apps. In this paper, we present TeleGapper, a black-box dynamic analysis framework to assess the privacy posture of Mini Apps by capturing runtime network traffic, identifying third-party communications, and comparing observed data flows against disclosed privacy information. We evaluated 278 working Mini Apps collected from tApps Center, a community-driven catalogue for discovering third-party applications in Telegram. Our analysis found that 59.4% of the analyzed Mini Apps exhibited at least one undisclosed data flow under the applicable privacy-policy regime, 78.8% relied exclusively on Telegram’s default privacy policy, and none displayed an observable in-app consent or opt-out mechanism at launch during the measured sessions.

all.title: DDQN-MLP: An explainable and adversarially robust DRL-Guided adaptive learning framework for ransomware detection
all.abstract: Ransomware detection remains challenging because modern variants exhibit heterogeneous, evasive, and partially benign-like behavioral patterns. Conventional supervised learning typically applies fixed optimization strategies in which all samples are treated uniformly during training. These strategies may inadequately address latent behavioral heterogeneity when subtle ransomware behaviors overlap with benign activities. To address this limitation, this study introduces a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework in training-time for ransomware detection using modern Windows 11 sandbox telemetry. The proposed system employs a DDQN as an adaptive sample-weighting controller during training. Using batch-level loss and prediction-confidence information, the DDQN adjusts sample weights to guide the lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifier. Crucially, after training, the DDQN component is fully decoupled, leaving only a lightweight MLP for low-latency inference. Using 5-fold stratified cross-validation on a balanced dataset of 2,000 executable profiles spanning 30 ransomware families, DDQN+MLP achieved the highest mean accuracy and F1-score among the evaluated models, both at 0.9930, with an ROC-AUC of 0.9991. Under family-disjoint GroupKFold cross-validation, in which the same ransomware family did not appear in both the training and validation partitions, the F1-score decreased to 0.9708, providing a stricter assessment of unseen-family generalization within the same Windows 11 ANY.RUN environment. Post-hoc SHAP and LIME explanations were complemented by a SHAP–gradient diagnostic to assess the consistency between feature attributions and classifier sensitivity. White-box adversarial evaluation further showed that adversarial training substantially improved resilience to bounded feature-space perturbations while retaining near-baseline clean-data performance. Overall, the framework combines adaptive training-time weighting, post-hoc interpretability diagnostics, bounded feature-space robustness evaluation, and lightweight inference for behavioral ransomware detection.

all.title: Detecção de fraudes em transações financeiras com Machine Learning: uma revisão da literatura
all.abstract: The growing digitalization of financial transactions has significantly increased the occurrence of fraud, making its detection a central challenge for banking institutions and payment companies. Given the limitations of traditional rule-based systems, machine learning has gained a prominent position in recent scientific literature. This study aimed to analyze, through a narrative literature review, the main machine learning techniques applied to fraud detection in financial transactions, with emphasis on credit cards. The research, qualitative and exploratory in nature, was based on the critical analysis of eight scientific works published between 2018 and 2026, found in databases such as IEEE Xplore, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. Results indicate the recurrent use of ensemble algorithms, such as Random Forest and boosting, alongside classical models, such as Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, and Support Vector Machine, with no universally superior algorithm. The extreme data imbalance is addressed through undersampling, SMOTE and its variants, and decision threshold adjustment. It was also found that metrics such as F1-Score, AUC-ROC, and the area under the precision-recall curve are more suitable than accuracy alone, and the tension between opaque models and the right to review automated decisions set out in the Brazilian General Data Protection Law was discussed. It is concluded that gaps remain regarding model interpretability, adaptation to emerging fraud patterns, and the scarcity of real and public data for validation, pointing to relevant directions for future research.

all.title: Financial Fraud Detection in Nigerian Banks: Data Mining Approach
all.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN
all.abstract: This research investigates the application of data mining techniques, specifically logistic regression and random forest, to detect financial fraud within Nigerian banks. Using individual bank statements and statutory bank charges, the study focuses on developing a robust system for identifying fraudulent transactions. The data preprocessing involves extracting key features such as transaction type, amount, balance, and transaction date. The dataset is split into training and testing sets, and both machine learning models are trained and evaluated based on metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores.The results indicate that the Random Forest model outperforms Logistic Regression, achieving higher accuracy and better handling of complex relationships within the data. Visualization tools like Matplotlib are used to present prediction probabilities, enhancing understanding of model behavior. The system's implementation includes secure access features, detailed transaction analysis, and comprehensive fraud summaries. Challenges such as data imbalance are addressed with techniques like SMOTE and advanced preprocessing methods. This study highlights the potential of using advanced machine learning models for effective fraud detection in financial transactions. The findings suggest that further improvements in feature extraction, data expansion, and exploring more sophisticated models can enhance system performance. This research contributes to the ongoing efforts to secure financial systems against fraudulent activities, offering valuable insights and practical solutions for the banking sector

all.title: Artificial Intelligence and Fraud Detection of Listed Deposit Money Banks in Nigeria
all.venue: JOURNAL OF ACCOUNTING AND FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT
all.abstract: The study examined the impact of artificial intelligence on fraud detection of listed deposit money banks in Nigeria. Fraud detection was used as independent variable while Artificial intelligence was used as the independent variable. The determinants of artificial intelligence in this study will be automated chatbot, deep learning machine, machine learning solutions and natural language processing. The geographical coverage of this study will be in Nigeria. The study will cover 11years spanning from 2012 to 2022; within this period CBN introduced cashless policy into the Nigerian Financial system. More so, a lot of Banks introduced artificial intelligence into their operations within this period. This study employ survey design, Therefore the study employed a survey method of data collection, via a self-administered questionnaire. The data was collected from deposit money banks in Kaduna state. Out of the 14 Listed Deposit money Banks in Nigeria, 10 banks will be selected based on simple random Sampling Technique. The tool will be statistical Package for Statistical sciences (SPSS) version 20. Regression analysis will be used to predict the effect of the independent variable on the dependent variable and also used to either accept or reject null hypothesis. Validity and reliability test will be carried out. The result from Table 4.6 reveals that automated chat boat has a coefficient value of 0.413 and P-value 0.000. This signifies that automated chat boat has a positive and significant influence on deposit money banks. The regression model in Table 4.6 indicated that deep learning machine has a coefficient value 0.212 and P value 0.009. This signified that deep learning machine is positively and significantly impacting fraud detection among deposit money bank. From the Table 4.6 it was observed that machine learning solution has a coefficient value 0.172 and P value 0.069. This shows that machine learning solution is positively but not significant in detecting fraud. From the Table 4.6 the finding shows that natural learning process has a coefficient value -.207 and P value 0.230 this indicates that natural learning process is insignificant on fraud detection. Huge investment in acquisition of deep learning machine should be ensured in order to boost fraud detection and protection in credit issuing and assessment in order to improve corporate performance of banks.

all.title: FraudBench-NG: A NIBSS-Calibrated Synthetic Dataset and Generator for Nigerian Inter-Bank Fraud Detection
all.abstract: Research on inter-bank fraud detection in Nigeria is limited by the lack of shareable transaction data, and synthetic benchmarks can mislead if they leak information or hide their assumptions. FraudBench-NG is a reproducible framework for studying fraud detection under explicitly documented modelling assumptions. It is a parametric simulation calibrated to 2023 NIBSS aggregates, with a released dataset of 2.1~million transactions from 25{,}000 customers and 0.1\% fraud. Fraud is generated as incidents, matching NIBSS counts and loss per case; every parameter is marked as NIBSS or assumed; and every behavioural feature uses only prior transactions, verified by row-by-row recomputation and a label-permutation test. Logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost reach a PR-AUC of 0.016--0.036 (no-skill 0.0007), with wide customer-level bootstrap intervals, so the models cannot be ranked. At a 1\% false-positive rate they raise about 70 false alerts per fraud row caught and flag only about 19\% of incidents at their first transaction. Results depend strongly on the assumptions: a model trained with takeover bursts transfers only partly to data with a different burst probability, and performance differs between burst settings mainly because of how an incident's loss is split across its transactions. Fraud prevalence is a design choice that cannot be compared with the NIBSS case-to-transaction ratio, and no real Nigerian transactions were available for validation.

all.title: The Human-centric Algorithm: Synergising AI-Driven Fraud Detection with Ethical Human Oversight to Optimise Sustainable Banking Integrity
institutions: Arab Academy for Science, Technology, and Maritime Transport
all.abstract: Purpose: The research aims to analyse whether Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) alone are efficient and self-sustainable in detecting financial fraud, or if they need human intervention and supervision for better fraud detection activity in digital finance. Design/Methodology/Approach: The Kaggle credit card fraud dataset of 284,807 transactions was used to determine the grey zone of suspicious flagging. To analyse the occurrence of false positives, a linear regression model was applied to the first 1,000 anonymised banking transactions. Findings: Results demonstrated a high degree of false-positive exposure in automated anomaly-detection systems. The regression analysis also yielded a statistically significant model (F = 4.255; p < 0.001); this underscores the complexity and unpredictability of fraud behaviour in online banking contexts. Original/Value of the Paper: The current research advances the investigation into the likelihood of false positives detected by AI and whether further human supervision is required to intervene in the detection or validation of suspicious flagging. Research Limitations/Implications: The study is limited to the first 1,000 observations from the dataset to ensure manageable statistical interpretation and analytical consistency. Practical Implications: The research offers a transformational roadmap for applying human contextual judgement to banking ecosystems, balancing the predictive accuracy of AI with the moral responsibility of human intelligence to create a resilient, inclusive, and sustainable financial future. Keywords: Digital Fraud Detection; Suspicious Transactions; Online Banking; Fraud Monitoring; Credit Card Fraud; Digital Finance Citation: Masanawa, A.U. and Shaheen, A. (2026): The Human-Centric Algorithm: Synergising AI-Driven Fraud Detection with Ethical Human Oversight to Optimise Sustainable Banking Integrity. In Ahmed, A. (Ed.): World Sustainable Development Outlook 2026, Vol. 22, pp. 195-213. WASD: London, United Kingdom.

all.title: A Development of Advanced Credit Card Fraud Detection Through Deep Learning Approaches with Data Analytics for Secured Banking Application
all.venue: The International Journal of Maritime Engineering
all.abstract: Credit Card Fauld Detection in Banking application technological advancements complicate cybercrime and hinder credit card fraud detection. Traditional methods are ineffective. A company developed an event-based temporal graph (ETG) to detail transactions among users, cards, devices, and accounts. This review examines machine learning algorithms for detecting financial fraud amid rising digital transactions. We examine many forms of fraud, such as money laundering, insurance fraud, credit card fraud, and financial statement fraud, as well as the unique detection difficulties associated with each new model Credit Card Fauld Detection Through Deep Learning Approaches with Data Analytics (CCFDDA). A method for credit card fraud detection that integrates deep learning and traditional machine learning with data preprocessing. Using a Kaggle dataset of 284, 807 transactions (492 fraudulent), we perform Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for feature anonymization and address class imbalance. Our analysis identifies key fraud indicators through statistical methods, and we enhance data completeness by removing incomplete rows, improving model learnability. In the Feature Normalization phase, Min-Max scaling normalizes numerical attributes to the range of 0 to 1 to mitigate scale bias. The cleaned transaction data is represented using overlapping sliding windows to maintain temporal dependencies. The machine-learning fraud detection component evaluates several models, including Decision Trees (DT), Random Forests (RF), Support Vector Machines (SVM), XGBoost, CatBoost, and Logistic Regression (LR), to identify fraudulent transactions and addresses class imbalance through various classification and ensemble techniques. Softmax assigns class probabilities, while a class-weighted loss function addresses class imbalance. The architecture employs machine learning, statistical analysis, structured preprocessing, and temporal graph-based deep learning for fraud detection. Its Deep Learning module utilizes a Dynamic Graph Neural Network (DGNN) for time-dependent classification and message passing, enabling it to model changing transaction interactions over time for effective fraud detection.

all.title: From Detection to Resilience: A Review of Explainable AI Trust and Real-Time Response in AI-Driven Bank Fraud Detection
all.abstract: Background: Banks use machine learning to flag fraudulent transactions at a scale that rule-based systems cannot match. Detection accuracy has received most of the research attention. Much less is known about whether better detection produces a more resilient institution.Purpose: This review examines how AI-driven fraud detection capability relates to the cybersecurity resilience of banks, and what role explainability-based trust and real-time response capability play in that relationship.Method: A narrative review of research on statistical and machine-learning fraud detection, explainable AI, human trust in automation, cyber resilience, and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) studies in banking. A recent U.S. banking survey study (Rimi et al., 2025) is used as an applied reference point.Findings: Three themes emerge. First, detection capability is well documented, but its link to organizational resilience is mostly assumed rather than tested. Second, explainability affects outcomes through human trust and reliance, not through model performance alone. Third, response speed is a weak predictor of resilience when it is not tied to recovery, governance, and learning. The reference survey study found that detection capability predicted resilience directly (β = 0.444) and through explainable AI trust (indirect β = 0.206), while real-time response capability had no significant effect (β = −0.002, p = 0.959).Conclusion: Banks should treat explainability, analyst training, and recovery integration as part of the fraud detection investment. Future work needs longitudinal designs, objective resilience measures, and tests of governance as a moderator.

all.title: Online Payment Fraud Detection Using Machine Learning
all.venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
authors: Akshay Ajalsonde, Om Auti, Vedant Ghadge
M. N. Pimple,  K. D. Jamkar, Dr. H. B. Jadhav, Ajay Kapse
all.abstract: The rapid growth of digital payments, including UPI, cards, net banking and e-wallets, has been accompanied by a sharp rise in online payment fraud. Rule-based filters adapt slowly and raise many false alarms, while fraud itself is extremely rare, so automated detection is a highly class-imbalanced learning problem. This paper presents a complete machine learning framework for online payment fraud detection covering data preprocessing, imbalance handling, model training, threshold selection and evaluation with metrics suited to rare events. Six classifiers (Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting and a Multi-Layer Perceptron) and an unsupervised Isolation Forest are compared on a simulated dataset of 100,000 transactions with 1.25% fraud. At the default threshold, Random Forest gave the best F1-score (0.380), precision (0.507) and ROC-AUC (0.837), with a PR-AUC (0.336) practically equal to that of the neural network (0.332), which achieved the highest recall (0.565) at the price of low precision. Further experiments show that SMOTE and random oversampling raise PR-AUC to 0.434 and 0.457, that the decision threshold changes the precision-recall balance more than the choice of model, and that the unsupervised detector is close to random on this data. The results confirm that ensemble methods are well suited to rare-event fraud detection and that accuracy alone is a misleading measure in this domain.

all.title: Real-Time Behavioural Fraud Prevention in Financial Institutions Using Adaptive Machine Learning
all.venue: International Journal of Scientific Research and Modern Technology.
institutions: SRM Institute of Science and Technology
all.abstract: The proliferation of digital financial channels has exponentially increased the attack surface for financial fraud, with global card fraud losses reaching USD 33.45 billion in 2022. Conventional rule-based fraud detection systems are inherently incapable of adapting to fast-changing fraud tactics, leading to high levels of undetected fraud and too many false positives impacting customer experience. This paper proposes a real-time behavioural fraud prevention framework based on Adaptive Machine Learning (AML) and CRISP-DM methodology. In this study, three classification algorithms, Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) are trained, evaluated and compared using an anonymised dataset of 499,999 financial transactions extracted from a Zimbabwean commercial bank on imbalanced and class-balanced datasets. We engineer novel behavioural features from raw transactional attributes, namely errorBalanceOrg, errorBalanceDest and hourOfDay that account for 71% of the feature importance of the Random Forest model. The Decision Tree classifier gives the best Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.9633361 on the balanced data set, which is a significant improvement over the estimated rule-based baselines. Current adaptive ML trends including federated learning, graph neural networks, transformer based anomaly detection, and concept drift adaptation are also discussed in this paper. In addition, a cloud-native deployment architecture on Microsoft Azure is proposed. The results demonstrate the viability of adaptive machine learning as a high-performance alternative to static rule-based fraud detection in developing-economy banking environments.

all.title: Adaptive Confidence-Aware Transformer–Graph Fusion Network for Robust Credit Fraud Detection
all.venue: Istanbul University - Journal of Electrical & Electronics Engineering
all.abstract: Currently, finding fraudulent transactions made with credit card systems is a major concern for the research community. The growth of online payment systems has increased transaction volumes. Attackers use increasingly sophisticated techniques, including identity theft, card cloning, and the compromise of online transactions, making fraud detection challenging for financial institutions. Traditional detection models rely on fixed rules and thresholds, which limit their ability to adapt to emerging fraud patterns; these systems are not flexible to deal with new and dynamic types of fraud. The literature shows growing interest in the development of datadriven intelligent systems for the analysis of transactional behaviors and the automatic recognition of suspicious activities. In this context, an adaptive confidence-aware transformer–graph fusion network model is proposed for reliable fraud detection in imbalanced financial transaction datasets. This study empirically investigates the two publicly available financial transaction datasets: ULB credit card and PaySim synthetic dataset which is a commonly used standard in the literature, examining fraud detection; these datasets have realistic distributional characteristics and anonymized variables. The graph-based fusion model is evaluated on PaySim, where it obtains 99% in accuracy, 96 % in F1-score, and 99 % in receiver operating characteristic-area under the curve (ROC-AUC). It improves recall and F1-score compared to individual transformer and Graph Sample and Aggregate (GraphSAGE) models and conventional machine-learning methods.

all.title: A Survey of Temporal, Financial and Behavioural Patterns for Corporate Tax Fraud Detection Using Machine Learning
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Corporate tax fraud persists and is increasingly sophisticated globally, at the cost of governments. Though machine learning has enhanced fraud detection, most current work uses static indicators of financial transactions and cross sections within a period to detect fraud, which is not suitable to detect fraudulent behavior that changes over time. This paper reviews the machine learning methods used for corporate tax fraud detection in a systematic way with an emphasis on financial, temporal and behavioural indicators. According to PRISMA guidelines, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore and ScienceDirect databases were searched for peer reviewed scientific studies published from 2017 to 2025. A newly developed Financial Temporal Behavioural Feature Taxonomy was used for 31 empirical studies and analyzed. Results indicate that financial measures are the most common predictors with AUC ranging from 0.85 to 0.96. Temporal models, such as LSTM and Transformer architectures, enhance the ability to detect new fraud trends, whereas behavioural models, like network analysis and textual disclosures, reveal coordinated fraud activities. But only two studies have combined the three dimensions in a comprehensive framework. This review highlights key areas where feature integration, model explainability and cross jurisdiction validation are lacking. Future research is suggested to focus on creating a transparent, adaptive and multidimensional fraud detection and prevention system that integrates financial, temporal and behavioural data, enhancing the predictive power and enabling efficient tax administration.

all.title: AI on Both Sides of Financial Crime: A Review of Fraud Detection, Criminal Misuse, and Cybersecurity Resilience
all.abstract: Financial institutions now process transactions faster than human reviewers or rule-based controls can follow, and criminals work through the same digital infrastructure. This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI), big data analytics, and cybersecurity practice affect financial crime from both directions. It synthesizes five studies on AI-based fraud detection, AI-enabled criminal activity, and cyber resilience in financial markets, and it connects their findings to related work on graph-based detection, explainable alert review, and synthetic identity fraud. The literature shows that machine learning and deep learning detect anomalies in transaction data in real time, that big data aggregation supports risk scoring before an account is opened, and that AI-driven simulation can test defenses before an attack. It also documents AI-assisted phishing, deepfake-based social engineering, adaptive malware, and synthetic identities. Current systems are limited by opaque model decisions, biased or incomplete training data, a resource gap between large and small institutions, and regulation that trails adoption. We conclude that AI is a necessary but incomplete defense whose value depends on explainability, regular auditing, and shared standards. Directions for future work include explainable models, multidisciplinary governance, and standards that smaller institutions can adopt.

all.title: EMPLOYEE AWARENESS, TRAINING, PERCEIVED FRAUD DETECTION AND PREVENTION EFFECTIVENESS: EVIDENCE FROM ECOBANK GHANA LIMITED
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This study examined the relationship between employee awareness and training programmes and perceived fraud detection and prevention effectiveness at Ecobank Ghana Limited. Guided by Fraud Triangle Theory, a pragmatic single-bank case study combined questionnaire responses from 184 employees in Tema with qualitative staff accounts. Simple linear regression showed a positive association between awareness/training and perceived fraud-control effectiveness (R = .619, R² = .383, adjusted R² = .380; F(1, 182) = 113.067, p< .001; B = .341, β = .619, t = 10.633). Thus, the model accounted for 38.3% of variation in reported effectiveness, not independently verified fraud outcomes. Participants described practical examples and timely refreshers as useful for recognising unusual activity, but noted inconsistent access and potentially repetitive training. The evidence is compatible with the view that informed personnel can help identify and report opportunities for fraud; the study did not directly measure fraud opportunity or establish a causal training effect. The findings support risk-based, role-specific training integrated with controls, protected reporting channels and assessment of learning. Generalisation is limited by the single-bank setting, self-reported measures and the absence of independent fraud-incidence data.

all.title: Construction and Evaluation of Credit Card Fraud Detection Model Based on Logistic Regression — A Case Study of Kaggle Dataset
all.abstract: The widespread use of online payment has led to frequent credit card fraud incidents, causing significant economic losses to financial institutions and users. Efficient fraud detection models are the focus of research in financial risk control. Based on the publicly available credit card transaction dataset from Kaggle, this paper constructs a logistic regression fraud detection model. The study involves data exploration of the dataset, handling of imbalanced data, feature selection, as well as model training and tuning. This study uses stratified sampling, StandardScaler normalization, and cross-validation to enhance data processing and model reliability. Model evaluation is conducted using confusion matrices, precision, recall rate, and AUC values. Experimental results show that the model achieves high recall but low precision under SMOTE oversampling. This model achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.9708 for the fraud category, with a recall rate of 0.92, but the accuracy rate of this model is only 0.06, which indicating a significant trade-off between detecting fraud and controlling false positives.

all.title: Reassessing Unsupervised Anomaly Augmentation for Fraud Detection: The Roles of Distribution Shift, Learner Instability, and Run-to-Run Variability
all.abstract: Unsupervised anomaly scores are often added to supervised fraud classifiers, but an apparent gain may stem from learner instability or from the mere addition of a column rather than from anomaly information. We propose a controlled evaluation protocol that combines temporal splitting, multi-seed replication, uninformative negative-control columns, learner-stability checks and prespecified equivalence margins. It is applied to LightGBM and XGBoost with six anomaly representations on the Bank Account Fraud (BAF) benchmark and the chronologically split CreditCard dataset, including rolling-origin windows. On BAF, a single-seed gain of 3.5% in mean-variant AUPRC shrank to 1.2% under multi-seed evaluation, matching the 1.1% gain of a random-noise column. On CreditCard, changing only the LightGBM bagging seed moved baseline AUPRC between 0.004 and 0.742. Bounding leaf values reduced collapses from 77% of runs to none, and a reverse experiment reproduced the collapses in XGBoost once both of its leaf-value safeguards were removed. With stable learners, every anomaly representation was equivalent to a random-noise column within prespecified margins of about 1% (CreditCard) and 4% (BAF) of baseline AUPRC. Negative controls, multi-seed evaluation and learner-stability checks should precede any attribution of a gain to anomaly information.

all.title: Explainable AI for Financial Fraud Detection in India: A Conceptual Framework Integrating Machine Intelligence, Chartered Accountancy Judgement, and the Emerging Indian Regulatory Architecture
all.abstract: Indian financial institutions now deploy machine-learning systems at unprecedented scale -the Unified Payments Interface alone processes transaction volumes that make manual fraud surveillance infeasible -yet the opacity of these models sits uneasily beside three distinctly Indian demands: the engineering imperative for interpretable outputs; the chartered accountancy profession's standards of professional scepticism codified in SA 240; and a regulatory architecture that has shifted from advisory soft law (NITI Aayog's Responsible AI principles) to binding instruments (the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, the RBI Digital Lending Directions 2025, and SEBI's 2025 amendments assigning responsibility for AI-tool outputs).The scholarly literature addresses these demands separately: explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) research optimises explanation fidelity without engaging Indian audit practice; accountancy research on AI adoption in India remains descriptive; and compliance commentary analyses each instrument in isolation.This article develops TEA-India -an adaptation of the Tripartite Explainability Alignment framework -comprising a technical-explainability layer, a judgement-alignment layer anchored in ICAI's Standards on Auditing, and a compliance layer mapped to India's sector-specific instruments, connected through an explanation audit trail.The analysis identifies five India-specific gaps, including the absence of any automated-decision provision comparable to GDPR Article 22 in the DPDP Act, the consultative (not yet binding) status of RBI's modelrisk guidance, and the near-complete absence of Indian empirical research on how chartered accountants actually consume model explanations.Five propositions and a comparative analysis against global frameworks are advanced.The framework offers Indian banks, NBFCs, auditors, and regulators a common vocabulary for designing frauddetection systems whose explanations are simultaneously technically faithful, professionally usable, and legally defensible.

all.title: Generative AI in Financial Systems and Banking Forensics
all.abstract: The constantly rising technology adoption in the financial sectors has shown more dynamic patterns in their fraud activities, making them increasingly complex. Despite the presence of class imbalance in fraud detection scenarios in the real world, increasing label latency, the dynamics of fraud attack patterns, and the rise of sensitive data in financial data sets act as barriers for applying rule-based machine learning techniques in financial products for precise fraud detection. Generative Artificial Intelligence refers to a revolution in the analysis of financial fraud because it encompasses all the critical processes involved in legitimate as well as fraudulent financial operations. The use of representation learning and simulation of transactions achieved by generative models enables the prior detection of financial fraud. The use of generative AI is applicable in various financial security systems such as transaction risk evaluation, identification of payment fraud, analysis of anti-money laundering (AML), Know Your Customer (KYC) automation, identification of synthetic identities, and evolutionary patterns of financial fraud identification. The current chapter offers an in-depth analysis of the application of generative AI in financial systems and banking forensics. The use of generative techniques for behavioral simulations, aggressive fraud simulations, fraud analysis and simulations through graphs and time-series analysis, and finally, design and implementation issues and regulations in integrating generative AI in financial systems. The above topics and considerations put together create a comprehensive framework through which one can apply and understand the application of generative AI in the financial and banking system for fraud analysis and detection.

all.title: Risk-Aware AI Deployment Architecture for Secure and Regulated Banking Environments
all.abstract: With an increasing imperative for banks to use AI at scale and regulatory requirements becoming more sophisticated and faster-paced, most organizations treat core security, explainability, and regulatory aspects as post-deployment bolt-ons. Instead, we propose a new, integrated, risk-driven AI architecture where these concerns are integral from day one. The framework categorizes each AI use case into one of three risk tiers. Each risk tier incorporates mandated security via hardware protection with Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), comprehensive explainability via tools like SHAP, LIME, and explainable boosting models (EBMs), and an increasing level of calibrated human oversight, ranging from human-in-the-loop to human-in-command configurations. A successful year-long pilot at a U.S. regional bank (approximately $45 billion in assets) involving 47 production models validated our framework. Compared to before the pilot, the average AUC of fraud detection models increased from 0.74 to 0.81, the AML false-positive rate reduced from 12.4% to 7.6%, and the average regulatory audit review time fell by 38%. This document outlines the architecture and three specific case studies from the pilot-two: one used in real-time production and two used to review historical decisions, providing an end-to-end walkthrough. The key differentiating factor of this framework is treating regulatory compliance as a continuous operating component rather than a compliance checkpoint, which we refer to as living compliance .

all.title: Optimizing Banking Security: A Comparative Study of Biometric Authentication Methods
all.venue: REST Journal on Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence
all.abstract: The impact of biometric authentication on banking security Biometric authentication is revolutionizing banking security by offering a highly secure, accurate, and convenient method of user verification. Unlike traditional passwords and PINs, biometrics such as fingerprints, facial recognition, iris scans, and voice recognition are unique to individuals, making fraud and identity theft significantly harder. Research significance: This research on banking security is significant as it addresses critical challenges in financial security, fraud prevention, and user authentication. Methodology: This study employs a mixed-methods approach to analyze the impact of biometric authentication on banking security. Primary data is collected through surveys and interviews with banking professionals and customers to assess their perceptions of biometric security, convenience, and fraud prevention. Secondary data is gathered from academic journals, industry reports, and case studies on biometric authentication. A comparative analysis of different biometric modalities, including fingerprint recognition, facial recognition, and iris scanning, is conducted based on security effectiveness, accuracy, and implementation challenges. Statistical tools are used to evaluate fraud reduction rates, customer adoption, and the cost-effectiveness of biometric security systems. Alternative: Fingerprint Recognition, Facial Recognition, Iris Scan, Voice Recognition, Palm Vein Recognition, Behavioral Biometrics, Retina Scan, Hand Geometry Evaluation preference: Accuracy (%), Security Level, User Convenience, Implementation Cost ($), Processing Speed (ms), Fraud Detection Effectiveness Results: Fingerprint Recognition is getting top of the table and Retina Scan is getting bottom of the table

all.title: Explainable and Multimodal AI for Financial Fraud Prevention: Advancing Trust and Cybersecurity in Digital Banking
all.abstract: Digital banking has made financial services faster, more accessible, and cheaper to run. It has also widened the opening for financial fraud, identity theft, social engineering, synthetic identity attacks, and deepfake-enabled cybercrime. Rule-based security systems often struggle with threats that are sophisticated and change quickly, which has increased interest in adaptive artificial intelligence (AI) solutions. This review examines how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) and multimodal AI can strengthen fraud prevention, support decision-making, and improve cybersecurity resilience in digital banking. It looks at the integration of multiple data modalities, real-time threat detection, explainable fraud alerts, and organizational trust in AI-generated decisions. The review synthesizes two empirical studies, one on U.S. digital banking and one on the U.S. banking sector. The first reports that multimodal deepfake detection, real-time detection, and explainable AI are each positively associated with fraud detection effectiveness and cybersecurity resilience. The second reports that explainable AI trust is a significant link between AI-driven fraud detection and banking cybersecurity resilience, while its proposed real-time fraud response mediation was not statistically supported. The review also covers methodological limitations and challenges involving data privacy, model transparency, false positives, adversarial attacks, and organizational readiness. It concludes that AI-based financial security needs interpretable decisions, human oversight, timely operational action, and responsible governance in addition to accurate detection.

all.title: Legal and Ethical Implication Framework for Artificial Intelligence Application in Centenary Bank Uganda Limited
all.venue: DS Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics
all.abstract: This manuscript examines the legal and ethical implications framework for the application of Artificial Intelligence in Ugandan Centenary banks, with a case study focus on the Lango Sub-Region of Northern Uganda. As banks increasingly deploy AI for credit scoring, fraud detection, customer onboarding, chatbots, anti-money laundering monitoring, and risk analytics, the technology promises greater efficiency, lower operating costs, and improved financial inclusion. However, these benefits are accompanied by significant legal and ethical concerns, including privacy infringement, algorithmic bias and opacity in automated decision-making, cybersecurity exposure, unlawful profiling, data localization issues, and uncertainty around accountability when AI systems cause harm. The manuscript situates these concerns within Uganda’s emerging legal and regulatory environment, including the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, the Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019, the Computer Misuse Act, 2011, the Financial Institutions Act, and sectoral supervision by the Bank of Uganda. It further engages ethical principles of fairness, transparency, accountability, explainability, non-discrimination, human oversight, beneficence, and proportionality. Using the Lango Sub-Region as a contextual lens, the paper argues that AI adoption in commercial banking must be governed by a hybrid framework combining statutory compliance, internal bank governance, regulatory supervision, and context-sensitive ethical safeguards. The manuscript concludes that Uganda requires clearer AI-specific rules, stronger supervisory guidance, institutional audit mechanisms, and bank-level governance protocols to ensure that AI innovation does not erode consumer rights, trust, and financial stability.

all.title: A Deep Learning Framework with Multiple Models for Detecting Credit Card Fraud Using Transaction Data and UAV Surveillance
all.abstract: Credit card fraud recognition is a critical challenge for financial institutions and service providers, as fraudulent activities result in significant monetary victims and reputational risks. Existing approaches primarily rely on predictable machine learning performances like Random Forest, Multilayer Perceptron, AdaBoost, and Gradient Boosting, which, although effective, face limitations in capturing complex, high- dimensional patterns. To discourse this, we recommend a multimodal deep learning structure that associations contextual information obtained from transactions with Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) surveillance. The dataset includes transaction attributes such as time, amount, and anonymized features (V1– V28), along with UAV-based visual embeddings to capture suspicious physical activities in transaction zones (e.g., ATM tampering, loitering, or skimming). Advanced to improve feature abstraction and categorization, models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Support Vector Machines(SVM) are used. The CNN automatically learns deep hierarchical representations from both transaction and UAV inputs, while the SVM makes use of its ability to efficiently separate high-dimensional data. The proposed fusion frame work aims to reduce false positives and improve fraud detection accuracy compared to transaction-only baselines. This strategy illustrates the possibility of combining financial analytics with UAV-enabled surveillance for secure and reliable fraud prevention.

all.title: Examining the Role of Digital Platforms in Mitigating Financial Fraud in Nigeria
all.venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF FINANCE AND INVESTMENT RESEARCH
all.abstract: This study examined the role of digital platforms in mitigating financial fraud in Nigeria. The study was motivated by the increasing adoption of digital financial services, as well as the growing incidence of technology-enabled financial fraud. The study specifically examined the extent to which digital platforms contribute to the prevention and detection of financial fraud, identified the security mechanisms used in mitigating fraudulent activities, and examined the challenges affecting the effectiveness of digital platforms in fraud control. Data for this study were obtained from Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS), Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC), and National Bureau of Statistics (NBS)The study adopted ARDL to evaluate the relationship between digital platform variables and financial fraud in Nigeria. The findings revealed that digital platforms play significant roles in mitigating financial fraud. The study concluded that digital platforms are essential instruments for preventing and detecting financial fraud; however, technology alone cannot completely eliminate fraudulent activities. Effective fraud mitigation requires a combination of advanced technology, strong internal controls, customer education, effective regulatory oversight, and collaboration among banks, fintech companies, telecommunications operators, and law-enforcement agencies. The study therefore recommended continuous investment in advanced fraud-detection technologies, stronger cybersecurity measures, improved customer awareness, enhanced authentication mechanisms, and greater cooperation among relevant stakeholders to reduce financial fraud and strengthen confidence in Nigeria's digital financial system.

all.title: Ethics, Fairness, and Explainability in Generative Fraud Models
all.abstract: Many teams consider generic AI as a tool for fraud detection to stop criminals. This view ignores the core problem. The main problem is trust. Account freezes a few minutes before fare payment. No explanation comes. The damage spreads rapidly. The relationship between the bank and the customer breaks. This chapter focuses on responsibility in financial AI. Accuracy alone fails as a goal. Interpretations matter as much as predictions. A system without reason causes harm even when the metrics appear strong. Fairness is revealed through clear mathematics. Bias shows up in measurable terms. Trade-offs appear in data rather than slogans. Tools like SHAP and LIME highlight how features make decisions. These tools support clarifications for clients, auditors, and regulators. Regulation shapes system design. The EU AI Act defines risk categories and liability limits. The GDPR implements the rights of explanation and challenge. These rules influence model selection, data management, and deployment path. By the end, the standard changes. The question is no longer asked whether a system works or not. The question asks whether a system works correctly.

all.title: Cross-Industry Case Studies and Applied Frameworks
all.abstract: This chapter specifies cross-industry case studies and generative AI-based methods that illustrate how the technology has completely changed fraud detection by linking theory with practice in various industries. Capital One and Swedbank, as examples of banks, make use of GANs to create synthetic transactions and consequently reduce fraud by half through real-time anomaly detection in their credit card transaction streams, as well as through KYC synthetic identity verification, further enabling risk scoring that is dynamic via integration with FinTech APIs. Insurance companies like Allianz employ VAEs for the simulation of rare claim frauds, and a 40% false positive rate reduction is attained by multimodal document forensics and federated learning that is compliant with HIPAA/GDPR. UnitedHealth in healthcare uses transformers for NLP, powered claim narrative scrutiny, and GAN-augmented datasets, increasing detection accuracy in billing scams to 35% while also ensuring privacy is maintained. Major e-commerce companies (Amazon, Shopify) are utilizing diffusion models to create behavioral profiles in retail scams that lead to account takeovers, which are then countered by multi-agent ensembles resulting in a total of 25% loss prevention. Cybersecurity companies such as Chainalysis are adopting graph-based GenAI for blockchain analytics, in which NFT scams and crypto laundering networks are traced using 90% traceability that is further improved by SOC integrations.

all.title: Impact of Generative AI on Cybersecurity Risks, Phishing, and Digital Defense in the US
all.venue: Journal of Engineering and Computational Intelligence Review
all.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has reduced the expenses of creating natural, personalized and context-relevant content, thus challenging defenses based on the linguistic weaknesses of traditional phishing. This paper explores the effects of GenAI on cybersecurity risk and phishing and digital defense in the United States with a structured synthesis of 23 studies and a controlled detection experiment. The synthesis is structured around offensive and defensive applications of GenAI. The experiment evaluates six different detectors (keyword rules, word and character n-gram classifiers, header/URL metadata model, metadata-plus-intent model, and fused model) against traditional phishing, GenAI-style phishing, and GenAI phishing from compromised accounts. Pre-GenAI mail was trained on the detectors, which were then evaluated at a 0.5% false-positive rate, using five different seeds. GenAI-style messages did not include any misspellings or classic lure words and were lexically nearer to legitimate messages (median cosine similarity 0.22 compared to 0.13 for traditional phishing). None of them were detected by keyword rules and the word-level classifiers dropped from 1.0 on traditional phishing to 0.508. Metadata was effective in detecting 97% of GenAI phishing messages originating from attacker infrastructure, but just 3.6% of messages originating from compromised accounts. Adding 1,500 defender-generated examples of phishing using GenAI improved the results of fused-model recall from 0.149 to 0.790 on the compromised-account case with no corresponding increase in false positives. The results suggest that GenAI has transformed the phishing threat from content to identity and context; thus, U.S. organizations need to implement email authentication, defender-side generative augmentation and continuous retraining, and account-takeover controls. all.title: Securing Digital Transactions: Machine Learning for Credit Card Fraud Detection
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The rapid growth of digital payments has increased the importance of reliable credit card fraud detection systems. Traditional rule-based approaches can struggle to identify com plex and evolving fraud patterns, particularly when fraudulent transactions represent only a small proportion of transaction data. This paper presents a machine learning-based framework that combines data preprocessing, class-imbalance handling, autoencoder-based feature representation, and XGBoost clas sification. The study uses the publicly available credit card transaction dataset containing 284,807 transactions, including 492 fraudulent transactions. Robust scaling is used to reduce the influence of extreme values, while the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) is applied only to the training data. An autoencoder learns a compact representation of trans action features and calculates reconstruction error; these outputs are combined with the prepared features for downstream clas sification. XGBoost is used to distinguish legitimate transactions from potentially fraudulent ones. The framework is evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, area under the precision recall curve (PR-AUC), and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). The paper also describes an API-oriented deployment workflow. Numerical results should be reported from the final reproducible experiment; illustrative or previously obtained values must not be treated as independently verified without rerunning the implementation.

all.title: Enhancing Credit Card Fraud Detection Using Generative AI-Based Data Augmentation
all.abstract: Credit card fraud detection is challenging due to the extreme class imbalance and the limited number of fraudulent transactions. To address this problem, this paper proposes a fraud detection framework that combines generative AI-based data augmentation with machine learning classification models. We generated synthetic fraud samples at augmentation ratios of 1%, 5%, and 10% using three generative approaches: a Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP), a Variational Autoencoder (VAE), and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based data generator. The generated samples were evaluated using the Discriminator Test, Distance-to-Closest-Record (DCR) analysis, and t-SNE visualization to compare them to real fraud data and identify differences in their distributions. The augmented datasets were then used to train Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM classifiers. The baseline models trained on the original dataset achieved F1-scores of 0.857 for Random Forest, 0.856 for XGBoost, and 0.877 for LightGBM. After adding synthetic fraud samples to the training data, the results showed improvements in fraud detection performance in some cases. LightGBM achieved the highest F1-score of 0.897 when trained with VAE-generated data at the 10% augmentation ratio. Similarly, XGBoost achieved an F1-score of 0.880 using VAE-generated data at the 5% ratio. Overall, the findings demonstrate the potential of generative AI-based augmentation to improve fraud detection performance in highly imbalanced financial datasets, particularly when combined with LightGBM and XGBoost classifiers.

all.title: 1313-GC SparkGuard: A Big Data Pipeline for Credit Card Fraud Detection
all.venue: DigitalCommons - Kennesaw State University (Kennesaw State University)
all.abstract: Fraud poses a significant threat to both organizations and individuals, making effective detection critical for protecting society. In this project, we evaluate various machine learning approaches to credit card fraud detection- including support vector machines (SVM), XGBoost, random forest, neural networks, and a voting ensemble approach aggregating multiple models.
