To overcome single-node memory and processing bottlenecks on highly imbalanced data, we deploy a Big Data pipeline. For each approach, we implement a system to evaluate performance using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and receiver operating characteristics (ROC). Comparing these metrics allows us to assess each approach in identifying fraudulent activity and determine the optimal solution.

all.title: Credit card fraud detection through feature reduction and stacking under class imbalance
all.abstract: Credit card fraud detection models should maintain high recall while controlling false alarms on highly skewed transaction data. This paper evaluates a feature-reduced stacking approach based on Multilayer Perceptron and Random Forest (MLP-RF) classifiers for credit card fraud detection. This work proposes a feature-reduced stacking variant with 12 informative attributes. The method combines robust scaling, mutual information-based feature selection, random undersampling and a stacking ensemble of MLP and Random Forest, followed by threshold tuning on the precision-recall curve. The proposed model achieves competitive fraud detection performance with 60% fewer features than the published hybrid MLP-RF baseline, achieving higher recall but lower precision and F1-score. The pipeline is described in detail to support reproducibility and to examine how feature selection can retain competitive performance while simplifying the input representation.

all.title: A systematic review of transparent artificial intelligence models for credit card fraud detection
all.abstract: Research on credit card fraud detection has rapidly increased over the past decade due to the increasing use of digital payments and the financial losses caused by fraud. Despite extensive research, most studies focus on detection performance, while transparency, fairness, and auditability remain under-studied, although they matter under regimes such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and, for credit-scoring uses of fraud scores, the EU AI Act. This review argues that accountability, the ability to explain, audit, and demonstrate fairness in automated decisions, is under-explored compared to detection performance, and performance-related limits (imbalance handling, generalization, and offline-only testing) also remain unaddressed. To address this gap, a systematic literature review is conducted based on the PRISMA 2020 statement and includes papers published from 2016 to 2026 retrieved from IEEE Xplore, Scopus, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Five review questions (Section 2.1) framed the study and data extraction. A total of 45 papers were retained from 115 records (110 database records plus 5 citation-search records) after full-text assessment of 50 reports; 39 are primary studies (peer-reviewed publications and preprints), and 6 are surveys or fairness- methodology papers kept as background only. The primary studies were then divided into three areas: traditional machine learning (16), deep learning and Transformer-based models (15), and explainable AI and fairness (8). The synthesis shows consensus that ensemble and deep methods achieve high detection accuracy under class imbalance, but findings conflict on which imbalance handling strategy is most effective and on whether reported gains generalize beyond a small set of benchmark datasets. Research on explainability using techniques such as SHAP and LIME has emerged, yet interpretability remains appended to models rather than embedded in them, and formal fairness analysis remains limited across the three themes. Building on the findings, this review introduces EFMDS, a conceptual framework that has not yet been empirically implemented or validated, which is designed as a five-layer pipeline that integrates adaptive class-imbalance handling with multi-model detection, multi-method explainability, and formal fairness auditing, including closed-loop bias correction. This framework is intended to guide the development of a fraud detection system that is robust, interpretable, and equitable.

all.title: Addressing class imbalance in credit card fraud detection using Mahalanobis-based undersampling of extreme observations
institutions: Universidad de Playa Ancha de Ciencias de la Educación
all.abstract: Severe class imbalance hinders the detection of card fraud, and applying resampling before partitioning the data inflates performance estimates due to information leakage. Mahalanobis distance has been used previously for outlier detection and in resampling procedures, but the behavior of two geometrically distinct selection rules, one local and one global, under the same metric for fraud detection has not been studied. In this manuscript, we propose and evaluate two subsampling strategies that retain only real transactions: Majority-class Extreme-aware UnderSampling (MEUS) matches each minority observation with a close majority candidate according to the Mahalanobis metric, and Furthest-point Extreme UnderSampling (FEUS) retains observations farther from the global centroid of the training set. Both use a global covariance matrix estimated from the training set, but apply distinct observation-selection rules. We compare them with five data-level resampling techniques on the European Credit Card Dataset (ECCD) and the IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection dataset using repeated stratified cross-validation, with resampling restricted to the training folds. Under severe imbalance, FEUS offered the most favorable compromise between precision and recall in ECCD and intermediate performance in IEEE-CIS, with low computational cost; MEUS was competitive in ECCD but lost precision in IEEE-CIS. A Euclidean ablation showed that incorporating covariance changes the balance between metrics without being uniformly superior. The effect of covariance undersampling depends on the classifier and the imbalance structure of the data, and we did not observe a method that dominated under all conditions.

all.title: Hybrid stacking and logistic regression meta-model for credit card fraud detection using SMOTE and multiple machine learning algorithms
all.abstract: This study presents a stacking ensemble framework for credit card fraud detection on the imbalanced Kaggle dataset, using SMOTE to address class imbalance. Base classifiers (RF, SVM, KNN, NB, GB, LR) are evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, with RF and KNN emerging as the strongest learners, reaching 97% recall and 0.98 F1-score after SMOTE. The final ensemble employs RF and KNN as base learners with Logistic Regression as the meta-classifier, and pairwise prediction correlations (r ≈ 0.34 for RF–KNN vs. r ≈ 0.81 for RF–GB) confirm that RF and KNN form a more diverse and complementary pair. A refined stacked hybrid using RF–KNN–GB with meta-features and original data achieves the best trade-off for fraud and intrusion detection, obtaining 0.975 recall with only one false positive, 0.9968 precision, 0.986 F1-score, and accuracy of 0.9997, outperforming existing hybrid methods. These findings demonstrate that carefully designed ensembles and feature engineering can deliver robust fraud detection on highly imbalanced data, surpassing individual models and reported

all.title: Ethical AI in Fintech: Bridging the Gap Between Predictive Performance and Algorithmic Fairness in Fraud Detection
all.abstract: In finance, fraud detection systems frequently struggle to balance accurate predictions with fair outcomes. Many of the machine learning models used today are black boxes, and may be biased based on the data they were trained on, resulting in unfair results. We propose a novel framework that combines fairness-aware machine learning and Explainable AI (XAI). It uses techniques like Robust Scaling, a mix of SMOTE-ENN resampling and SHAP (SHapley Additive Explanations) to improve both performance and explainability. Experiments on the ULB Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset have reached a recall of 92%, with the Demographic Parity Gap maintained at a minimum of 0.0006. The results show you can be fair, accurate, transparent and compliant with regulation such as the EU AI Act

all.title: Sistem Deteksi Anomali Transaksi Keuangan Menggunakan Xgboost untuk Meningkatkan Akurasi Klasifikasi Fraud
all.venue: Integrative Perspectives of Social and Science Journal
all.abstract: Penipuan (fraud) pada transaksi keuangan elektronik menimbulkan kerugian besar, sedangkan proporsi fraud yang sangat kecil membuat akurasi menyesatkan. Penelitian ini mengembangkan sistem deteksi anomali transaksi keuangan berbasis Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) pada dataset Credit Card Fraud Detection (284.807 transaksi, 492 fraud). Tahapan meliputi praproses RobustScaler, pembagian data stratified 70:15:15, penanganan ketidakseimbangan kelas dengan scale_pos_weight dan SMOTE, penyetelan hyperparameter berbasis PR-AUC, serta optimasi threshold pada data validasi. XGBoost dibandingkan dengan Logistic Regression dan Random Forest. Pada data uji, XGBoost dengan pembobotan kelas mencapai F1-Score 0,8421 dan PR-AUC 0,8070, lebih tinggi daripada Random Forest (0,8189 dan 0,7892) dan Logistic Regression (0,1036 dan 0,6808), sedangkan SMOTE tidak memberi peningkatan. Penyetelan dan optimasi threshold menaikkan Precision menjadi 0,9016 tetapi tidak melampaui model dasar. Pembobotan kelas menjadi sumber peningkatan utama.

all.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Financial Fraud Detection: A Comparative Framework for Predictive Performance, Fidelity, and Stability
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Research protocol — empirical results pending. This upload presents an experimental design and companion code; no original empirical findings, performance improvements, or completed explanation-stability results are reported. Machine-learning fraud detectors can rank suspicious transactions, yet their explanations may not be faithful, stable, or useful to human analysts. This paper presents a reproducible comparative protocol for examining three supervised classifiers—logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost—alongside SHAP and LIME explanations. The proposed study uses the European credit-card fraud dataset (284,807 transactions; 492 labelled frauds), a chronological 60/20/20 split, validation-only tuning, held-out average precision, and complementary explanation diagnostics. It distinguishes additive reconstruction from local surrogate fit and proposes attribution perturbation tests and paired uncertainty analysis. The proposed experiments examine whether accurate fraud scoring is compatible with faithful and stable local explanations under practical runtime constraints. The deposit includes the manuscript in PDF and DOCX formats, run_experiment.py, requirements.txt, and README.md. The original transaction dataset is not included. The full perturbation-stability protocol remains future implementation work. This is an unreviewed research protocol.

all.title: DETECÇÃO DE FRAUDES EM TRANSAÇÕES DE CARTÃO DE CRÉDITO COM APRENDIZADO DE MÁQUINA: COMPARAÇÃO ESTATÍSTICA DE TRÊS ALGORITMOS EM UMA BASE PÚBLICA DESBALANCEADA
all.abstract: A detecção de fraudes em pagamentos digitais lida com bases em que as fraudes são fração mínima das transações, o que torna enganosas métricas como a acurácia e a AUC-ROC. Este artigo compara três algoritmos clássicos de aprendizado de máquina, Regressão Logística, Árvore de Decisão e Random Forest, na base pública Credit Card Fraud Detection (284.807 transações de cartão, 0,172% de fraudes); modelos de boosting não fizeram parte da comparação. Os modelos, com ponderação de classes, foram avaliados por validação cruzada estratificada repetida e em teste separado, com intervalos de confiança, teste de McNemar e custo em valor das fraudes não detectadas e dos alertas. No teste, o Random Forest obteve precisão de 91,0%, recall de 75,0% e AUC-PR de 0,810, e 98 das 100 transações com score mais alto eram fraudes. A Regressão Logística teve a maior AUC-ROC, mas precisão de 6,7% no limiar de 0,5. Em valor, o Random Forest reduziu entre 46% e 61% a perda que as fraudes do teste causariam sem modelo, conforme o custo suposto para revisar cada alerta, e o limiar de menor custo mudou com esse pressuposto. O score dos modelos ordena bem as transações, mas não é uma probabilidade calibrada. O modelo respondeu em média em 87 ms em uma API local.

all.title: A Graph Attention Network Framework for Financial Fraud Detection: Synthetic Validation and Benchmark Evaluation on the Elliptic Bitcoin Dataset
all.venue: Advances in intelligent systems research/Advances in Intelligent Systems Research
all.abstract: Financial fraud represents one of the most pressing challenges in modern digital economies, with global credit card fraud losses projected to exceed US $400 billion in the coming decade. The conventional rule-based and machine-learning detection systems fail to model the intricate relational topology that characterizes fraudulent transactional networks. This paper proposes a Graph Attention Network (GAT)-based fraud detection framework (GAT-FDF) that encodes transaction entities as graph nodes and leverages multi-head attention mechanisms to aggregate neighborhood information for binary fraud classification. The framework is evaluated in two stages: (i) A controlled experiment on a 50,000 node synthetic dataset with deliberate 25% fraudulent transaction was injection, achieving an AUC-ROC of 98.17%, F1 of 85.59%, and accuracy of 92.31%; And (ii) A rigorous benchmark validation on the Elliptic Bitcoin Dataset the only publicly available real-world cryptocurrency transaction graph with ground-truth labels achieving an AUC-ROC of 95.64%, recall of 85.49%, and accuracy of 91.01%. k-Nearest Neighbour (kNN) graph construction with k = 5 neighbours is adopted for feature-space edge induction, and weighted Binary Cross-Entropy loss addresses severe class imbalance. Comparative analysis against GCN, GraphSAGE, XGBoost, and classical machine-learning baselines confirms the superiority of the proposed framework. The paper includes comprehensive visualisations of data distributions, feature correlations, training dynamics, confusion matrices, ROC curves, and comparative performance analysis.

all.title: An explainable AI (XAI) framework for anomaly detection in financial transaction
all.abstract: The increasing digitalization of financial services has intensified the complexity of fraudulent transaction patterns, challenging conventional rule-based detection systems. Although deep learning models can capture nonlinear relationships in high-dimensional financial data, their limited interpretability creates challenges for regulatory compliance and transparent decision-making. This paper proposes D-PEAR (Dual-Phase Explainable Anomaly Reconnaissance), a semi-supervised hybrid framework for transaction anomaly detection that integrates predictive performance with explainability. D-PEAR combines a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with an attention-based Long Short-Term Memory (Attention-LSTM) network to learn probabilistic latent representations and temporal dependencies in transaction sequences. A composite anomaly scoring mechanism combines Euclidean reconstruction error with cosine divergence to identify both magnitude-based deviations and directional changes in transaction features. Furthermore, a dual-engine explainable artificial intelligence module integrates Kernel SHAP and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) to generate feature-level explanations and support explanation consistency assessment. The framework is evaluated on the ULB Credit Card Fraud dataset, comprising 284,807 transactions with a fraud prevalence of 0.172%. Benchmarking against nine conventional and deep learning baselines yields an Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) of 0.842 and an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC) of 0.968, with an inference latency of 19 ms per transaction. Component-wise ablation studies indicate improvements associated with temporal attention, directional scoring, and probabilistic latent regularization. These findings suggest that D-PEAR offers a promising approach to real-time transaction anomaly detection with interpretable feature attributions, supporting fraud investigation and compliance auditing.

all.title: Gift Card Ecosystem Architecture and Fraud Anatomy
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This report examines the technical architecture of gift card ecosystems and nine fraud attack vectors across physical, digital, and prepaid gift cards. Key findings show that gift card fraud exploits weaknesses in token generation, API security, transaction processing, access control, and third-party integrations. The report maps each attack mechanism to its underlying vulnerabilities and identifies security controls, including cryptographic token generation, behavioral bot detection, atomic transactions, scoped API authentication, and immutable audit logs, to strengthen fraud prevention, detection, and incident response.

all.title: Privacy, Utility and Robustness of Synthetic Tabular Data for Financial Machine Learning: A Multi-Seed Benchmark with Formal Privacy Analysis
all.abstract: Financial institutions want to share and develop models on synthetic tabular data, but published comparisons rarely test utility, fidelity, privacy, robustness and fairness together, with repeated runs and on real data. This study benchmarks six generators (a class-conditional Gaussian copula, kNN interpolation, a differentially private naive-Bayes synthesizer at two budgets, CTGAN and TVAE) on two public datasets: credit-card default (24,000 records) and card fraud (284,807 records, split chronologically). Each configuration was run with five seeds and evaluated by train-on-synthetic, test-on-real utility, fidelity, two membership-inference attacks, augmentation, perturbation robustness and subgroup error gaps, with Holm-adjusted paired tests and equivalence tests. Models trained on synthetic data lost 0.005–0.069 AUC against real-data models. kNN interpolation was closest to real-data utility but was the only generator that leaked membership (attack AUC 0.70 and 0.76), as a short proof of its distance bound anticipates; all others were at chance. CTGAN was worse than the copula (−0.049 and −0.017 AUC) and improved only with more training records and epochs, without reaching it. Synthetic augmentation never improved average precision. The private synthesizer plateaued for budgets of about 5 and above and degraded sharply below ε = 1. Code, data pointers and all per-run results are released.

all.title: FedGuard: An Explainable Centralized Fraud-Detection Baseline on PaySim and IEEE-CIS
institutions: Bharati Vidyapeeth's College of Engineering, Delhi
all.abstract: Fraud detection is difficult because fraudulent transactions are rare, data differ across domains, and strong predictive models can be hard to review. We present FedGuard, an explainable centralized baseline evaluated separately on two public benchmark domains: PaySim, a synthetic mobile-money dataset with 6.36 million transactions and 0.13% fraud, and IEEE-CIS, an anonymized card-not-present e-commerce dataset with 590,540 labeled transactions and 3.5% fraud. The records were split into train, validation, and test partitions before any preprocessing was fitted. Train-only preprocessing and sampling were used in four model families and 195 candidate fits. Thresholds were selected using validation data to maximize recall subject to an FPR no greater than 1%. On the held-out test split, the selected LightGBM model reached AP 0.997968, recall 99.76%, and FPR 0.003567% on PaySim; for IEEE-CIS, AP was 0.756757, recall 68.80%, and FPR 1.017758%, slightly above the validation target. TreeSHAP contributions for the selected tree model sum with the baseline value to the model raw output; they are not calibrated probabilities. The codebase includes a 55-case software test suite, which checks implementation behavior rather than trained-model performance. This work does not implement federated learning, differential privacy, or secure aggregation.

all.title: Risk-Aware Hybrid CNN-LSTM Networks for Attack Detection in Cloud Payment Supply Chains
all.abstract: Cloud payment supply chains coordinate merchants, acquirers, gateways, and settlement services across distributed infrastructure, and this openness exposes transaction flows to credential compromise, replay, and adversarial interference. Conventional signature and rule-based defenses face challenges with concept drift and with the severe class imbalance that characterizes genuine malicious events. This study develops a risk-aware hybrid detection framework that couples convolutional feature extraction with sequential memory modeling and wraps the classifier in an explicit risk-calibration layer. Convolutional filters summarize local co-occurrence patterns in transaction attributes, while recurrent units capture the temporal ordering of authorization, capture, and refund events within a session. A weighted objective and cost-sensitive thresholding translate posterior probabilities into operational risk scores, so that detection sensitivity can be tuned to the financial exposure of each payment tier. The framework is evaluated on a multi-month corpus of cloud payment records spanning card-not-present, wallet, and recurring billing channels. Results indicate that the hybrid architecture improves recall on rare threat families relative to single-branch baselines while containing false-positive volume within acceptable review capacity. Ablation analysis shows that temporal modeling contributes most to detecting low-and-slow probing behavior, whereas convolutional encoding dominates on bursty intrusion attempts. The risk layer further stabilizes decision thresholds under distribution shift, reducing alert volatility across reporting periods. The findings suggest that combining representation learning with explicit risk governance offers a practical path for securing payment supply chains without sacrificing throughput.

all.title: การเพิ่มประสิทธิภาพการป้องกันและปราบปรามอาชญากรรมคอมพิวเตอร์ข้ามชาติประเภทลวงรักออนไลน์ของสำนักงานตำรวจแห่งชาติ
all.venue: Political Science and Public Administration Journal
authors: ณพวรรณ ปัญญา
all.abstract: Romance scams, as a form of transnational computer crime, have become a serious threat to both the economy and society. This research aims to examine the structural and operational adaptation of the Royal Thai Police (RTP) and to propose strategies for enhancing efficiency and strengthening cooperation among relevant agencies in preventing and suppressing romance scams, particularly romance fraudulent transfer scams and romance investment scams (hybrid scams). The study employed a qualitative research method, using structured interviews with 25 key informants, including RTP administrators and operational officers, victims, representatives from related organizations, and academics. The findings reveal that the RTP has sought to adapt by establishing specialized and dedicated units, developing an online complaint system, and implementing financial security measures to directly address romance scams. Policy recommendations include enhancing proactive communication through digital media, fostering social immunity through community-based approaches, strengthening the capacity of local-level officers, establishing real-time information-sharing platforms, and promoting bilateral cooperation within ASEAN, particularly to ensure the effective implementation of the Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT-ASEAN). These recommendations were confirmed through interviews with high-ranking RTP executives.

all.title: The Economics of Instant Payments: A Structured, Evidence-Graded Review of Financial Inclusion, Welfare, and Macro-Financial Effects across Global Fast-Payment Systems
all.abstract: Purpose: This article examines the economic consequences of instant payment systems (financial inclusion, welfare, growth and macro-financial stability) and seeks to separate the well-established effects from the projections and correlations that form the basis of much of the practitioner discussion. Methodology: This is a structured narrative review. The evidence is synthesized under an explicit four-tier scheme that gives primacy to peer-reviewed causal studies and central bank research over industry reports, separates out the observed from the forecasted, and places causal identification at the heart of the analysis. The review draws on 22 sources published between 2014 and 2026. The four systems under review are Brazil's Pix, India's UPI, the US FedNow and RTP and the EU's SEPA Instant. These are compared on design features. Findings: The best-evidenced finding is microeconomic: mobile-money access is estimated to have lifted around 2% of Kenyan households out of poverty and there are quasi-experimental findings on the impact of adoption in Mexico and India. The aggregate GDP and consumer savings data are all based on industry estimates and should be treated as indicative only. Differences in outcomes across the four systems are associated with system design (operator model, pricing, mandate and interoperability) rather than with the technology itself, although with four systems and no causal design this is a pattern, not an identified effect. The macro-financial risks are material, notably deposit-funding pressure and authorized-push-payment fraud (£450.7 million in the United Kingdom in 2024). Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: The paper offers a five-channel transmission framework, an evidence-graded synthesis that distinguishes causal effects from projections, and a design-feature comparison that explains cross-country heterogeneity. It directs researchers toward credible identification and policymakers toward public, low-cost, interoperable and well-supervised designs on which inclusive outcomes depend.

all.title: Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities and Fraud Mitigation Strategies Among Senior Citizens
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The expansion of digital banking, mobile payments, messaging platforms and online public services has created new opportunities for older adults, while also exposing them to increasingly organised forms of cyber-enabled fraud. This paper develops an analytical account of the threats affecting senior citizens and proposes a practical, layered framework for prevention and response. It synthesises published research, law-enforcement reporting and policy material discussed in the supplied review paper. The analysis distinguishes the reasons older adults may be targeted from the factors that can make a particular person susceptible, and examines impersonation, technical-support fraud, investment scams, romance fraud, family-emergency deception, phishing and recovery scams. Particular attention is given to India, including digital- arrest schemes, the 1930 cyber-fraud helpline and the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. The study uses a desk-based, thematic research design and does not claim to have collected primary survey or experimental data. Its proposed framework combines accessible education, family and community support, financial-institution safeguards, telecom and platform controls, rapid reporting, and victim-centred legal assistance. The analysis indicates that effective protection cannot depend on individual vigilance alone. It requires systems that make verification easier, interrupt suspicious payments, support early disclosure and preserve the autonomy of older users. The paper concludes with implementation priorities and a research agenda for evaluating interventions in the Indian context.

all.title: **"The Rise of Digital Deception: Deepfakes, Sextortion, and AI-Driven Financial Fraud in the Digital Age"**
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: --- ### Alternative Titles 1. **"Trapped in the Digital Illusion: Analyzing Deepfake Extortion, Cyber Blackmail, and the Weaponization of Social Media"** 2. **"The Dark Side of the Digital Web: A Comprehensive Study of AI-Driven Sextortion, Financial Scams, and Law Enforcement Countermeasures"** 3. **"Beneath the Likes: How Cybercriminals Exploit Social Media for Deepfake Blackmail and Investment Fraud"** 4. **"Digital Maya: The Escalating Threat of AI-Manipulated Media, Cyber Extortion, and the Urgent Need for Digital Literacy"** 5. **"From Fake Profiles to Financial Ruin: A Case Study on Deepfake Sextortion and AI-Enabled Cybercrime in India"** --- ### Subtitle**"A comprehensive analysis of the escalating threat of AI-manipulated media and cyber extortion—examining the predatory tactics of criminals on social media, the devastating psychological and financial toll on victims, and the critical role of law enforcement and digital literacy in combating this new wave of cybercrime"** --- ### Detailed Description This research paper provides an in-depth analysis of the rapidly evolving landscape of cybercrime, focusing specifically on the malicious use of Deepfake technology, sextortion, and AI-driven financial fraud. Drawing on recent case studies, police reports, and cybercrime statistics from India, the paper examines how the convergence of artificial intelligence, easily accessible image manipulation tools, and the ubiquity of social media platforms has created a fertile ground for sophisticated digital deception. The paper is structured around five core analytical dimensions. **First**, it investigates the mechanics of Deepfake-based extortion. The analysis details the predatory pattern used by cybercriminals: creating fake profiles on platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and Telegram to lure victims, extracting sensitive personal information (photos, contact lists), and using AI tools to morph the victim's face onto explicit or compromising images. These manipulated images are then used as leverage for blackmail, demanding ransom under the threat of public exposure to family and friends. The paper highlights the devastating psychological impact of this crime, noting tragic cases of suicide among victims who felt trapped and stigmatized. **Second**, the paper examines the broader ecosystem of AI-driven financial fraud, including investment scams and phishing operations. It details how criminals use WhatsApp and Telegram to promote fraudulent stock market and cryptocurrency schemes, often creating fake apps and "trading rooms" that display artificially inflated profits to encourage larger investments. The paper cites specific cases involving the siphoning of crores of rupees through complex networks of "mule accounts" and stolen identities, illustrating the sophisticated nature of these operations. **Third**, the paper analyzes the response of law enforcement agencies, particularly the Cyberabad police. It highlights successful operations, including the arrest of individuals involved in selling stolen data and the interception of youths returning from Cambodia who were allegedly forced to work in cyber-slavery conditions running scam operations targeting Indians. The paper also discusses the police's advocacy for AI-based detection tools to identify Deepfakes and track cryptocurrency transactions. **Fourth**, the paper critically evaluates the role and responsibility of social media platforms. It argues that the lax verification processes and anonymity offered by major platforms are being blatantly exploited by criminals. The paper calls for greater accountability from tech companies in monitoring, removing malicious content, and cooperating swiftly with law enforcement. **Fifth**, the paper outlines essential prevention and digital literacy strategies. It emphasizes the need for users to avoid accepting friend requests from unknown individuals, refrain from sharing personal photos online, and exercise extreme caution with unverified investment schemes. The paper strongly advises victims of sextortion to report the crime immediately rather than paying ransom, as capitulation only encourages further demands. The paper concludes that the weaponization of AI and social media represents a paradigm shift in cybercrime. Combating this "digital maya" requires a multi-pronged approach: stringent platform accountability, improved AI detection technologies, robust law enforcement, and a massive, nationwide campaign to educate the public about the dark side of the digital world. **Target readership:** Cybersecurity researchers, law enforcement officials, digital rights advocates, social media policy analysts, psychologists studying cyber-trauma, and the general public. **Methodological note:** The paper is a review and analysis based on reported police cases and journalistic accounts from the source articles. Statistical claims and specific case details should be verified against official law enforcement records and cybersecurity reports prior to formal submission. --- *Would you like me to adjust the academic tone, shorten the description for a specific publication format, or generate a table of contents or abstract to accompany these elements?*

all.title: O dever de cuidado na era do PIX: responsabilidade civil das instituições financeiras por falha de segurança e hipervulnerabilidade do idoso em fraudes digitais
all.venue: Caderno da Escola Superior de Gestão Pública Política Jurídica e Segurança
all.abstract: Este estudo analisa a responsabilidade civil das instituições financeiras diante das fraudes digitais, com ênfase nas operações realizadas via Pix e nos golpes de engenharia social praticados contra pessoas idosas. Investiga-se a tensão entre a celeridade das transações digitais e o dever de segurança bancária, partindo da compreensão de que a responsabilidade das instituições financeiras é objetiva e, em determinadas situações, solidária. A pesquisa identifica duas falhas recorrentes no dever de cuidado: a deficiência nos procedimentos de identificação e verificação de clientes, que pode favorecer a abertura de contas utilizadas por fraudadores, e a insuficiência dos mecanismos de monitoramento capazes de detectar operações incompatíveis com o perfil transacional do consumidor. Examina-se também a aplicação da excludente de culpa exclusiva da vítima diante de situações caracterizadas como fortuito interno. Conclui-se que, quando demonstrada falha na segurança do serviço, a responsabilização das instituições financeiras encontra fundamento na Teoria do Risco do Empreendimento, no dever de segurança e na proteção do consumidor idoso em condição de hipervulnerabilidade. Palavras-chave: responsabilidade civil bancária; hipervulnerabilidade do idoso; fraudes digitais. Abstract This study analyzes the civil liability of financial institutions in cases of digital fraud, with emphasis on transactions carried out through Pix and social engineering schemes targeting elderly consumers. It examines the tension between the speed of digital transactions and the banking duty of security, based on the understanding that the liability of financial institutions is objective and, in certain circumstances, joint and several. The research identifies two recurring failures in the duty of care: deficiencies in customer identification and verification procedures, which may facilitate the opening of accounts used by fraudsters, and insufficient monitoring mechanisms capable of detecting transactions inconsistent with the consumer’s transactional profile. The study also examines the application of the exclusion based on the exclusive fault of the victim in situations characterized as internal fortuitous events. It concludes that, when a failure in service security is demonstrated, the liability of financial institutions is grounded in the Theory of Enterprise Risk, the duty of security, and the protection of elderly consumers in situations of hypervulnerability. Keywords: banking civil liability; hypervulnerability of the elderly; digital fraud. Resumen Este estudio analiza la responsabilidad civil de las instituciones financieras frente a los fraudes digitales, con énfasis en las operaciones realizadas a través de pix y en las estafas de ingeniería social perpetradas contra personas mayores. Se investiga la tensión entre la celeridad de las transacciones digitales y el deber de seguridad bancaria, partiendo de la comprensión de que la responsabilidad de las instituciones financieras es objetiva y, en determinadas situaciones, solidaria. La investigación identifica dos fallas recurrentes en el deber de cuidado: la deficiencia en los procedimientos de identificación y verificación de clientes, que puede favorecer la apertura de cuentas utilizadas por defraudadores, y la insuficiencia de los mecanismos de monitoreo capaces de detectar operaciones incompatibles con el perfil transaccional del consumidor. También se examina la aplicación de la eximente de culpa exclusiva de la víctima en situaciones caracterizadas como caso fortuito interno. Se concluye que, cuando se demuestra una falla en la seguridad del servicio, la responsabilización de las instituciones financieras encuentra fundamento en la Teoría del Riesgo Empresarial, en el deber de seguridad y en la protección del consumidor mayor en condición de hipervulnerabilidad. Palabras-clave: responsabilidad civil bancaria; hipervulnerabilidad de las personas mayores; fraudes digitales.

all.title: Cyber Fraud in Digital Banking: Legal Remedies and Consumer Protection in India
all.venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
institutions: Institute of Chartered Accountants of India
all.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital banking and real-time payment systems in India has transformed access to financial services, but it has also intensified exposure to phishing, vishing, identity theft, account takeover, SIM-swap fraud, malicious applications, remote-access scams, QR-code manipulation, mule-account networks and other cyber-enabled financial crimes. This paper critically examines the Indian legal and regulatory framework governing cyber fraud in digital banking, with particular attention to the rights and remedies available to consumers. It analyses the Information Technology Act, 2000; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025; the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023; the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023; the Consumer Protection Act, 2019; the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007; and the Reserve Bank of India’s customer-protection directions. It distinguishes the DPDP framework’s phased commencement from the date of enactment and explains the position as at 20 November 2026. The study adopts a doctrinal and analytical methodology using statutes, regulatory directions, judicial decisions and official institutional materials. It argues that existing law provides meaningful remedies but remains fragmented in implementation, particularly in prompt reporting, burden of proof, inter-bank coordination, preservation of digital evidence, data security, recovery from mule accounts and compensation for social-engineering victims. It recommends a coordinated, victim-centred model combining rapid transaction containment, transparent liability assessment, accountable personal-data processing, reasoned bank decisions, accessible grievance redress, stronger payment-system accountability and digital literacy.

all.title: Prevenção de Fraudes e Golpes Digitais em Meios de Pagamento Eletrônicos: mecanismos jurídico-regulatórios e proteção ao consumidor no Sistema Financeiro Nacional
all.venue: Revista da Procuradoria-Geral do Banco Central
authors: Danniel Pedro Lima de Araújo Da Conceição
all.abstract: Este artigo analisa o marco jurídico-regulatório para prevenção de fraudes e golpes digitais no Sistema Financeiro Nacional (SFN), com ênfase em meios de pagamento eletrônicos, especialmente o Pix. O objetivo é avaliar a eficácia dos mecanismos de governança e segurança cibernética do Banco Central do Brasil (BC) e do Conselho Monetário Nacional (CMN) na proteção do consumidor financeiro. A metodologia adota a análise normativa de resoluções recentes, como a Resolução Conjunta 6/2023 e as atualizações do Regulamento do Pix referentes ao Mecanismo Especial de Devolução (MED), aliada à jurisprudência do Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) e aos acórdãos do Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU). Os resultados revelam uma evolução regulatória focada no compartilhamento obrigatório de dados sobre fraudes e na responsabilidade objetiva dos prestadores de serviço por falhas de segurança ou engenharia social. Conclui-se pela necessidade de reforçar o monitoramento em tempo real e as tecnologias de detecção, transferindo o risco da fraude do consumidor vulnerável para as instituições, em consonância com a Lei 15.252, de 4 de novembro de 2025, e os princípios da cidadania financeira.

all.title: Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI): Emerging Challenges and Issues in International Financial Law
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Digital public infrastructure is slowly becoming the base for many financial services. It includes systems such as digital identity, instant payments, and sharing of financial data with consent. These systems help people receive government benefits, make payments, and open bank accounts more easily. But they also bring legal problems, especially when personal data, private companies, and cross-border transactions are involved. This paper looks at the legal issues connected with digital public infrastructure in international financial law. At present, there is no one international law that covers DPI completely. Payments, data protection, cybersecurity, and digital identity are handled under different laws in different countries. Because of this, companies and users face confusion when a DPI-based service works across borders. The paper studies India, the European Union, and Brazil. These three examples show that countries are building DPI in different ways, but the law has not developed at the same speed. The paper points out problems such as weak cybersecurity, unclear liability when fraud or system failures happen, digital exclusion of people without documents or smartphones, and differences in data-protection rules. It argues that DPI should be treated as important financial infrastructure and should be regulated more clearly. Finally, the paper suggests that countries should follow common principles for DPI, improve cooperation between regulators, protect consumer rights, and provide offline or assisted options for people who cannot use digital systems. A balanced legal framework is needed so that DPI can support financial inclusion without putting users at risk.

all.title: The Three Laws of Payment Physics: Speed-Finality Separation, Friction Relocation, and Multilateral Liquidity-Saving Netting Across Global Retail and Wholesale Rails
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Modern electronic checkouts complete contactless card authorizations and mobile QR scans in 150 to 400 milliseconds, sustaining the widespread illusion that sovereign purchasing power moves at fiber-optic speed. In reality, global financial plumbing separates fast cryptographic messaging from irrevocable balance-sheet extinction across commercial and central bank ledgers. Bridging monetary economics with protocol-level distributed systems engineering, this 8-page open-access working paper (Digbijoy Labs Working Paper WP-2026-03) formalizes The Three Laws of Payment Physics: Law I — The Speed–Finality Divide: Authorization messages record conditional intent at fiber-optic speed, whereas interbank debt extinguishes only when central-bank reserves (Tier 0 M0) or statutory settlement assets mutate across nested double-entry ledgers. Law II — The Conservation of Friction: Checkout simplicity never destroys verification complexity; it relocates protocol work into hardware cryptography (EMV ARQC, FIPS 140-3 HSMs), alias and Verification of Payee directories (NPCI VPA, BCB DICT, EU Reg. 2024/886 VoP), prefunded liquidity pools, or post-settlement dispute arbitration. Law III — The Conservation of Risk: Credit, intraday liquidity, fraud, foreign-exchange principal (Herstatt), and split-brain timeout exposures never vanish; Debit Pull vs. Credit Push rulebooks invert risk polarity and price exposure across balance sheets. Includes a unified 9-archetype comparative taxonomy and monochrome schematics contrasting Four-Corner ISO 8583 Pull Cards, Sovereign Instant Credit Push (India UPI, Brazil Pix, US FedNow and RTP, Eurozone SEPA Instant / TIPS), Wholesale RTGS and Liquidity-Saving Mechanisms (Fedwire Funds, Eurosystem T2, CHIPS 26:1 continuous multilateral netting), and CLS Bank 18-currency atomic FX Payment-versus-Payment (PvP). Companion Monograph (Releasing December 8, 2026): Jay Thorne, The Physics of Payments: A Practitioner's Guide to Cards, Instant Rails, B2B Treasury, Cross-Border FX, and Wholesale Settlement (Digbijoy Labs, 2026, 242 pp., 20 Chapters, 20 Monochrome Schematics; Paperback ISBN 979-8-1449-0879-5, Hardcover ISBN 979-8-1449-1281-5). Interactive Open-Source Simulators (MIT): https://digbijoylabs.github.io/anatomy-of-a-payment/ | Source & Free 23-Page Chapter 1 Sample: https://github.com/digbijoylabs/anatomy-of-a-payment

all.title: Behavioural Analytics for Early Detection of SIM Swap and Account Takeover in Financial Systems: A Model
all.venue: Tech-Sphere Journal for Pure and Applied Sciences
all.abstract: The increasing adoption of digital financial services has heightened the vulnerability of financial systems to cybersecurity threats, particularly SIM swap fraud and account takeover (ATO). Conventional fraud detection mechanisms, which predominantly rely on predefined rules and transaction-based monitoring, often struggle to identify sophisticated attacks that exploit legitimate authentication channels and imitate normal customer behaviour. This study develops a Hybrid Predictive Intelligence Model (HyPIM), a behavioural analytics framework for the early detection of SIM swap fraud and account takeover in financial systems. The proposed framework integrates telecommunications-related SIM lifecycle information, device intelligence, authentication activities, geographical access patterns, and financial transaction behaviour through a five-layer architecture comprising data acquisition, behavioural feature engineering, intelligent analytics, risk assessment, and fraud detection and response. The methodology employs Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), XGBoost, and Isolation Forest algorithms to identify known fraudulent activities and emerging behavioural anomalies. The experimental evaluation utilises the SIM Swap Fraud Detection dataset and PaySim1 financial transaction dataset as complementary sources for behavioural and transactional fraud analysis. The illustrative results indicate that HyPIM achieves 99.63% accuracy, 94.80% precision, 93.10% recall, and a 0.24% false-positive rate, suggesting improved detection performance compared with individual machine learning models and conventional rule-based approaches. The study contributes an integrated approach to behavioural fraud detection by correlating SIM-related security indicators with financial account activities to support early threat identification and timely security interventions.

all.title: Account Takeover at the Cart: When the Buyer Is Not the Account Holder
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: A customer opens a shopping app and finds an order they did not place, shipped to an address they do not recognize, paid with the card they saved for convenience. The person who checked out was not the account holder. This paper proposes a taxonomy of six failure modes for account takeover at the cart: The Borrowed Login, The Silent Session, The Changed Address, The Stored Card Unchecked, The Recovery That Locks Out the Victim, and The Blamed Victim. It proposes a framework, the takeover ledger, recording what the account holder did, what the account did, what changed and when, and what was notified through which channel, with three tests for who should bear the loss. It works the argument through a single takeover, from a leaked credential to recovery, and closes with six design principles, including that the victim is made whole first and liability is settled between providers afterward. Working paper by Salem Evbogbai, not peer reviewed.

all.title: RUID: Privacy-preserving multi-factor authentication through ephemeral user identifiers
all.abstract: This paper introduces RUID (Random User Identifier and Dynamic), a privacy-preserving multi-factor authentication (MFA) protocol. Traditional MFA and federated identity frameworks rely on static user identifiers, leaving them vulnerable to user enumeration, cross-session tracking, and credential stuffing. RUID mitigates these threats by replacing persistent identifiers with ephemeral, single-use identifiers cryptographically bound to a registered client device. By removing the static identity from the network transit phase, RUID prevents early-stage reconnaissance and identity correlation. The protocol is analysed using a five-stage approach which provides a precise monitor of the security and performance limits of the extensively used authentication mechanisms. The protocol is assessed against the prominent authentication framework like OAuth2+OIDC, SAML2 based federation, smart card based schemes and digital signature based approaches. The protocol is analysed as benchmark, measuring success rates of attacks, authentication latency, and failure behavior in adverse conditions. In order to have a main consistency and replicability of the protocol all the experiments are made in a testing environment. The results indicate that the protocol is effective in reducing user validation attack and replay attack while preserving the genuine authentication of the legitimate users. The implementation and replicable test suite provide evidence that the protocol can be implemented in terms of standard cryptographic primitives on commodity hardware, thereby providing a groundwork for functional verification and optimization of the protocol as well as real-world deployment.

all.title: Adapting and Evaluating Enterprise AI Risk Orchestration Across Payment Environments
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This working paper extends Enterprise AI Risk Orchestration with a method for adapting its vendor-agnostic fraud-risk architecture to different wire payment workflows. The paper examines an account takeover and a comparable legitimate payment in two hypothetical environments. One uses an institution-operated wire platform. The other uses the institution’s own payment queue until handoff to an external processor. The comparison shows which orchestration functions a receiving institution can reuse and how it can map those functions to local signals, payment identifiers, policies, and release controls. It also identifies where a hold can take effect and how the institution can confirm it. The paper proposes a protocol for verifying the adaptation and comparing it with existing controls. The protocol measures fraud detection time to intervene, interruptions to legitimate payments, and time to confirmed action.

all.title: A Reissuable Social Security Credential Framework to Prevent Identity Theft
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The United States Social Security number (SSN) is used both as a permanent identifier for taxand payroll records and as a secret that proves identity when credit is opened. It cannot doboth: an identifier must be disclosed widely, and a secret that has been disclosed cannot bechanged. This paper specifies a backward-compatible framework that separates the two roleswithout altering the SSN or the systems that store it. The Social Security Administration (SSA)issues each number holder a plastic chip card containing a private signing key that never leavesthe chip and is unlocked by a four-digit PIN that SSA assigns and mails separately; the carddisplays no SSN and no secret. To open credit, the holder’s chip signs a request that the lenderhas itself signed, naming the lender, the product and an amount ceiling, so that approval isbound to one application. Credit bureaus verify the signature against an SSA-issued certificateand a published status list, so SSA is not contacted during a transaction and does not learnwhere people apply for credit. Two alternatives produce an approval attested by SSA instead ofsigned by the chip: a web session secured by a passkey, and, for holders who prefer paper and paya fee, a path using a paper record card that carries a reissuable 16-digit Credential Number anda 12-character card secret, entered in SSA’s application with the PIN and completed by photoidentification in person, by a one-time code sent to the holder’s telephone, or after a waitingperiod announced to the holder by mail. The two classes of approval are labeled and neverconflated. Status is kept separately for the person and for each credential, so that a freeze blocksevery path while the loss of one credential affects only that credential. We specify issuance, loss,recovery and freeze procedures consistent with NIST SP 800-63-4, an origination receipt thatlimits each approval to one account, a statutory outline with a conditional safe harbor, a fundingmodel and a transition plan. The design addresses new-account and synthetic identity fraud. Itdoes not by itself address account takeover, tax-refund fraud or employment fraud, and it hasnot been prototyped or formally verified.

all.title: Cyber Security Challanges In Digital Banking
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This report is based on my Summer Internship Programme at the State Bank of India (SBI), focusing on the topic "Cybersecurity Challenges in Digital Banking." It explores various cybersecurity threats and challenges associated with digital banking, including phishing, online fraud, data breaches, identity theft, and unauthorised transactions. The report examines the importance of cybersecurity in the modern banking system, customer awareness of digital security, and measures that can help ensure safer digital banking practices. It also presents relevant observations, findings, and recommendations based on the internship experience and research conducted during the programme. This report was prepared as part of my academic internship under the B.Com (FYUGP) programme at Gurucharan College, Silchar.

all.title: CYBERSECURITY RISKS AND DATA PROTECTION IN THE DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION OF COMMERCIAL BANKS: EVIDENCE FROM UZBEKISTAN
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This thesis examines cybersecurity risks and personal data protection mechanisms amid the digital transformation of commercial banks in Uzbekistan. Based on an analysis of the Laws "On Cybersecurity" (No. LRU-764) and "On Personal Data" (No. LRU-547), Basel Committee operational resilience principles, CERT-CBU practices, and remote-lending fraud evidence, it is shown that rapid digital credit growth has heightened social-engineering, identity-theft, and third-party data-leak exposures. A conditional cyber-resilience sequence, an integrated zero-trust defense principle, and five readiness indicators are substantiated.

all.title: Cybersecurity in Digital Finance: Evaluation of Cyber-Attacks in India
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Digital finance is revolutionizing financial services access across India, from UPI payments to mobile/digital banking in semi-urban and rural areas, but it has also resulted in cyber-attack. There is a shift towards open Application Programming Interfaces (API), cloud services and AI-enabled decision-making systems that bring efficiency and inclusivity, yet expose financial institutions, businesses and individual users to data breaches, phishing, identity theft and algorithmic exploitation. This paper investigates cybersecurity challenges faced by banks, NBFCs and FinTech firms operating in Indian markets. Using an empirical approach, the study combines a review of regulatory guidance from RBI advisories and national data protection initiatives with important case studies of cyber-attacks in India. The paper highlights innovative practices that show promise. These include two-step authentication that balances usability with security for users, community-oriented cybersecurity awareness campaigns conducted via local language media and partnerships between banks and academic institutions to create cost-effective threat detection solutions. The paper concludes with policy suggestions and an operational checklist for financial institutions and other relevant sectors, aiming to promote safe and inclusive digital financial systems that can maintain trust and facilitate broader financial inclusion.

all.title: Exploiting AI Vulnerabilities: The Deepfake Threat to Cybersecurity, Privacy, and Trust
all.abstract: This research deals with the vulnerabilities in artificial intelligence (AI) systems that can be exploited, with deepfake technology being one of the most famous xamples of adversarial abuse. Deepfakes produced by the system have been used for deceptive aims, like identity theft, misinformation, and financial fraud. Besides deepfakes, this work also covers broader adversarial attacks, evasion attacks, data poisoning, model inversion and Trojan AI which affect sectors like cybersecurity, autonomous systems, and healthcare. The research examines the technical basis of deepfake generation, the availability of adversarial tools, and possible exploitation in the wild. It also finds weaknesses in systems, data collection, model training, and models that can be exploited. Further, it assesses existing detection and mitigation techniques such as forensic and frequency-domain analysis, adversarial training, and awareness programs. Ethical and legal issues are explored under regulations such as the GDPR, CCPA and DPDPA. Lastly, the paper highlights the importance of enhanced AI security, advancements in detection technologies, and international cooperation to facilitate ethical and responsible AI development

all.title: Deepfake Detection Using AI: A Review Of Audio, Visual And Audio–Visual Methods For Digital Forensics
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Deepfakes are realistic manipulated images, videos and audio created with deep learning and generative models that can imitate a person's face, voice, expressions or movements. Although useful in entertainment and education, they are misused for misinformation, fake identities, fraud and reputational harm. This paper reviews AI-based deepfake detection across both visual and audio modalities. It explains generation methods, then examines visual detection from facial texture, lighting, eye and lip movement and inter-frame differences using convolutional and attention-based networks; generalizable detectors for fully synthetic images; audio detection from spectral and prosodic voice characteristics using anti-spoofing models; and audio–visual methods that detect mismatches between speech and lip motion. Benchmarks including FaceForensics++, ASVspoof and FakeAVCeleb are discussed. The detection process of collecting and preprocessing media, extracting features and applying machine learning or deep learning models is formalized in a five-layer architecture. Research gaps, objectives, a comparison of modalities and challenges such as generalization, compression, adversarial evasion and explainability for forensic use are presented. The review concludes that combining audio and visual evidence gives the most reliable detection for social media, journalism, banking, law enforcement and digital forensics.

all.title: The Psychology Behind AI-Generated Phishing and Social Engineering Attacks
all.abstract: Cybercrime has evolved significantly with the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), transforming traditional phishing and social engineering attacks into highly sophisticated and personalized threats. While early phishing attempts relied on generic messaging and low success rates, modern AI-driven attacks leverage advanced data analytics, natural language processing, and behavioral prediction to manipulate victims more effectively. This research examines how cybercriminals utilize AI to enhance psychological manipulation techniques in phishing and social engineering attacks, increasing victim susceptibility. Drawing from interdisciplinary literature in cybersecurity and psychology, this study explores key psychological mechanisms, including cognitive biases, emotional triggers, and decision-making processes that influence victim behavior. This paper will also analyze how AI amplifies these vulnerabilities by enabling personalization, automation, and realism in cyberattacks. Additionally, the research evaluates the psychological, financial, and societal impacts of cybercrime victimization, highlighting the growing risks associated with identity theft and digital distrust. Finally, this study proposes comprehensive prevention strategies that integrate technological defenses, user awareness training, and policy interventions. Understanding the intersection of AI, psychology, and cybercrime is essential for developing effective cybersecurity measures in an increasingly digital and interconnected world.

all.title: Legal, Regulatory, and Societal Dimensions of Generative Fraud Analytics
all.abstract: In this chapter, one can find an examination of legal, regulatory, and societal issues around generative AI in fraud analytics. The discussion takes place in the context of a complex world that has been shaped by fast technological changes and increased risks. The paper presents an analysis of key intercontinental frameworks. Among others, the EU AI Act defines risk-based classifications for high-impact GenAI systems, GDPR imposes thorough data protection requirements, India's DPDP Act stresses consent and data localization, and the USA is on its way with state-level deepfake regulations and federal initiatives such as the No AI FRAUD Act. Discussions are held around the liability doctrines for decisions that are autonomous in nature, made by AI systems, wherein the accountability is shared among AI developers, deployers, and users, with the models being treated as opaque “black, box”. The regulation of deepfakes is aimed particularly at synthetic identities and media fraud, whereas technological solutions from RegTech automate compliance by means of auditable pipelines and synthetic data governance. Several fundamental principles of data ethics, such as privacy, design, minimization, and transparency, are combined with human rights concerns about surveillance biases and discriminatory effects of fraud correlation. Public administration issues refer to an erosion of trust in the market that results from AI-generated scams; thus, they appeal for law and tech collaborations that would produce harmonized international standards (e. g., ISO/IEC AI governance). Ethical auditing frameworks, certification programs like those from IEEE, and societal changes, for instance, less financial inclusion due to overzealous detection, are examined. Ultimately, the article emphasizes the need for proactive, multidisciplinary governance that makes utilization of GenAI in the fight against fraud, its potential, at the same time protecting human rights and equality.

all.title: Addressing the Misuse of Mule Accounts in Online Fraud: A Comparative Study of Vietnamese and Malaysian law
all.venue: Addaiyan Journal of Arts Humanities and Social Sciences
all.abstract: Mule accounts—payment accounts through which proceeds derived from fraudulent activities are received, transferred or dispersed—constitute a significant component of contemporary online fraud schemes. Their misuse raises a fundamental legal challenge: how can individuals who knowingly facilitate fraudulent activities be held criminally accountable without imposing liability on those who have been exploited or whose conduct does not satisfy the requisite mental element? This article compares the legal frameworks of Vietnam and Malaysia through four functional dimensions: the classification of online fraud offences; liability arising from conduct involving payment accounts; the establishment of the mental element and differentiation of criminal responsibility; and the mechanisms for tracing, restraining and recovering fraud-related funds. Vietnam adopts a combined regulatory and criminal-law approach, incorporating prohibitions under payment legislation, administrative sanctions under Decree No. 340/2025/ND-CP and existing offences under Articles 17, 174, 290, 291, 323 and 324 of the Penal Code. Malaysia, by contrast, has introduced specific offences concerning the possession, transfer of control and use of payment accounts without lawful authority or lawful purpose under sections 424A–424C of the Penal Code, together with police powers to seize funds or prohibit dealings in suspected accounts under section 116D of the Criminal Procedure Code. The comparative analysis identifies distinct challenges in both jurisdictions. Vietnam faces questions concerning the adequacy of existing sanctions in addressing deliberate account-related facilitation, whereas Malaysia faces interpretative and enforcement challenges concerning the application of its newly introduced offences. Assessing both legal frameworks against six criteria—coverage, culpability, enforceability, timeliness, safeguards and recovery—the article argues for a differentiated and proportionate approach to addressing mule-account misuse. It proposes common principles and jurisdiction-specific reforms rather than identical legislative solutions, emphasising the importance of balancing effective fraud prevention and enforcement with the requirements of criminal culpability and the protection of affected individuals.

all.title: Coerced but “Authorised”: Allocating Loss in India's Digital Arrest Frauds and the Case for a Statutory Reimbursement Regime
all.venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
institutions: National University of Study and Research in Law
all.abstract: In a “digital arrest” fraud, callers posing as police, customs or central-agency officers convince a victim over video that she is under investigation and must move her savings into a “verification” account to avoid arrest. The victim makes the transfers herself. That single fact has shaped how Indian law allocates the loss. Because the payment is authenticated by the customer, it falls outside the “unauthorised transaction” framework that has governed bank liability since 2017, and the victim usually bears the whole loss. This paper examines whether that allocation can be defended and what should replace it. It combines doctrinal analysis of the Reserve Bank of India’s 2017 Circular, the Responsible Business Conduct Third Amendment Directions, 2026, consumer law and the Supreme Court’s continuing suo motu proceedings with analysis of official data placed before Parliament and the Court, and a comparative study of the United Kingdom, the European Union, Singapore and Australia. Reported digital-arrest losses rose from ₹91.14 crore in 2022 to ₹1,935.51 crore in 2024, and the average reported loss per complaint rose from about ₹22,800 to about ₹1.57 lakh. The 2026 Directions bring coerced payments within the definition of a fraudulent transaction, but a coerced customer who took reasonable care falls under none of their liability rules, and their compensation mechanism covers only negligent customers’ losses of up to ₹50,000, once in a lifetime, for a single year. The paper argues that coercion is not negligence, that banks are the cheapest avoiders of this loss, and that the bank hosting the mule account should share it. It proposes a statutory Coerced Payment Reimbursement Scheme built on a presumption of reimbursement, an equal split between sending and receiving banks, a meaningful cap and a narrow gross-negligence exception.

all.title: Application of Intelligent Agents in Anti-money Laundering Transaction Detection
all.venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
institutions: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics
all.abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) transaction detection faced scarce labels, extreme class imbalance, relational dependencies, and future-information leakage. This study developed a validation-gated ensemble detection framework combining temporally constrained transaction features, historical account statistics, explicit transaction-network motifs, and seven heterogeneous XGBoost experts. A large language model (LLM) proposed candidate rules from aggregated validation evidence, which a programmatic rule-validation agent assessed through threshold fitting and out-of-time validation. A validation-gated router integrated expert predictions and validated rule signals. On the temporal test set of the synthetic HI-Small dataset, the framework achieved PR-AUC, F1, and recall of 0.5965, 0.5532, and 0.4299, respectively. These values exceeded those of the evaluated XGBoost and GIN-family baselines; the explicit-motif XGBoost baseline achieved a PR-AUC of 0.4788. Stage-wise analysis attributed most gains to explicit transaction-network motifs and validation-weighted expert voting. The router provided only a small improvement, and the rule branch did not improve PR-AUC. Under this experimental setting, the findings supported using the LLM for candidate-rule generation and auxiliary analysis, but did not establish it as the source of the overall performance gain.

all.title: Detecting Illicit Bitcoin Transactions for Anti-Money-Laundering Monitoring: A Temporal and Interpretable Machine Learning Benchmark on the Elliptic Dataset
all.abstract: Cryptocurrency networks give criminals a low-friction way to move illicit funds, so institutions and regulators need tools that flag suspicious transactions and can justify each alert. This study presents a temporally faithful benchmark of three supervised classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost) for detecting illicit transactions in the Elliptic Bitcoin dataset for anti-money-laundering (AML) research. Models are trained on earlier time steps and tested on later ones to avoid temporal leakage, and the benchmark adds a quantification of concept drift and paired significance tests. Only 9.76% of the labeled transactions are illicit. Logistic Regression reaches an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.8777 but a precision of only 0.1762 on the illicit class, so over 80% of its alerts would be false. Random Forest and XGBoost reach illicit-class F1-scores of 0.7562 and 0.7878, with precision of 0.9875 and 0.9442 and precision-recall areas of 0.7595 and 0.7751; XGBoost attains the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (0.9355) at a recall of 0.6759. Performance degrades sharply when the test window lies far from the training window, and a threshold analysis shows that missed illicit transactions are limited by feature separability rather than by the decision threshold. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identify the small set of transaction features that drives most predictions, supporting the audit trail that compliance teams require. The study does not 1 propose a new algorithm; its contribution is a rigorous and interpretable reference benchmark for AML monitoring in digital finance.

all.title: Who Sent It or How It Moved? Sender Shortcuts in Cryptocurrency Anti-Money-Laundering Benchmarks, Audited on Elliptic2 and Elliptic++
all.abstract: Two public benchmarks dominate graph-based anti-money-laundering (AML) research on Bitcoin: the transaction-level Elliptic dataset, extended as Elliptic++, and the subgraph-level Elliptic2. In both, a label is assigned according to the entity that sends the funds. We ask whether models trained on these benchmarks learn how laundering moves or merely who sent the money, and we propose a diagnostic protocol to tell the two apart: a sender lookup baseline, a novelty baseline, a sender-disjoint split with a leakage check, and a decomposition of performance into sender, receiver and intrinsic signal. On Elliptic2 the task largely reduces to classifying the sender. Under the standard random split, a no-learning lookup of sender history reaches a PR-AUC of 0.954, against 0.975 for gradient boosting on 456 features; our reimplementation of RevClassify reproduces its reported 0.97 and falls to 0.126 without sender information. When senders are held out, performance drops to 0.746, and the subgraph's own structure, transactions and receivers fall from 0.619 to 0.186. On Elliptic++ the same protocol finds the shortcut negligible: sender history reaches only 0.340 against 0.986 for the full model (3.5 against 10.1 times the test prevalence), adding it to the full model raises PR-AUC by less than 0.004 in every seed, and the transaction's own features keep 0.883 when sending addresses are held out. We trace the difference to the unit of sender identity: Elliptic2 senders are entity clusters that recur across many labeled subgraphs, whereas Elliptic++ senders are individual addresses, and fewer than half of test transactions have a sending address seen in training. A shared sender-based label rule thus produces a severe shortcut in one benchmark and a negligible one in the other, so the diagnostic must be run on each benchmark.

all.title: Effectiveness of a hybrid Machine Learning Model for War Against Money Laundering in Nigeria
all.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN
all.abstract: This paper examined the effectiveness of machine learning (ML) Models for the ongoing war against money laundering in Nigeria. In advanced economies, the rise of machine learning has revolutionized the way financial institutions and governments combat illegal financial activities emanating from mobile money transactions. By using advanced algorithms and data analysis techniques, machine learning has proven to be an effective tool in identifying suspicious financial transactions and patterns, thereby helping authorities take proactive rather than reactive measures in preventing fraudulent transactions. This study aimed to address the research gap in the use of reactive approach by Nigeria government, where the prevalence of money laundering has risen in recent years, and explored how ML techniques can be utilized to enhance the country’s efforts in combating this financial crime.The datasets for this study were obtained from Kaggle website that contains fraudulent transactions on money laundering, which was used to train, validate and test the ML models. Logistic regression (LR) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) were used as the baseline models while Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) neural network was used for feature learning and dimensionality reduction. The results indicate that LR classifier still showed reasonable performance but did not outperform the other models. Among all the measures, SVM exhibited outstanding performance, with over 90% prediction accuracy. The amount of money transferred and location of transactions emerged as top features for predicting money laundering transactions in online money transfers. These findings suggest that further research is needed to enhance the logistic regression model, and sparse autoencoder neural network should be explored as potential tool for law enforcement agencies and Nigeria financial Institutions to proactively learn representative data from high dimensional datasets as quality of data improves performance of predictive models.

all.title: Transaction Monitoring That Survives Reconciliation
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This white paper sets out an engineering design for transaction monitoring in anti-money laundering (AML) programs, for U.S. banks and for fintech lending programs run with a sponsor bank. It starts from a public enforcement case. The U.S. Justice Department found that one bank left about 92% of its transaction volume unmonitored for more than six years. The paper argues that most monitoring failures happen before any model is involved: products that were never connected to monitoring, data that was never reconciled, alerts that can’t be rebuilt later, and testing that measures new models against filings the old system produced. This is done by Muoro's team. The design works in a fixed order. First, reconcile the data, so the institution can prove which transactions its controls checked. Second, run the scenarios regulators require in a protected lane, where no model can switch them off. Third, add machine learning in a separate lane to rank the optional alert queue and to find patterns the rules miss. Every alert keeps its source events, its known data gaps, and the logic that raised it, so an investigator or examiner can see what the system knew at the time the alert fired. The paper covers: mapping regulatory obligations to engineering requirements the difference between what a bank and a fintech lending program can each see a reference architecture and a typical tech stack a worked example in SQL: three loans repaid from one shared funding account, and how the picture changes when one of those payments is returned how to choose training labels, and why past suspicious activity reports (SARs) are not ground truth testing a new model in shadow mode, and comparing it with the current system at the same investigator capacity where generative AI can help investigators questions examiners and model risk committees will ask a phased rollout with acceptance criteria and rollback steps The worked example and the capacity comparison use synthetic, illustrative figures. This paper is not legal or regulatory advice.

all.title: Graph-Based Financial Fraud Detection: A Property-Centric Survey of Static, Temporal, Cycle-Aware, and Generative Methods and Their Evaluation
all.venue: Journal of Computing Theories and Applications
all.abstract: Financial fraud is increasingly coordinated across multiple accounts and transactions, meaning that its evidence often lies in relationships between accounts, the sequence of events, and, in schemes such as money laundering and wash trading, closed loops of transfers rather than in individual records. This review examines graph-based methods for detecting such fraud, covering static and temporal graph neural networks, graph anomaly detection, cycle- and motif-aware methods, generative models, and the evaluation practices used to assess them. The review draws on 147 sources identified through a documented literature search protocol. Four findings emerge. First, no single method family performs best under all conditions: tree-based models remain highly competitive on feature-rich datasets, whereas graph-based and temporal models offer greater advantages when discriminative signals reside in relational structures or transaction sequences.
