Second, detecting cyclic laundering is fundamentally a representational problem: standard message-passing architectures have limited ability to capture cycle structures, while recent performance gains have been associated with representations that preserve the directed multigraph structure of transactions rather than simply increasing model complexity. Third, evaluation practices, including temporal leakage and threshold selection using test data, can inflate reported performance and undermine the reliability of comparisons. Fourth, a taxonomy of eight method families evaluated against four properties required for coordinated, temporal, and partially observed fraud detection—temporal awareness, probabilistic generation, cycle awareness, and intrinsic explainability—reveals that none of the reviewed families provides all four properties. This identifies a central research gap in the current literature. Building on these findings, the review proposes cyclic fraud as a structural stress test for future detection methods and provides an evaluation checklist to address the methodological weaknesses identified.

all.title: Artificial Intelligence for Financial Crime Detection: Economic Efficiency, Accountability, and Legal Responsibility
all.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning and Data Analytics
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied to financial crime detection, offering potential efficiency gains over traditional rule-based systems while raising important questions concerning algorithmic accountability and criminal liability. This review examines 25 scholarly and institutional sources across law, criminology, computer science, and regulatory policy. It focuses on three areas: (1) the economic efficiency of AI in anti-money laundering (AML) and fraud detection; (2) criminal liability issues associated with false negatives, algorithmic opacity, and the due diligence responsibilities of system deployers; and (3) governance challenges relating to explainability, human oversight, and cross-jurisdictional regulatory harmonization. The review indicates that machine learning approaches offer potential advantages in identifying complex financial crime patterns and reducing false-positive alerts. However, the available evidence on overall cost-effectiveness and measurable crime reduction remains limited. False negatives represent a particularly significant challenge because undetected suspicious transactions may create regulatory, reputational, and legal risks. The analysis further highlights fragmented liability frameworks and the importance of due diligence in determining responsibility for AI-related failures. The review concludes that effective AI-based financial crime detection requires a human-machine collaborative governance approach supported by explainability, systematic false-negative monitoring, appropriate human oversight, and stronger international regulatory coordination.

all.title: Early Detection of Financial Crime Risks: A Conceptual Framework for Incorporating Heuristic Decision Rules into Suspicious Activity Reporting
all.abstract: This conceptual article advances anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT) research by proposing a novel, explainable framework for embedding simple heuristic decision rules into internal suspicious transaction reporting (STR) and suspicious activity reporting (SAR) workflows. Existing transaction-monitoring tools often suffer from massive false-positive burdens (frequently exceeding 90–95%) and operate primarily ex post, struggling to provide timely pre-execution risk indicators. I argue that formal heuristic decision rules—including recognition, take-the-best, fast-and-frugal decision trees (FFTs), tallying, and satisficing—can structure front-line inquiry and analyst triage to support early risk assessment under severe conditions of dynamic uncertainty. Crucially, I establish clear operational boundaries by distinguishing front-line customer due diligence (CDD) and internal compliance escalation from formal institutional STR filing to financial intelligence units (FIUs). I emphasize that customer answers and behavioral anomalies provide initial indicators of risk rather than conclusive evidence of criminal intent (mens rea). Furthermore, I outline strict legal, privacy, and anti-discrimination safeguards under international Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards and domestic regulatory regimes (e.g., European Union General Data Protection Regulation (EU GDPR), anti-tipping-off provisions). Finally, I present a concrete 4-step prototype questionnaire mapped directly to objective verification rules, alongside a rigorous, multi-stage validation methodology utilizing temporal holdout testing, synthetic counterfactual simulation, and asymmetric loss functions.

all.title: SMART BANKING SYSTEM (GREEN BANKING) A UNIFIED, SECURE AND INTELLIGENT CORE BANKING PLATFORM FOR CUSTOMERS, COMPLIANCE OFFICERS, AND ADMINISTRATORS
all.abstract: Modern financial operations and digital banking exist in a mission-critical area where security vulnerabilities, unauthorized overdrafts, fraudulent transactions, money laundering risks, and manual credit underwriting delays can profoundly undermine institutional integrity and customer trust. This paper proposes Green Banking (Smart Banking System), a unified, secure, and intelligent core banking platform connecting retail customers, compliance officers and bank administrators through a real-time digital financial ecosystem. The system is focused around an atomic double-entry General Ledger bookkeeping engine, two-step OTP multi-factor authentication, real-time AI Neural Sentinel fraud and anomaly detection, automated Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance monitoring, CIBIL-based loan underwriting with reducing-balance EMI amortization schedules, ISO/IEC 7812 Luhn Mod-10 card lifecycle management and standardized identifier generation (IFSC, UPI VPA and ISO 13616 IBAN). The platform is built using a four-tier architecture encompassing a presentation tier, an Express REST API gateway tier, a business services tier and an ACID-compliant persistence tier utilizing SQLite in Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode. Security is enforced through JWT-based Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), bcrypt password hashing and tamper-evident audit logging and the API is documented with OpenAPI/Swagger. The primary aim of the system is to transform every banking operation into an atomic, verified and auditable lifecycle in which no transaction is committed without balance verification, AML screening and fraud-risk scoring. The proposed design also serves as the foundation for future technologies including blockchain-based ESG bond tokenization, IoT smart-meter verification, Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) settlement and biometric authentication.

all.title: Artificial Intelligence and Cryptocurrency-Enabled Organized Cybercrime: Criminal Typologies, Investigation, and Digital Evidence
all.abstract: This chapter focuses on the recent merging of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), cryptocurrencies, and cybercrime, especially on the dark web and crime using cryptocurrencies. It examines how, while cryptocurrencies allow for easy, secure, and low-cost digital and financial transactions and transfers, they enable criminal and illegitimate activities such as fraud, money laundering, terrorism financing, ransomware, and cybercrimes. The chapter assesses how AI and ML help unearth illegitimate cryptocurrency transactions, detect suspect transactional patterns, trace financial transactions on the blockchain, and support digital and cryptocurrency forensics. It examines the use of privacy and anonymity-enhancing technologies (including darknet markets), mixers, privacy-focused cryptocurrencies, decentralized systems, and crypto wallets to obscure identities and transactional traces. The chapter assesses legal and regulatory frameworks, as well as technological responses, and suggests an integrated approach of legal, regulatory, investigative, and forensic frameworks.

all.title: Privacy and security preservation of bitcoin digital currency transactions on mixing services using enhanced heuristic-aided optimal weighted features and hybrid deep learning network
institutions: SRM Institute of Science and Technology
all.abstract: Bitcoin (BTC) is a Peer-to-Peer (P2P) digital currency that facilitates transactions using pseudonymous identities. Mixing services improve the anonymity of transactions but are misused for illicit activities such as money laundering, raising security concerns in the BTC ecosystem. This research implements a hybridized deep learning approach for privacy preservation in BTC transactions. The required data are gathered from Elliptic Dataset and Ethereum Fraud Detection dataset, and these datasets are used for evaluation. The features are extracted from these datasets, followed by weighted attribute selection. The optimal feature selection and fine-tuning of the weights are implemented using the Improved Current Mussel Time-based Eurasian Oystercatcher Optimizer (ICMT-EOO) algorithm. The weighted attributes are classified using a Faster Regions-based Convolutional Neural Network with Dilated Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (FRCNN-DBi-LSTM). Experimental evaluation is performed using existing classifiers and optimization algorithms to demonstrate the efficiency of the approach. The proposed method achieves an accuracy of 95.2%, an F1-score of 92.98%, a recall of 95.21%, and a precision of 90.84%, respectively. The results confirm that the developed model achieves improved performance and enhanced security compared to existing methods.

all.title: Clean-Account Banking, Zero Hidden Money, and Multi-Tier Protection Against Corrupt Agencies: Reclaiming Cryptographic Ledgers From Speculative Coin Schemas
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Eliminating Illicit Money Laundering, Proof-of-Work Speculative Waste, and Unchecked Institutional Snooping Through Provenance-Closed Double-Entry OMVFS01 Ledgers, Four Graduated Secret Tiers, and Adversarial Threshold Quorum Warrants (OMVFS-BANK-V1) Cryptographic hash chains and Merkle trees were invented for a noble, natural purpose: tamper-evident accounting, double-spend prevention, and mathematical auditability. Speculative cryptocurrency schemas hijacked that breakthrough — attaching Proof-of-Work coin mining and anonymous token casinos that burn nation-scale electricity while serving ransomware cartels, wash traders, and dirty-account money laundering. Yet the state-surveillance alternative — centralized Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) or unchecked agency databases — hands a single ministry god-mode visibility over every citizen's life, turning into an extortion weapon whenever an agency or official becomes corrupt. OMVFS-BANK-V1 solves both sides simultaneously: clean accounts form a mathematically closed Kirchhoff conservation graph where unattributed dark-silo money cannot enter (binding ordinary citizens, corporations, and public officials under the exact same math), while honest people are shielded by four graduated OMVFS secret-protection tiers, (t, n) adversarial multi-institution quorum warrants, single-field Merkle openings, and unforgeable reverse-audit scars that expose any corrupt snooping. Reclaiming Blockchain's True Purpose Without Speculative Coins: Delivers mathematical double-entry conservation, non-repudiation, and public timestamp finality on standard object storage at near-$0 transaction cost and zero Proof-of-Work energy waste. Clean-Account Provenance Closure (Zero Hidden Dirty Money): Every credit in a clean account must reference a counter-signed upstream clean transaction or regulated issuance node — dark-silo bribes, cartel proceeds, and unattributed shells fail lineage verification on contact. Symmetric Accountability for Officials & Treasuries: Connects commercial banking directly to WP-0005's public-treasury conservation DAG so corrupt officials cannot siphon public funds or launder off-ledger kickbacks back into the clean economy. Four Graduated Secret-Protection Tiers: Formalizes Tier 1 (blinded clean-standing proof), Tier 2 (PRIVATE .omenc vault), Tier 3 (SECRET protected multi-key custody), and Tier 4 (SECRET | HEADER_ENCRYPTED + .fstab.omenc topology cloaking against insider graph analysis). Defeating Corrupt Agencies ("Watching the Watchmen"): Eliminates unilateral agency backdoors via (t, n) adversarial quorum warrants (Independent Judiciary + Citizen Ombudsman + Regulator), single-leaf Merkle disclosure, and mandatory APPEND_ONLY reverse-audit receipts. all.title: Explainable Graph Neural Networks for Detecting Coordinated Fraud in Digital Transaction Networks
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Coordinated fraud in digital transaction networks involves interconnected accounts that distribute illicit activity across multiple transfers, making suspicious behaviour difficult to identify through isolated transaction analysis. This paper proposes an explainable graph neural network framework for detecting such activity by jointly examining account characteristics, transaction behaviour, and relationships among participants. Digital transactions are represented as a directed graph in which nodes correspond to accounts and edges represent fund transfers, with features capturing transaction amounts, frequency, timing, and account activity. A graph neural network learns neighbourhood representations to estimate account-level fraud risk, while suspicious connections among high-risk accounts are examined to identify candidate fraud groups. An explanation module highlights the account features and transaction subgraphs that contribute most strongly to individual predictions, providing investigators with interpretable evidence for reviewing flagged activity. The proposed evaluation compares the framework with conventional machine learning and graph-based baselines using precision, recall, F1-score, and precision–recall area under the curve. Explanation quality is assessed through fidelity, sparsity, and stability, while chronological data partitioning limits information leakage. The study investigates whether relational learning can improve the identification of coordinated fraudulent behaviour while producing concise and useful explanations. The framework is intended to support transparent fraud screening and human investigation, with particular attention to incomplete coordination labels, changing transaction patterns, and the computational demands of large transaction networks.

all.title: Cross-Institution Cooperative Detection Model of Insurance Fraud Based on Graph Neural Networks and Federated Learning
all.abstract: The core challenge in cross-institution insurance fraud detection is that fraud-ring connectivity crosses institutional boundaries, while privacy regulations prohibit the centralized aggregation of raw claims data. This paper proposes CFGFraud, a federated graph detection framework for partially observable graphs. In this framework, a virtual-node placeholder mechanism makes the local model aware of cross-institutional hub entities; institutional attention mask separates the parameterization of real and virtual connections and imposes a learnable attenuation coefficient; and a federated attention alignment strategy constrains drift in each institution’s attention pattern during aggregation. The non-IID experiment with five clients on the IEEE-CIS dataset shows that CFGFraud achieves an AUPRC of 0.791, 0.057 higher than FedAvg+GAT. Fraud-ring recall reaches 0.723, 24.4% higher than FedAvg+GAT. The standard deviation across clients is compressed from 0.029 to 0.012. Single-round computation costs increase by about 8%, while communication overhead increases by less than 0.01%. Ablation experiments show that the virtual-node mechanism accounts for 31.1% of the fraud-ring recall gain, and collaboration gain is positively correlated with entity overlap across institutions. This framework provides a deployable technical path for cross-agency relational fraud detection under the constraint of data confinement.

all.title: Temporal Graph Learning for Robust Detection of Coordinated Fraud in Dynamic Transaction Networks
all.venue: International Journal of Advanced Engineering and Technology Research
all.abstract: Coordinated fraud can produce repeated, synchronized transfers whose signatures are obscured by heterogeneous activity, missing edges, and evolving behavior. This paper studies a lightweight temporal graph learning strategy based on account-level transaction attributes, static neighborhood descriptors, and eight-bin temporal coordination statistics. Static and temporal feature variants are each trained with the same simulated edge-deletion augmentation to disentangle the effects of timing descriptors and robustness training. Experiments are conducted on a controlled, fully specified synthetic benchmark containing 4,800 accounts, approximately 15,000 transfers per run, and simulator-assigned coordinated actors; the benchmark is not a real-world labeled fraud dataset. Three independent runs use chronological, nonoverlapping train/validation/test snapshots. The edge-augmented static graph achieves test average precision 0.631, while the identically augmented temporal feature model reaches 0.602; their nonaugmented counterparts score 0.571 and 0.569, respectively. At 20% and 40% test-edge removal, augmented static-graph average precision is 0.518 and 0.389, respectively. A matched augmentation control, fixed-budget top-100 precision, and timestamp shuffling separate the roles of training robustness and within-snapshot timing. The study provides an efficient, transparent protocol for evaluating coordinated-pattern detection in evolving transaction networks.

all.title: Cyber Intelligence, Blockchain Defenses, and Web3 Fraud Prevention
all.abstract: Generative AI has been a key enabler for cyber intelligence, blockchain defenses, and Web3 fraud prevention, mainly through simulating adversarial threats and allowing for proactive analytics in decentralized ecosystems. This chapter is a deep dive into the cyber fraud terrain, which is rapidly shifting, and the various fraud techniques being used range from APTs and ransomware to highly sophisticated scams that are exploiting smart contracts, cryptocurrencies, NFTs, and DeFi protocols. Generative models such as GANs help in creating very realistic attack simulations, which in turn lead to better-trained defenses that are capable of handling novel exploits like oracle manipulations or 51% attacks, whereas diffusion models predict risk patterns in volatile on-chain behaviors. Moreover, some of the major breakthroughs are blockchain analytics, which help in pattern visualization and wallet clustering that lead to the mapping of fraud networks, along with predictive vulnerability detection of smart contracts through the application of transformer- based NLP to codebases. On the other hand, the detection of cryptocurrency fraud is made possible through the use of synthetic data augmentation in cases of imbalanced transaction streams with the main focus being to counter pump, and, dump schemes as well as mixer obfuscation. Moreover, NFT fraud and Web3 phishing are analyzed through the use of behavioral anomaly models, and the usage of generative forensics is illustrated by the tracing of illicit funds through the employment of graph neural networks. Besides that, the integration within Security Operations Centers (SOCs) is done through a multi-agent AI system for real-time monitoring, which combines on-chain data with off-chain threat intelligence. Evaluation is done against global datasets such as Chainalysis reports, whereas policy frameworks are concerned with regulatory enforcement. Issues like scalability, quantum threats, and adversarial robustness are discussed in the paper, which ends by offering a hybrid GenAI, blockchain model that promises resilient and tamper- proof Web3 security.

all.title: How Much Do Foundation Models Add to Gradient Boosting on Financial Event Sequences?
all.abstract: Foundation models pretrained on raw transaction sequences are proposed for credit, fraud and churn modeling, with reported gains over gradient boosting, but the data and baselines behind these gains are rarely public. We measure how much the pretraining and adaptation recipes of these models add to a baseline of point-in-time window aggregates and LightGBM, and we propose TBS (Temporal Boosting-Sequence ensemble), which averages the ranks of a boosting model enriched with label-free event-transition features and of a pretrained sequence network fine-tuned jointly with the aggregates. On a synthetic credit-card dataset, the public MBD-mini banking dataset and two proprietary datasets of trade credit and B2B churn, we compare 27 methods at three label budgets with five seeds and paired bootstrap intervals, using sequence models of about 0.4 million parameters pretrained per dataset. Frozen self-supervised embeddings rarely improve the baseline, and a fine-tuned sequence network alone clears it in 9 of 21 target-budget cells. TBS clears it in 19 of 21 cells (18 after FDR adjustment), with a median gain of +1.8 AUC points, and the controls suggest that combining boosting with the pretrained network is the main source of the observed gain. Gains shrink as labels grow and with rich tabular data: with both, the gain on the proprietary datasets is +0.7 and +0.8 points, the latter with an interval including zero. We also re-examine two benchmarks. On IBM TabFormer, the test follows a change in the fraud pattern and the published baseline has no history; with the training period the vendor states, our history-aware LightGBM and our own foundation model stay below the published scores of a commercial model. On IBM AML, a simulation artifact lets a date rule reach F1 0.482, and a point-in-time LightGBM reaches the F1 of graph neural networks whose test graph includes later transactions.

all.title: Deepfake and Voice Clone Identity Shield System
all.abstract: Synthetic videos and cloned voices can be easily created nowadays, and are being used for impersonation, fraud and spreading misinformation.Manually determining whether video content or audio has been manipulated is not reliable.The Deepfake and Voice Clone Identity Shield System (DFVCISS) is a web-based solution that provides detection of video deepfakes, analysis of voice clones and combined audio/video analysis using a single Flask application.It will provide predictions, confidence and evidence from the model instead of just a category.All analysis will be logged within an SQLite history.A PDF can then be generated using the information stored.The video detection uses a trained convolutional neural network.Inspection of the FakeAVCeleb dataset was performed to determine audio/video examples.This project is a prototype to allow initial verification of media.The reliability of the results depend upon the models being used, training dataset and independent testing.

all.title: DEEPFAKES AND THE LAW: A GROWING LEGAL CHALLENGE
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Deepfakes are AI-generated synthetic media that convincingly depict a person saying or doing things they never did. Though they have lawful uses in entertainment, education and accessibility, their misuse for impersonation, fraud, harassment, non-consensual sexual imagery and disinformation threatens autonomy, privacy, consent and reputation. This article examines how deepfakes are created, the harms they cause and the Indian legal framework that applies to them: Article 21 of the Constitution, the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the IT Rules, 2021, as amended in February 2026 to cover synthetically generated information. It argues that these laws punish the consequences of deepfakes but do not regulate deepfakes themselves. It proposes stricter penalties, quick and affordable remedies, stronger personality and likeness rights, careful scrutiny of digital evidence and greater public awareness, so that individual rights are protected without stifling legitimate uses of AI.

all.title: FRAMEWORK GAIA-FIS: GOVERNANÇA DE IA PARA MITIGAÇÃO DE FRAUDES POR DEEPFAKES DE ÁUDIO E IDENTIDADES SINTÉTICAS
all.abstract: A proliferação da IA generativa criou um novo vetor de risco corporativo, deepfakes de áudio para fraudes financeiras. Paralelamente, o Brasil discute a regulação do setor por meio do PL nº 2.338/2023, que propõe deveres de governança. Este artigo apresenta o Framework GAIA-FIS, modelo prático de governança desenhado para organizações brasileiras. Adotou-se abordagem qualitativa, baseada em análise documental e mapeamento cruzado entre requisitos regulatórios e controles da ISO/IEC 42001:2024. Baseado no PL, na LGPD e na ISO/IEC 42001:2024, o framework propõe 20 controles operacionais estruturados em cinco dimensões e guiados pelo ciclo PDCA, com o propósito de reduzir a lacuna entre a conformidade legal e a defesa técnica contra identidades sintéticas. Por se tratar de uma proposta ainda não validada empiricamente, recomenda-se sua aplicação experimental em estudos futuros.

all.title: VeriFace: Automated Deepfake Recognition - From CNN and Temporal Models to Multimodal Transformers
all.venue: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
all.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has made deepfake videos increasingly realistic, creating serious concerns regarding digital security, identity theft, online fraud, and misinformation. Detecting manipulated videos has therefore become an important research challenge. This paper presents a deepfake detection platform that uses deep learning techniques to identify facial manipulations in video content. The proposed approach analyzes video frames by extracting facial features and examining visual inconsistencies across consecutive frames. Spatial analysis helps identify irregularities within individual frames, while temporal analysis detects unnatural changes that may not be visible in a single image. The system classifies the input video as real or fake, provides a confidence score, and uses visual heatmaps to highlight regions influencing the prediction. Its performance can be evaluated using benchmark deepfake datasets under different video quality and compression conditions. The paper also discusses key challenges related to detection accuracy, computational efficiency, model explainability, generalization, and data privacy. This approach aims to support reliable deepfake identification and improve trust in digital media.

all.title: An Ensemble Deep Learning Framework for Deepfake Video Detection Using ResNet Models
all.venue: Kocaeli Journal of Science and Engineering
all.abstract: Deepfake technology has raised growing concerns due to its potential to enable misinformation, identity fraud, and security threats through manipulated digital content. As these risks continue to increase, the development of reliable deepfake detection methods has become essential. In this study, a spatial feature-based ensemble deep learning framework is proposed to improve detection accuracy and classification stability. Facial regions were first extracted from video frames using the MTCNN algorithm to focus the analysis on relevant facial areas. The proposed framework focuses on spatial facial representations extracted from individual video frames rather than explicit temporal modeling. Subsequently, ResNet50 and ResNet101 were employed as the main spatial feature extractors to obtain deep facial representations at different abstraction levels. ResNet152 was also evaluated experimentally to examine the effect of a deeper feature extraction branch; however, it was not included in the final framework because it increased runtime without improving video-level classification performance. The extracted feature vectors were classified using independent multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifiers, and the final prediction was obtained using a two-model weighted soft voting ensemble. The proposed method was evaluated on a balanced subset of the Celeb-DF dataset using a video-level train-test split to reduce data leakage between training and test sets. Experimental results showed that the final ResNet50–ResNet101 weighted soft voting ensemble achieved 94.17% video-level accuracy, 0.986 AUC, 0.9440 F1-score, and 0.8864 MCC. The two-model ensemble achieved performance comparable to the three-model configuration while providing a more favorable runtime profile. These findings suggest that combining complementary spatial facial representations through weighted soft voting provides a reliable and computationally efficient approach for deepfake video detection.

all.title: VeriMedia: A Spatial-Temporal Deep Learning Platform for Video Deepfake Detection and Forensic Verification
all.abstract: The increase of hyper-realistic generative models, deepfakes, face-swapping algorithms, and neural rendering has severely compromised public trust in digital video media, helping centered political disinformation, financial fraud, executive impersonation, and non-consensual synthetic defamation, in many respects; synthetic artifacts are clearing heterogeneously across the microscopic pixel textures and inter-frame temporal transitions, when the facial video undergoes generative forgery, in real-world scenarios.Standard digital forensic workflows rely on static two-dimensional Convolutional Neural Networks (2D-CNNs) that are inspecting isolated frames; in fact, yet, frame-by-frame classifiers are fundamentally blind to temporal boundary flickers, physiological inconsistencies (such as irregular eye blinking flow and micro-expression dynamics), and motion discontinuities.Along these dimensions, suffering from acute vulnerability to lossy social media compression (such as H.264/H.265 codecs at high quantization parameters c23 and c40); in fact, also black-box deep models output uninterpretable scalar scores without spatial or temporal attribution, restricting their evidentiary admissibility in judicial and regulatory environments.Current methods across the digital media forensics, deep spatial representation learning, temporal sequence modeling, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) are reviewed by this survey paper, broadly speaking.In parallel with this, forensic feature acquisition mechanisms (handcrafted biological heuristics, frequency-domain changes, and deep convolutional backbones), temporal sequence learning pipelines, and emerging explainability frameworks, and benchmark leading industry platforms (Microsoft Video Authenticator, Intel FakeCatcher, Sensity AI) alongside academic systems (MesoNet, XceptionNet, EfficientNet-B4, C3D/I3D, LipForensics, FTCN are gauged), on the whole.To tackle key research gaps around temporal blindness, compression sensitivity, and ungrounded black-box outputs, we suggest the architectural design of VeriMedia, namely one full-stack, spatial-temporal forensic framework combining zero-trust video ingestion, MTCNN facial landmark alignment, any ResNeXt-50 (32x4d) clustered residual convolutional backbone, a further multi-layer Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) sequence modeling pipeline with dual-threshold confidence gating, and a dual-stream visual explainability engine delivering spatial Grad-CAM saliency heatmaps and temporal anomaly waveforms anchored by a tamper-evident cryptographic SHA-256 PDF dossier.Finally, open research challenges and position multimodal audio-visual synchronization are analyzed as a planned future extension.

all.title: The Dark Side of AI: Fraud, Deception, and the Erosion of Trust
all.abstract: Fraud and deception are not new. They have existed for as long as human civilization. What AI changes is the scale, speed, and sophistication at which deception can be conducted. Scams that once required a team of people can now be executed by a single individual deploying automated agents. AI has lowered the barrier to entry for creative work, for business, for education, and for fraud. A deepfake is an AI-generated or manipulated audio, video, or image designed to convincingly imitate a real person. AI can generate invoices, contracts, résumés, certificates, and legal documents that look entirely authentic. Creating a fake degree certificate, a forged reference letter, or a convincing but fraudulent contract is no longer a specialist skill. Phishing has always relied on tricking people into clicking links or handing over credentials, but it has historically been detectable by poor grammar, generic greetings, and implausible scenarios.

all.title: Multimodal Fraud Intelligence: Text, Image, Audio, and Video
all.abstract: The rise of communication platforms has significantly altered the fraud environment by allowing fraudsters to stage a sophisticated attack across different data types. Modern fraud attacks now encompass manipulative text, images, audio forgery, and deepfakes to increase their authenticity and bypass solutions designed to detect fraud via a single data type. This chapter provides a detailed investigation of multimodal fraud intelligence solutions that process text, image, audio, and video modality signals to ensure effective fraud detection. It discusses the application of Deep Learning-based architectures in multimodal learning and the dual-application process of Generative Models, including fraud generation and forensic methods for fraud discovery. The chapter studies cross-modal fusion techniques, multimodal alignment methods, and joint inference processes that allow for the discovery of orchestrated fraud in multimodal datasets. In addition to this, the chapter deals with threats to multimodal systems, real-time inference issues, and issues of deployment at scale. It also considers legal, ethical, and regulatory matters such as evidentiary support, privacy, explainability, and legal requirements. Thus, such topics form a body of work to create a unified technical and legal needs-based approach to designing, analyzing, and implementing multimodal fraud intelligence solutions.

all.title: Impact and Response of AGI Such as Sora on the Judicial Identification of Fraud
all.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial general intelligence (AGI), exemplified by Open AI’s Sora, has profoundly disrupted the judicial identification of fraud crimes. This study systematically examines how Sora’s high-fidelity text-to-video capabilities lower the threshold for fraud, enhance deceptive sophistication, and facilitate precise victim targeting, thereby significantly escalating criminal risks. It identifies two pivotal challenges in judicial practice: first, the complex attribution of criminal liability amid AGI’s transitional status as either a human-controlled tool (weak AI) or an autonomous actor (strong AI); and second, the severe evidentiary crisis triggered by deepfake technology, which fundamentally undermines traditional authentication standards and complicates the collection, preservation, and verification of digital evidence. In response, the chapter proposes a comprehensive regulatory framework encompassing a multi-dimensional governance system, prospective doctrinal adjustments to criminal liability, and the modernisation of evidentiary rules through advanced detection technologies and standardised authentication protocols. By integrating legislative foresight, technical countermeasures, and multi-stakeholder collaboration, this research offers actionable pathways to mitigate AGI-driven fraud risks while safeguarding judicial integrity and evidentiary reliability in the algorithmic era.

all.title: Ethical CV: Deep-Fake Detection Via Biological Signals
all.abstract: Deepfake videos are becoming more common and are often used for harmful purposes like identity fraud, political manipulation, and spreading false or misleading content. While modern deepfake generators create videos that look very realistic, they still struggle to copy subtle human behaviors like natural blinking, accurate lip-sync, and small facial movements. Most current detection tools focus on surface-level visuals such as lighting or video quality, which may not be reliable as deepfakes become more advanced. Ethical CV introduces a smarter solution by analyzing natural biological signals in the face to detect whether a video is real or fake. It uses computer vision to track these signals and machine learning to check if they follow real human patterns. Early tests show this method is more accurate than relying on visual cues alone. Ethical CV is flexible, easy to understand, and useful in areas like media verification, digital forensics, and the safe, responsible use of AI in digital content. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance with 94.2% accuracy, 92.8% precision, and 95.1% recall on benchmark datasets.

all.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Changing Patterns of Crime in Nigeria: Implications for Social Control
all.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
all.abstract: The increasing application of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming criminal activities and creating emerging challenges for mechanisms of social control in Nigeria. This study examined the changing patterns of AI-assisted criminality and their implications for crime prevention, institutional regulation and social control. Anchored in Social Control Theory and Routine Activity Theory, the study adopted a qualitative integrative literature review and documentary analysis of scholarly publications, institutional reports, Nigerian legislation and relevant policy documents. The findings revealed that AI is reshaping existing forms of cybercrime through automated financial fraud, identity impersonation, deepfake-enabled deception, social engineering and transnational criminal operations. Available evidence further indicated that socioeconomic pressures, weakened informal social controls, institutional capacity limitations and inadequate technological guardianship contribute to vulnerabilities associated with emerging digital criminal activities. However, existing Nigerian cybercrime statistics do not sufficiently distinguish AI-enabled offences from conventional cybercrime, limiting accurate assessments of their prevalence and economic consequences. The study also identified challenges involving digital evidence authentication, cross-border jurisdiction, data protection and inter-agency coordination. It argued that effective responses require the integration of technological safeguards with formal and informal mechanisms of social control. The study recommended specialised digital forensic training, strengthened cybersecurity legislation, improved financial fraud detection, community-based digital literacy, institutional accountability and international cooperation. It concluded that addressing AI-assisted criminality in Nigeria requires a preventive, technologically responsive and socially inclusive approach that strengthens crime prevention while safeguarding fundamental human rights

all.title: Communication Abuse: Why Spam and Scam Calls, Texts and Emails Persist — and What It Would Take to Stop Them
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Scam and spam calls, texts, emails and ads, which this paper calls communication abuse, drive much of the 15.9 billion dollars in fraud losses Americans reported to federal authorities in 2025. That figure is nearly five times the 2020 total. Because most victims never report, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) estimates the true cost could be as high as 195.9 billion dollars. The paper asks why the problem persists despite decades of laws, fines and blocking tools. Its core finding is that enforcement targets scam callers, who are mostly overseas and almost never pay. Meanwhile, the carriers, platforms and payment companies that carry the traffic are paid on volume and face little liability. Courts have narrowed the 1991 Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA), Congress has not updated it, and no single agency owns the problem from first contact to stolen dollar. The abuse has also moved to social media, messaging and dating apps, and political texting, where the rules are weakest. It now runs on bot farms, dark-web phishing kits, forced-labor scam compounds and AI voice cloning. Older adults and people with disabilities lose the most per person and get the least help recovering. The paper is written to be useful to the aging and disability networks already on the front line: Adult Protective Services, area agencies on aging, Senior Medicare Patrol, the National Elder Fraud Hotline and disability service providers. Drawing on approaches in the United Kingdom, Singapore and Australia, the paper recommends a Communication Abuse Accountability Framework of nine actions. They are led by a modern Communication Abuse Prevention Act, a shared-responsibility duty of care for banks, carriers and platforms, collectible penalties, authentication for text messages, a single accountable national lead, and default protections for people at greatest risk. The paper is meant to complement the Aspen Institute’s United We Stand: A National Strategy to Prevent Scams (October 2025), not compete with it. The paper is a synthesis of published sources current to November 2026; it presents no original data. Research and drafting were assisted by AI tools (Anthropic’s Claude and Perplexity) under the author’s direction, and vendor-sourced figures are flagged. Version 1.0; corrections are welcome and will be reflected in later versions.

all.title: Language and Back-Translation Effects in Multi-Class Smishing Classification: A Controlled 16-Language Benchmark
all.abstract: Smishing is a cyberattack in which fraudulent Short Message Service (SMS) messages are used to obtain personal or financial information by deceiving users. For a Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT), identifying the smishing type (bank/financial, delivery, or e-commerce) helps determine the impersonated entity. However, existing datasets are English-centric, leaving other languages underexplored. We present a controlled benchmark to study automatic translation on multi-class smishing classification, along two complementary lines: multilingual classification and back-translation augmentation for English. We introduce MIMICS-3500-16L, comprising 3500 seven-class smishing messages translated into 15 languages, and MIMICS-56000-BT, containing 56,000 original and back-translated variants. We present four experiments: (1) evaluation of multilingual models (XLM-RoBERTa, mBERT) on 16 languages, (2) comparison of six embeddings (TweetEval, FastText, USE, SMS-Bert, SentenceBert, RoBERTa) as input for SVM, LR, RF, and XGB, (3) proposal for fusion of embeddings, and (4) evaluation of back-translated sample selection using ROUGE and METEOR. XLM-RoBERTa reaches F1-scores of 0.8619 in English and 0.8612 in Italian, whereas mBERT exhibits lower cross-language dispersion. TweetEval–RoBERTa fusion obtains a 0.8765 F1-score on MIMICS-3500. Training with back-translated variants does not consistently improve performance on original messages, where RoBERTa obtains a 0.8606 F1-score. These findings provide a benchmark for studying language and translation in multi-class smishing classification, while highlighting the need for validation on naturally occurring non-English messages.

all.title: Emerging Cyber Crimes in India: Trends, Impact & Regulatory Evaluation
all.abstract: India’s rapid digitalization has transformed banking, commerce, governance, and public services, but it has also increased the risk of cybercrime. This study examines major cybercrime incidents in India, including the Cosmos Bank cyber heist, Aadhaar data breaches, ransomware attacks on AIIMS Delhi and Tata Technologies, and phishing scams. The research analyzes the methods used by cybercriminals, identifies common vulnerabilities, and highlights emerging cyber threats. The study evaluates the social and economic impact of cybercrime on individuals, organizations, and critical infrastructure. It also examines the roles of law enforcement agencies, cybersecurity institutions, and government bodies in responding to cyber incidents. Furthermore, the effectiveness of existing cybersecurity laws, policies, and technological safeguards is reviewed. The research identifies key challenges in cybercrime prevention and investigation, such as limited awareness, inadequate digital literacy, and evolving attack techniques. Based on the findings, it recommends stronger cybersecurity practices, improved public awareness, enhanced legal frameworks, and greater collaboration among stakeholders. The study emphasizes that a coordinated effort by government, institutions, and citizens is essential to strengthen cyber resilience and ensure a secure digital future for India.

all.title: **The Digital Paradox: Analyzing the Surge in Cybercrime, Financial Fraud, and the Critical Need for Digital Literacy in Modern India (A Case Study of the November 2026 Eenadu Report)**
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: ### Alternative Titles 1. **From Connectivity to Vulnerability: A Comprehensive Study of Cyber Threats and Public Awareness in the Indian Digital Ecosystem**2. **Securing the Digital Frontier: An Analysis of Cybercrime Trends, Societal Impact, and the Imperative of Digital Intelligence**3. **The Human Firewall: Addressing the Digital Literacy Gap to Combat Rising Cyber Fraud in India**4. **Digital India at Risk: Navigating the Complexities of Cyber Security, Fraud Prevention, and Public Education** --- ### Sub-titles (Section Structure) 1. **Introduction: The Illusion of a Secure Digital Space**2. **The Landscape of Cybercrime in India** * 2.1 The Evolution of Cyber Threats * 2.2 Financial Frauds and Digital Payment Vulnerabilities3. **The Human Element: The Digital Literacy Deficit** * 3.1 Why Technology Alone Cannot Save Us * 3.2 Vulnerable Demographics4. **Societal and Economic Impact** * 4.1 Financial Losses and Psychological Trauma * 4.2 Erosion of Trust in Digital Systems5. **Institutional and Technological Countermeasures** * 5.1 Law Enforcement and Cyber Cells * 5.2 Technological Safeguards (2FA, AI Detection)6. **The Way Forward: Strategies for a Secure Digital India** * 6.1 Nationwide Awareness Campaigns * 6.2 Integrating Cyber Hygiene into Education7. **Conclusion: The Need for a "Digital Suraksha" Movement** --- ### Detailed Description #### 1. Introduction: The Illusion of a Secure Digital SpaceThe rapid proliferation of the internet and smartphones has fundamentally transformed Indian society, integrating digital tools into every aspect of daily life—from banking and shopping to governance. However, this massive shift toward digital dependency has created a dangerous paradox. As the November 2026 report in *Eenadu* highlights, the very devices that empower citizens have become portals for sophisticated cybercriminals. This paper explores the current cybersecurity landscape, arguing that the rapid adoption of technology has outpaced the public's ability to use it safely, resulting in a severe vulnerability crisis. #### 2. The Landscape of Cybercrime in India**2.1 The Evolution of Cyber Threats:** Cybercriminals are no longer isolated individuals but operate as organized syndicates. The methods have evolved from simple email scams to complex social engineering, phishing, and ransomware attacks. The article notes a staggering rise in these incidents, with criminals constantly adapting their tactics to bypass security measures. **2.2 Financial Frauds and Digital Payment Vulnerabilities:** A significant portion of cybercrime focuses on financial theft. As Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and net banking become ubiquitous, fraudsters exploit user ignorance. Common tactics include sending malicious links via SMS or WhatsApp, creating fake customer service numbers, and using "vishing" (voice phishing) to extract OTPs (One-Time Passwords) directly from victims. #### 3. The Human Element: The Digital Literacy Deficit**3.1 Why Technology Alone Cannot Save Us:** The core thesis of the article is that while security software is vital, the "human firewall" is often the weakest link. The gap between technological advancement and "digital intelligence" (digital literacy) is the root cause of most successful cyberattacks. Citizens often lack the fundamental knowledge to identify fraudulent links, secure their devices, or recognize social engineering tactics.**3.2 Vulnerable Demographics:** The report indicates that specific groups—the elderly, rural populations, and first-time internet users—are disproportionately affected. These groups are often targeted because they are less familiar with the red flags of digital fraud, making them easy prey for manipulative tactics. #### 4. Societal and Economic Impact**4.1 Financial Losses and Psychological Trauma:** The immediate impact of cybercrime is financial loss, which can run into millions of rupees collectively. However, the article emphasizes that the damage is not just monetary. Victims often suffer from severe psychological trauma, stress, and a sense of violation.**4.2 Erosion of Trust in Digital Systems:** A broader consequence is the erosion of public trust. If people feel unsafe using digital payment apps or online services, the overarching goals of a "Digital India" are undermined. Fear of fraud can push citizens back toward cash-based transactions, hindering economic progress. #### 5. Institutional and Technological Countermeasures**5.1 Law Enforcement and Cyber Cells:** The article points out the need for stronger law enforcement responses. While cybercrime cells exist, they are often overwhelmed by the sheer volume of cases. There is a critical need for better training, upgraded forensic tools, and faster cross-border coordination to track down criminals.**5.2 Technological Safeguards:** On the technical front, service providers and users must adopt stricter security measures. This includes mandatory two-factor authentication (2FA), biometric locks, and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) by financial institutions to detect and block suspicious transactions in real-time. #### 6. The Way Forward: Strategies for a Secure Digital India**6.1 Nationwide Awareness Campaigns:** The article strongly advocates for massive, nationwide public awareness campaigns. These campaigns must move beyond technical jargon and use accessible language to teach citizens basic "cyber hygiene"—like never sharing OTPs or clicking unverified links.**6.2 Integrating Cyber Hygiene into Education:** To create a long-term impact, digital safety must be integrated into the school curriculum. Teaching children how to navigate the internet safely will build a generation of responsible digital citizens. #### 7. Conclusion: The Need for a "Digital Suraksha" MovementThe transition to a digital economy is inevitable and beneficial, but it must be accompanied by a parallel "Digital Suraksha" (Digital Security) movement. The *Eenadu* report serves as a clarion call: without equipping the average citizen with the tools of digital literacy, the dream of a safe and secure Digital India will remain incomplete. The responsibility lies not just with the government or tech companies, but with every individual to remain vigilant and informed.

all.title: Securing the Modern Workforce: A Zero Trust Blueprint for Oracle Cloud HCM
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Enterprise HCM platforms store the most critical workforce information that an organization can't afford to lose: locators, banking and payroll information, personal identifiers, tax identifiers, and even executive compensation. With that focus, they are prime targets for credential phishing, payroll diversion and bulk data theft, and most of the attacks are through the front door with valid credentials. Perimeter security, which trusts a session upon initial authentication is never designed for this. The goal of this white paper is to explain a working Zero Trust architecture for Oracle Cloud HCM based on NIST SP 800-207 that re-authenticates every request for data, every integration, every device, and every user. Five pillars that support each other drive the design: Adaptive identity with MFA resistant to phishing login in OCI IAM identity domains; Least-privilege RBAC via Security Profiles and Oracle Access Governance; Default-deny network segmentation via OCI Zero Trust Packet Routing; Encryption with life cycle masking for non-production copies; Continuous object-level monitoring with automated response. The model is then translated into a program in a 90-day roadmap and the necessary control matrix through a reference architecture, which can be executed by CISOs, HR tech leaders, and Oracle Fusion security architects.

all.title: Profile Poisoning and Selective-Update Bias in Online Behavioral Biometric Authentication
all.abstract: Behavioral continuous authentication can update a user’s profile during operation, but accepted-only adaptation links access errors to future model states. Prior biometric work established separate authentication and update thresholds and quantified erroneous impostor inclusion and genuine-update misses. We examine their coupled security and adaptation consequences in score-level mobile authentication using frozen HMOG long short-term memory scores, a synthetic feature-space shift, and an independent two-day McGill Gait protocol. Poisoning samples were separated from future impostor probes. The strongest benchmark assumed access to claimant scores and presented up to eight initially accepted samples ranked near the authentication boundary; reconnaissance and candidate screening were not counted. At the reference operating points, blind exponential moving-average (EMA) updating increased post-poison attack success rate from 22.92% to 53.96% on HMOG and from 12.37% to 32.09% on McGill. An enrollment-anchored Guarded EMA condition kept the reference-point result close to Frozen. This direction did not persist across recalibrated policies. Under the nominal-1% calibration condition, the mean Blind-minus-Frozen effect was negative on both datasets for the tested boundary strategy. On the same HMOG conditional cohort, Blind EMA reduced attack success by 0.447 percentage points but increased false rejection by 6.89 points and the half-total-error rate by 3.22 points. Full-cohort false rejection at this strict condition was 80.79% on HMOG and 90.25% on McGill. The Guarded rule added no update margin when the current authentication threshold reached or exceeded the enrollment mean. In separate temporal evaluations, Guarded did not improve late genuine acceptance relative to Frozen. A label-aware, non-deployable Oracle-all diagnostic changed profile trajectories and reduced false rejection, but increased false acceptance. The results show that poisoning effects, genuine rejection, update-gate activity, calibration transfer, and attack feasibility depend on the operating point and should be evaluated together.

all.title: The residual victim: Crypto-asset fraud, restitution and the limits of criminal procedure in the MiCA era
all.abstract: European Union law now licenses the firms that hold and exchange crypto-assets and calls this investor protection. It does not require any scheme to compensate their clients. No other licensed retail financial market in European Union law has such a floor. This article asks why such an elaborate enforcement architecture returns so little to the people it names as its beneficiaries. That fraud victims struggle to obtain both recognition and restitution is well established. The argument here is narrower. Four features make the failure structural rather than contingent. Transfers cannot be reversed, because irreversibility is designed in. Offender anonymity is a property of the technology, not a shortfall in investigation. The Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation has no equivalent to the Investor Compensation Schemes Directive. The collective redress presupposes a named trader who frequently does not exist. Recognition fails too: these victims meet none of the usual criteria for victimhood. Meanwhile, new reimbursement rights in Europe exclude the crypto payment rail by design. As protection improves for other fraud victims, crypto-fraud victims are becoming the residual class. The article proposes five adjustments and states plainly which of them are new and which adapt established instruments.

all.title: Beyond the Trafficker–Victim Dyad: Examining Peer Relationships and Trauma Bonding Across Victim Pathways into and out of Commercial Sexual Exploitation
all.abstract: Commercial sexual exploitation (CSE) is a complex form of interpersonal victimization characterized by force, fraud, and coercion in which individuals engage in sexual activities that generate financial, material, or other benefits for third parties. Although trauma bonding has increasingly been used to explain why victims remain attached to exploiters, less attention has been devoted to the role of peer relationships in shaping pathways into and out of exploitation. This study examined how peer socialization and trauma bonding may influence victim pathways through a secondary qualitative analysis of 78 child sex trafficking investigative case files and 114 application files of adult women voluntarily seeking admission to a residential recovery program serving women currently or formerly involved in the sex industry or identifying as sexually exploited and/or trafficked. Using a theory-building thematic approach, four themes emerged: (1) relationship-based pathways into exploitation through peers, romantic partners, family members, and online contacts; (2) trauma bonding within exploitative relationships and social networks; (3) barriers to exit, including attachment to exploitative networks, substance use, homelessness, and trauma; and (4) recovery supported by recovery-oriented peers, family members, friends, and other supportive relationships. The findings indicate that peer relationships may function as both risk and protective factors. They also raise the possibility that trauma bonding processes may extend beyond trafficker–victim dyads to broader exploitative social networks, although this interpretation remains exploratory and warrants further empirical investigation.

all.title: E-BANKING, CYBERTHREATS AND DIGITAL FRAUD IN THE NIGERIAN FINANCIAL SECTOR: A LEGAL APPRAISAL OF REGULATORY FRAMEWORKS, INSTITUTIONAL ENFORCEMENT AND REFORM IMPERATIVES
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Abstract The electronic banking sector in Nigeria has been beset by cyber threats and digital frauds since its inception, with losses escalating from ₦2.9 billion in 2019 to ₦17.67 billion in 2023 alone. This article undertakes a doctrinal legal appraisal of the legislative and institutional framework designed to govern e-banking security, prevent digital fraud, and provide remedies to victims in the Nigerian finance sector. Drawing on the Deterrence Theory, Routine Activity Theory, and the Fraud Triangle Theory as its theoretical framework, the article examines the adequacy of the principal legislative instruments, including the Cybercrime (Prohibition, Prevention, Etc.) Act 2015 as amended, the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act 2020, and the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 alongside the institutional roles of the Central Bank of Nigeria, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, and allied regulatory bodies. The article finds that while Nigeria has constructed a multi-layered regulatory architecture, a systemic enforcement deficit produced by legislative fragmentation, weak institutional coordination, low prosecution rates, and inadequate technical infrastructure leaves e-banking customers structurally exposed to harm. Comparative analysis with the United Kingdom and South Africa identifies concrete legislative models capable of addressing this deficit. The article concludes with targeted recommendations for legislative reform, institutional coordination, and capacity building.

all.title: Financial Fraud and Cross-Border Legal Enforcement
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Financial Fraud and Cross-Border Legal Enforcement Vandana Yadav* Dr. Taru Mishra** Financial fraud has clearly turned into a global phenomenon, with financial transactions, digital banking, virtual assets and corporate set-ups now working across various jurisdictions. An individual fraud could have an originator in one country, victims in another, financial intermediaries in a third jurisdiction and proceeds in a number of other countries. This poses a major challenge to the law enforcement authorities as criminal jurisdiction, investigative power and rules of evidence are still largely territorial based. The paper draws upon the issue of cross border financial fraud and explores the legal mechanisms that can be adopted for tackling the problem, especially in relation to India and the international legal framework for cooperation among states. The study focuses on the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, the Companies Act, 2013 and other pertinent laws in India. It also takes into account the international instruments related to the Financial Action Task Force, the United Nations Convention against Corruption, the cooperation through mutual legal assistance and INTERPOL, financial intelligence cooperation. Uses a doctrinal research methodology, based on laws, judicial decisions, international instruments, institutional reports and secondary legal literature. It indicates that jurisdictional conflicts, procedural delays, differences in legal standards, beneficial ownership problems and virtual assets, as well as insufficient institutional resources, are significant challenges for effective enforcement. The study confirms that current laws and legal instruments are valuable instruments to tackle financial fraud but their effectiveness is heavily reliant on timely international cooperation and coordinated enforcement actions. Recommendations for the modernization of mutual legal assistance mechanisms, enhancement of financial intelligence sharing, transparency with regard to beneficial ownership, technological capacity building and harmonization of regulation of virtual assets. *Department of Law, Amity University, Lucknow Campus, LL.M. (Cyber Law and Cyber Security) **Department of Law, Amity University, Lucknow Campus, LL.M. (Cyber Law and Cyber Security)

all.title: Informal Guardianship, Data Privacy Risks, and Consumer Fraud Victimization in Social Media Marketplaces (WhatsApp and Instagram) in Southern Nigeria
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The rapid expansion of social media e-commerce has transformed commercial transactions in Nigeria, yet it has simultaneously exposed consumers to unprecedented risks of digital fraud and privacy violations. This study investigates the nexus between informal guardianship, data privacy risks, and consumer fraud victimization within social media marketplaces, specifically focusing on WhatsApp and Instagram in Southern Nigeria. Grounded in Routine Activity Theory, the research employs a quantitative cross-sectional survey design utilizing structured questionnaires administered via Google Forms to active online consumers. The study examines how platform-based informal control mechanisms (such as group admin oversight and user reviews) and consumer data-sharing habits influence vulnerability to fraudulent schemes. Data were collected from 50 online shoppers across Southern Nigeria using Google Forms and analyzed using simple frequency counts and percentages. Findings show that 52.0% of the respondents have been scammed or ghosted by online vendors, mainly after making direct bank transfers before delivery (78.8%). Also, 74.0% of shoppers routinely share their personal phone numbers and 52.0% share their full home addresses in chats, leading to 46.0% experiencing spam calls, harassment, or fake loan messages after transaction disputes. Although 70.0% of buyers warn others about scammers in comments, 60.0% reported that WhatsApp group admins do not verify sellers' ID cards or shop addresses. The study recommends that banks and social media platforms introduce simple escrow payment options and that group admins verify sellers before allowing them to post goods.

all.title: Shared Liability for Digital Fraud in an Emerging Economy: Evidence from Thailand
all.venue: Journal of risk and financial management
all.abstract: Technology-enabled financial fraud, including call center scams, has become a significant form of transnational crime operating through cross-border networks and digital infrastructure. This study analyses the personal and perceptual factors associated with self-reported financial loss from five types of digital fraud, including call center scams, together with the division of responsibility among state agencies, financial institutions, telecommunications providers, and users before, during, and after a fraud incident. A mixed-methods design was employed, applying binary logistic regression to questionnaire data from 1201 users of digital financial services and conducting in-depth interviews with 15 informants: 10 victims or persons with direct experience of fraud and 5 experts. Binary logistic regression analysis was used to examine the association between predictors and occurrence of fraud loss. Age and occupation were significantly associated with the occurrence of fraud loss. Sex, education, income, perceived security and perceived benefits were not significantly associated with the occurrence of fraud loss. The interviews show offenders relying on institutional credibility, fear, and urgency to steer victims, and assistance falling behind once transaction data, investigative authority, and the power to freeze funds are dispersed across several organizations. Drawing on the interviews and the legal analysis, the study proposes policy measures that allocate responsibility according to each party’s capacity to limit the damage, including a lead agency for victim assistance, clear criteria and time limits for suspending transactions, and verifiable standards for apportioning losses between providers.

all.title: BANKING COMPLIANCE TOOLS FOR INVESTIGATING CRIMINAL CRYPTOCURRENCY SCHEMES TARGETING SOCIALLY VULNERABLE INDIVIDUALS
all.abstract: The research is aimed at developing a conceptually new paradigm of risk-oriented banking supervision adapted to counter cyber fraud involving virtual currencies. The main objective is to form a set of proactive compliance tools to block shadow transactions at the stage of the legal fiat gateway, when criminal groups use social engineering to force socially vulnerable citizens to convert their cash savings into crypto assets through unlicensed CVC terminals. The study employs a comprehensive approach that combines methods of systemic and structural analysis to identify institutional vulnerabilities of financial monitoring and to model the life cycle of illicit transactions. Using synthesis methods, an updated security architecture has been constructed, which integrates behavioral profiling, geospatial tracking of infrastructure, and on-chain intelligence into a single matrix of banking control. Scientific novelty. The necessity of the conceptual transformation of banking compliance from a passive reporting function into an end-toend forensic mechanism is substantiated. An original model of synergistic application of tools is proposed, which shifts the focus of supervision from the retail victim-client to an in-depth audit of corporate crypto ATM operators. The exclusive role of the banking institution as the last controlled link before the anonymization of assets in the distributed ledger is highlighted. Conclusions. It is proven that conservative algorithms, such as threshold monitoring, payment screening, and anti-fraud systems, lose their preventive potential under conditions of psychological manipulation of victims and deliberate structuring of transactions. The implementation of the developed multi-level complex will allow banks to timely recognize anomalous patterns of cash withdrawals, protect the savings of elderly citizens, and generate a high-quality evidentiary base to neutralize transnational shadow networks of crypto asset exchange.

all.title: An Explainable Machine Learning Framework with Large Language Model Features for Predicting Monetary Redress in Bank Fraud and Scam Complaints
all.abstract: Liability for scam losses is shifting towards banks, yet few interpretable tools can anticipate which fraud and scam complaints will end in redress. This study develops SCAM-XD, an explainable framework that predicts whether a complaint to the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) flagged as possible fraud or a scam closes with monetary relief reported by the company. From the CFPB narratives archive, the study builds a benchmark of these complaints, about half of which human coders confirm as fraud or scams. A large language model (LLM) codes each narrative for scam type, payment rail, authorisation, manipulation cues and signals of the bank's response, agreeing closely with human coding on scam type. These features are combined with structured fields, company identity and text representations in a stacking ensemble, explained with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and linked to a cost-sensitive triage layer. Tested on a later period, SCAM-XD improves significantly on strong baselines across seeds, including a reimplemented topic model approach. LLM features yield a compact, interpretable model that nearly matches a high-dimensional text baseline but do not significantly improve the full model. Company identity is the strongest driver of predicted redress, yet firm identity alone predicts far less well, and payment rail and bank response cues act in directions consistent with liability rules. Under assumed costs, thresholds selected on validation data substantially reduce modelled expected cost relative to standard thresholds, whereas model choice matters much less. Redress depends on both the firm and the facts that determine liability.

all.title: The Genesis of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Fraud Detection
all.abstract: The greater digital transformation of today's economy has caused a considerable rise in the scale, speed, and complexity of fraudulent transactions, thus creating an even greater urgency for the development of sophisticated anti-fraud tools by which these needs will be met. Normally, the classical approach based on rule-based systems and traditional machine learning methods would not be able to cope with the changing nature of financial fraud tactics, the lack of labeled datasets, or the extremely imbalanced classes. Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) coming into being totally changes the way anti-fraud analytics is done, where it is not necessary to apply predetermined models, as this new AI simply figures out the overall data distribution. In short, generative AI aligns the data distribution that is hidden in the data with the distribution of the input so as to generate valid synthesized data. Going deeper into the chronological path of the development of anti-fraud methods using AI, the difference between discriminative methods and generative methods will be discussed. Also, the combination of synthesized data with anti-fraud analytics will be the subject of this paper. In addition, this discourse will touch upon the moral issues of AI usage in anti-fraud analytics. The ideas presented in this discussion will provide a good basis for the following two chapters, which delve into the evolution of advanced AI models from various architectural perspectives.

all.title: Explainable Machine Learning for Mobile Payment Fraud Detection
all.abstract: This repository contains the complete code, generated outputs, and reproducibility manifest for a cost-sensitive, explainable machine-learning pipeline for mobile payment fraud detection. The pipeline compares four classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) on a realistic synthetic mobile payment dataset from a Central Asian emerging market. The dataset has 150,000 transactions and a fraud rate of 3.47 percent. The market was selected as a proof-of-concept for Central and South Asia.The repository enables full reproduction of every table, figure, and number reported in the study. It also provides a reusable template for researchers and mobile payment operators who wish to apply the pipeline to their own transaction data.What the pipeline doesThe pipeline runs in 24 steps across five stages.Stage 1: data preparation. Steps 1 to 6 load the three source tables, merge them, select 12 real-time features, audit feature availability, preprocess the data, and split it into training (70 percent), validation (10 percent), and test (20 percent) sets. The split is stratified to preserve the 3.47 percent fraud rate.Stage 2: cost derivation. Step 4b derives the false-positive cost and false-negative cost from the dataset and from published Uzbek operational figures. The false-positive cost is USD 0.75. The false-negative cost is USD 21.70. The ratio is 28.93 to 1.Stage 3: model training and threshold optimisation. Steps 7 to 9 train four classifiers, sweep 99 thresholds on the validation set, lock the optimal threshold for each model, and evaluate once on the untouched test set. LightGBM achieves the lowest expected financial cost at USD 14,898.40 per 30,000 transactions, at threshold 0.48.Stage 4: robustness and leakage checks. Steps 10 to 19 run eight checks. These are optimism bias (validation versus test tuning), temporal validation (train 2023, test 2024), cost-ratio sensitivity (10 to 1, 29 to 1, 50 to 1, 100 to 1), fixed versus re-optimised threshold sensitivity, 5-fold cross-validation, single-feature leakage screen, train-validation-test overlap check, and feature-availability audit.Stage 5: explainability and comparison. Steps 13 and 20 to 24 produce the SHAP feature importance for the deployed model, all publication-ready tables and figures, the hyperparameter tuning comparison, the feature engineering comparison, and the final pipeline recommendation.Key findings reproduced by this repositoryThe deployed model is LightGBM at threshold 0.48. Test cost is USD 14,898.40 per 30,000 transactions. Cost at the default threshold of 0.5 is USD 14,941.30. The saving is 0.29 percent. Test AUC-PR is 0.0901. Test F2 is 0.2417. Test MCC is 0.1295. 5-fold cross-validation AUC-PR is 0.0900 plus or minus 0.0055. Temporal validation cost for LightGBM is USD 36,879.95 on 74,918 transactions. The maximum single-feature AUC-PR is 0.0569 from hour_of_day. There is zero overlap between train, validation, and test sets. SHAP analysis shows that login_attempts, risk_score, and hour_of_day are the top three predictors. Transaction amount ranks seventh with a relative importance of 9.3.Files in this repositoryThe repository contains the following files.Notebook and code. The Jupyter notebook or Python script that runs all 24 steps in sequence. The notebook runs end to end in Kaggle with the public dataset attached.Reproducibility manifest. A JSON file recording library versions (Python, numpy, pandas, scikit-learn, xgboost, lightgbm, shap), random seed, split sizes, cost parameters, deployed model name, and deployed threshold.Data outputs. CSV files for every intermediate and final table. These include the merged dataset summary, the feature-availability audit, the cost derivation, the split summary, the validation threshold sweep, the test results, the optimism-bias table, the temporal validation table, the cost-ratio sensitivity table, the fixed versus re-optimised threshold table, the 5-fold cross-validation table, the single-feature leakage table, the train-validation-test overlap table, the SHAP importance table, the tuning comparison table, the feature engineering comparison table, and the final pipeline comparison table.Publication-ready tables. Five tables in CSV and LaTeX format. Table 1 is performance metrics. Table 2 is default versus validation-optimal threshold. Table 3 is SHAP feature importance. Table 4 is cost parameter derivation. Table 5 is robustness and leakage checks summary.Figures. Publication-quality PNG figures. These include the SHAP summary plot, the SHAP bar plot, the validation cost curves per model, the test cost bar chart, the precision-recall curves, the ROC curves, the confusion matrices, the cost-ratio sensitivity heatmap, the model comparison chart, and the per-model threshold panels.Data sourceThe dataset used in this study is publicly available on Kaggle under a CC0 Public Domain license (Safarbek, 2025). The dataset contains synthetic transactions generated to mirror the statistical properties of a Central Asian mobile payment ecosystem. No real personal or financial data is included. The dataset citation is:Safarbek. (2025). Central Asia Fintech Fraud Detection Dataset. Kaggle. https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/safar1/central-asia-fintech-fraud-datasetReproducibilityTo reproduce the results, open the notebook in Kaggle, attach the dataset from Kaggle as input, and run all cells. All outputs will be written to the working directory. The reproducibility manifest records the library versions used in the original run. To reproduce the exact numbers reported in the study, install the same library versions listed in the manifest.Intended useThe repository is intended for researchers and mobile payment operators who wish to develop cost-sensitive fraud detection pipelines. The code is written to be adapted. Users can replace the dataset with their own transaction data and recalibrate the cost parameters to their institution's operational environment. The threshold optimisation and SHAP explainability components are dataset-agnostic.

all.title: An Explainable Hybrid CNN–Transformer Framework for Fraud Detection in Digital and Cryptocurrency Transactions
all.abstract: Fraud detection in digital payment and cryptocurrency systems is complicated by heterogeneous transaction records, class imbalance and limited model interpretability. This study proposed an explainable hybrid convolutional neural network (CNN)–Transformer framework for identifying suspicious transactions using the IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection and Ethereum Address Behavior datasets. Tabular features were transformed into spatial representations using the Image Generator for Tabular Data algorithm, while principal component analysis and rolling temporal sequences were employed to represent transaction behaviour. A dual-branch CNN–Transformer model was developed with cost-sensitive learning and hyperparameter optimisation using the Sparrow Search Algorithm. Model predictions were interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations, while an IPFS- and blockchain-based architecture was proposed for audit logging.
