TQ-HQNet: A Trainability-Aware and Qubit-Efficient Hybrid Quantum Neural Network for Cross-Domain Learning on Heterogeneous Data
all.abstract: Hybrid quantum neural networks are a promising direction for noisy intermediate-scale quantum computing, but their practical effectiveness is often limited by poor trainability, rigid circuit design, and weak robustness across heterogeneous real-world tasks. This paper proposes TQ-HQNet, a Trainability-Aware and Qubit-Efficient Hybrid Quantum Neural Network for cross-domain learning on heterogeneous data. The proposed framework combines three mechanisms: 1) adaptive latent compression to map domain-specific features into qubit-compatible representations, 2) trainability-aware search over compact variational circuit candidates, and 3) hybrid fusion of multiple shallow quantum experts to improve robustness without increasing qubit cost excessively. TQ-HQNet is evaluated on four public datasets spanning neurological screening, phishing detection, financial direction prediction, and DNA sequence classification. Across all domains, the proposed model consistently improves over a fixed hybrid quantum baseline, with balanced-accuracy gains of +0.280, +0.170, +0.071, and +0.060, respectively. Ablation and sensitivity studies confirm that gains arise from trainability-aware compact circuit selection and expert fusion, not circuit scaling. Although classical baselines outperform on some tasks, fixed-split results show consistent improvements over the fixed hybrid reference. These analyses support the practical role of compact selection and fusion, with repeated-split and hardware-aware studies left for future work.

all.title: Harvesting Apple's Orchard: A Security Analysis of On-Device CoreML Models Across the Apple Ecosystem
all.abstract: Apple ships hundreds of task-specific machine-learning models inside iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and tvOS. We present, to our knowledge, the first systematic security analysis of this on-device surface. We harvested 1,137 CoreML artifacts from six platform images and two device harvests, and a conversion pipeline recovered 155 previously opaque bundles as loadable mlpackage archives. Eight findings. (1) 368 of 1,137 artifacts expose plaintext learned parameters (281 blobs, 369.61 MiB) and 166 of 166 MIL bundles leak internal model-database tokens. (2) Specification versions 1-9 coexist and locale variants diverge architecturally. (3) Across 82,092 adversarial evaluations (221 model paths), worst-case flip rates reach 100%; zero-width spaces flip 65% of the Indian-English and 70% of the US-English SMS filter. (4) A 16-byte weight edit flips 7 of 8 probe inputs of a system model, with no runtime integrity check observed. (5) Loading Apple's own hand-gesture model crashes libBNNS through the public CoreML API (4/4 on production M2, also macOS 27.0); Apple ruled it a self-crash outside the security boundary. (6) Eleven bundles ship isUpdatable=1 hooks. (7) SMS text-classifier latency is 13.1-52.0 ms, 92.4% in the CPU-side NLP core, not the ANE. (8) The classifiers label 8-9 of 10 phishing messages Transactional. We filed three reports with Apple Product; all were declined as not crossing a security boundary, and we report the findings as robustness results.

all.title: Benchmarking Web Agent Defenses Against Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection
all.abstract: Multimodal web agents automate website interactions but remain vulnerable to visual prompt injection (VPI), where malicious webpage content manipulates their visual processing and induces unintended actions. Although several defenses focus on detecting injected instructions in screenshots, malicious destinations such as phishing URLs embedded in HTML can remain hidden yet accessible through agent interactions. Existing evaluations have also not sufficiently examined adaptive attackers who know the defense mechanisms. To address these limitations, we introduce AdaptiveVPI, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating adaptive VPI threats in web agents. Specifically, we present a dataset of 360 webpage instances spanning 6 distinct hijack strategies across 10 real-world websites, with malicious destinations not visible in screenshots. We design an adaptive attack framework that iteratively refines malicious instructions based on feedback from the defense mechanism being evaluated. We also introduce three metrics to measure the extent of agent hijacking at three different levels. Across 10 defense configurations for computer-use agents and 11 defense configurations for browser-use agents, our adaptive attacks achieve average success rates of 91.87% and 91.99%, respectively. These results reveal a gap between current VPI defenses and realistic threats and highlight the need for defenses designed with adaptive attackers in mind.

all.title: Development of an Effective Federated Learning-Based Defense System Against Phishing Attacks on Mobile Platforms
all.abstract: Phishing remains one of the most pervasive and damaging cyber threats, exploiting both technical flaws and human behavior to compromise sensitive data. We present a privacy-preserving, real-time defense that analyzes full webpage source code on mobile platforms. Our system combines a lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for end-to-end feature extraction with a Federated Learning (FL) framework that updates models collaboratively on user devices without transferring raw data-supporting regulatory compliance and personalization. Evaluated on a large and diverse dataset, the model attains 86.02\% accuracy, 90.35\% precision, 80.64\% recall, and 92.78\% ROC-AUC. While some centralized, classical approaches may report higher accuracy, our design emphasizes a practical balance among accuracy, user privacy, and real-time performance on resource-constrained devices. We further demonstrate an end-to-end integration within the open-source Lightning Android browser, achieving real-time detection with low computational overhead. This work shows that privacy-first, AI-driven phishing detection is both feasible and scalable across mobile and IoT settings, delivering robust protection while keeping user data on-device.

all.title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway
all.abstract: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .

all.title: Sequential Semantic-Non-Semantic Watermarking: Robustness Against UnMarker Attacks
all.abstract: Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have accelerated digital content generation and intensified concerns around fraud, misuse, counterfeiting, and content provenance. Defensive image watermarking provides a practical mechanism for identifying and tracing digital content, but recent watermark-removal attacks challenge its robustness. This study investigates Sequential Semantic Non-Semantic Watermarking (SSNSW), which combines HiDDeN and StegaStamp as complementary non-semantic and semantic watermarking schemes. Using 50 images from MS-COCO and CelebA-HQ, both embedding orders are evaluated, followed by UnMarker's non-semantic and semantic attacks applied individually and sequentially. Results show that both watermarks remain highly decodable after dual embedding, with only limited embedding-order effects. Under individual attacks, one watermark generally remains strongly decodable: StegaStamp under the non-semantic attack and HiDDeN under the semantic attack. Sequential attacks are therefore required to substantially reduce both watermark signals, while attack order has a limited and configuration-dependent effect. The semantic attack also shows a broader effect across the two watermark types than the non-semantic attack. LPIPS remains relatively low in several settings, although qualitative inspection reveals noticeable distortions, particularly in selected facial images, indicating that LPIPS should not be used alone to assess visual quality. Overall, the findings show that combining complementary watermark types can increase robustness against single-stage removal attacks and motivate broader multi-layer watermarking, stronger perceptual evaluation, and further study of sequential watermark-removal strategies.

sample.title: How Much Do Foundation Models Add to Gradient Boosting on Financial Event Sequences?
sample.abstract: Foundation models pretrained on raw transaction sequences are proposed for credit, fraud and churn modeling, with reported gains over gradient boosting, but the data and baselines behind these gains are rarely public. We measure how much the pretraining and adaptation recipes of these models add to a baseline of point-in-time window aggregates and LightGBM, and we propose TBS (Temporal Boosting-Sequence ensemble), which averages the ranks of a boosting model enriched with label-free event-transition features and of a pretrained sequence network fine-tuned jointly with the aggregates. On a synthetic credit-card dataset, the public MBD-mini banking dataset and two proprietary datasets of trade credit and B2B churn, we compare 27 methods at three label budgets with five seeds and paired bootstrap intervals, using sequence models of about 0.4 million parameters pretrained per dataset. Frozen self-supervised embeddings rarely improve the baseline, and a fine-tuned sequence network alone clears it in 9 of 21 target-budget cells. TBS clears it in 19 of 21 cells (18 after FDR adjustment), with a median gain of +1.8 AUC points, and the controls suggest that combining boosting with the pretrained network is the main source of the observed gain. Gains shrink as labels grow and with rich tabular data: with both, the gain on the proprietary datasets is +0.7 and +0.8 points, the latter with an interval including zero. We also re-examine two benchmarks. On IBM TabFormer, the test follows a change in the fraud pattern and the published baseline has no history; with the training period the vendor states, our history-aware LightGBM and our own foundation model stay below the published scores of a commercial model. On IBM AML, a simulation artifact lets a date rule reach F1 0.482, and a point-in-time LightGBM reaches the F1 of graph neural networks whose test graph includes later transactions.

sample.title: Who Sent It or How It Moved? Sender Shortcuts in Cryptocurrency Anti-Money-Laundering Benchmarks, Audited on Elliptic2 and Elliptic++
sample.abstract: Two public benchmarks dominate graph-based anti-money-laundering (AML) research on Bitcoin: the transaction-level Elliptic dataset, extended as Elliptic++, and the subgraph-level Elliptic2. In both, a label is assigned according to the entity that sends the funds. We ask whether models trained on these benchmarks learn how laundering moves or merely who sent the money, and we propose a diagnostic protocol to tell the two apart: a sender lookup baseline, a novelty baseline, a sender-disjoint split with a leakage check, and a decomposition of performance into sender, receiver and intrinsic signal. On Elliptic2 the task largely reduces to classifying the sender. Under the standard random split, a no-learning lookup of sender history reaches a PR-AUC of 0.954, against 0.975 for gradient boosting on 456 features; our reimplementation of RevClassify reproduces its reported 0.97 and falls to 0.126 without sender information. When senders are held out, performance drops to 0.746, and the subgraph's own structure, transactions and receivers fall from 0.619 to 0.186. On Elliptic++ the same protocol finds the shortcut negligible: sender history reaches only 0.340 against 0.986 for the full model (3.5 against 10.1 times the test prevalence), adding it to the full model raises PR-AUC by less than 0.004 in every seed, and the transaction's own features keep 0.883 when sending addresses are held out. We trace the difference to the unit of sender identity: Elliptic2 senders are entity clusters that recur across many labeled subgraphs, whereas Elliptic++ senders are individual addresses, and fewer than half of test transactions have a sending address seen in training. A shared sender-based label rule thus produces a severe shortcut in one benchmark and a negligible one in the other, so the diagnostic must be run on each benchmark.

sample.title: Large Payments Model
sample.abstract: Payment applications such as fraud detection, authorization prediction, and payment optimization draw on overlapping transaction information. This motivates a reusable payments intelligence layer that shares learned representations and predictive signals, rather than developing predictive models independently for each task. Realizing this shared capability requires handling heterogeneous transaction fields, high-cardinality identifiers, lifecycle-dependent attributes, long histories, and rare outcomes while meeting latency and cost constraints. We present Large Payments Model (LPM), a domain-specific foundation model designed for operational use and trained from scratch on large-scale structured transaction data to learn reusable representations for payment prediction tasks. LPM employs field-specific encodings and lifecycle-aware self-supervision in two complementary architectures: the Independent variant uses hybrid masking and supports efficient per-transaction inference, while the Sequence variant incorporates entity-linked histories through compact latent representations for richer temporal context. Optional distillation enables resource-constrained deployment. We pretrain LPM on up to 400 billion tokens and study scaling, downstream performance, and representation reuse. LPM improves over strong task-specific baselines across multiple prediction tasks in Merchant and Treasury Services, demonstrating applicability in distinct payment domains. Its representations also facilitate adaptation to a target not observed during pretraining through compact task-specific components. Together with production deployment, these results position LPM as a practical basis for reusable payments intelligence.

sample.title: Evaluating Ongoing Access Attacks on the Web
sample.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
sample.abstract: In ongoing access attacks, an adversary reconfigures security features on a compromised account to maintain access, despite victim attempts to remove them. Such attacks are particularly common in interpersonal violence where abusers often use them for continuous monitoring, surveillance, and stalking of their victims. Despite the severity and prevalence of these attacks in practice, we are aware of only one prior study that considers them, and only in the context of authentication via passkeys. We provide the first study of ongoing access attacks that holistically considers all available authentication mechanisms. First, we survey modern account security features to characterize 11 types of access routes: different ways in which a user can configure the account to obtain authenticated access. Many web services now offer a multitude of access routes, including single-sign on, passkeys, recovery mechanisms, and more, resulting in a rich attack surface even for adversaries that only use service-provided user interfaces. Using these access routes, we experimentally simulate ongoing access attacks for 20 popular services, showing that 14 of these offer an access route that is irrevocable or not properly remediated by service-provided guidance, leaving adversarial access intact.

sample.title: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Will LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam?
sample.abstract: Online fraud is traditionally limited by the cost of the human labor needed to talk to potential victims. We ask whether hosted large language models will now supply that labor. We prompted ten off-the-shelf models to play the seller in the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites, using a plain system prompt with no jailbreak. Each model played 30 conversations against each of four buyer personas, from credulous to guarded, with the same model playing the buyer (1,200 conversations). We label each conversation by what happened to the buyer's money, and validate the labels against two human coders. 737 conversations (61%) ended with the buyer paying in advance. Eight of the ten models played in almost every conversation, and running both sides cost about 2.5 cents per payment. Only the guarded buyer, who wanted a findable identity, resisted, and the most willing sellers got past it by inventing names and phone numbers. Sellers that recognized the scam still took the money in 133 conversations, usually reasoning about their own honesty rather than the buyer's risk. Several models protected the buyer without refusing, by conceding payment on delivery, so refusal rates alone misstate safety. We release the benchmark, prompts, code and labels.

sample.title: Maturity-Aware Dual-Timescale Replay for Delayed-Feedback Financial Fraud Screening
sample.venue: International Journal of World Economic Research
sample.abstract: Fraud-screening labels often arrive after a transaction, with fraudulent outcomes confirmed later than legitimate outcomes. This class-dependent observation process distorts conventional replay under concept drift. We instantiate the adaptive recent/global prioritized replay of DriftShield in a one-step cost-sensitive fraud controller, and extend it with maturity-gated access, transaction-time recency and capped inverse confirmation-visibility weighting. A second, arrival-driven scorer supplies a faster adaptation channel; its predictions are combined with the slow replay scorer using a fixed mixture. The system is tested prequentially on an explicitly synthetic 42,000-event stream with two changes in fraud signatures and asymmetric reporting delays. In the three-seed comparison, 42 model/delay runs include three component ablations and two stress-test delays. An additional 12-seed paired evaluation reports F1 0.262 and average precision 0.236 for the dual-timescale controller, versus 0.239 and 0.223 for arrival-time replay. A fast-only scorer with the same threshold controller instead reaches F1 0.265 and average precision 0.242: the slow branch does not improve that stronger comparator in this simulator. Paired intervals and a future-label nonanticipation test delimit the reproducible benefits of maturity-aware replay without implying production deployment gains.

sample.title: FraudBench-NG: A NIBSS-Calibrated Synthetic Dataset and Generator for Nigerian Inter-Bank Fraud Detection
sample.abstract: Research on inter-bank fraud detection in Nigeria is limited by the lack of shareable transaction data, and synthetic benchmarks can mislead if they leak information or hide their assumptions. FraudBench-NG is a reproducible framework for studying fraud detection under explicitly documented modelling assumptions. It is a parametric simulation calibrated to 2023 NIBSS aggregates, with a released dataset of 2.1~million transactions from 25{,}000 customers and 0.1\% fraud. Fraud is generated as incidents, matching NIBSS counts and loss per case; every parameter is marked as NIBSS or assumed; and every behavioural feature uses only prior transactions, verified by row-by-row recomputation and a label-permutation test. Logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost reach a PR-AUC of 0.016--0.036 (no-skill 0.0007), with wide customer-level bootstrap intervals, so the models cannot be ranked. At a 1\% false-positive rate they raise about 70 false alerts per fraud row caught and flag only about 19\% of incidents at their first transaction. Results depend strongly on the assumptions: a model trained with takeover bursts transfers only partly to data with a different burst probability, and performance differs between burst settings mainly because of how an incident's loss is split across its transactions. Fraud prevalence is a design choice that cannot be compared with the NIBSS case-to-transaction ratio, and no real Nigerian transactions were available for validation.

sample.title: Graph-Based Financial Fraud Detection: A Property-Centric Survey of Static, Temporal, Cycle-Aware, and Generative Methods and Their Evaluation
sample.venue: Journal of Computing Theories and Applications
sample.abstract: Financial fraud is increasingly coordinated across multiple accounts and transactions, meaning that its evidence often lies in relationships between accounts, the sequence of events, and, in schemes such as money laundering and wash trading, closed loops of transfers rather than in individual records. This review examines graph-based methods for detecting such fraud, covering static and temporal graph neural networks, graph anomaly detection, cycle- and motif-aware methods, generative models, and the evaluation practices used to assess them. The review draws on 147 sources identified through a documented literature search protocol. Four findings emerge. First, no single method family performs best under all conditions: tree-based models remain highly competitive on feature-rich datasets, whereas graph-based and temporal models offer greater advantages when discriminative signals reside in relational structures or transaction sequences. Second, detecting cyclic laundering is fundamentally a representational problem: standard message-passing architectures have limited ability to capture cycle structures, while recent performance gains have been associated with representations that preserve the directed multigraph structure of transactions rather than simply increasing model complexity. Third, evaluation practices, including temporal leakage and threshold selection using test data, can inflate reported performance and undermine the reliability of comparisons. Fourth, a taxonomy of eight method families evaluated against four properties required for coordinated, temporal, and partially observed fraud detection—temporal awareness, probabilistic generation, cycle awareness, and intrinsic explainability—reveals that none of the reviewed families provides all four properties. This identifies a central research gap in the current literature. Building on these findings, the review proposes cyclic fraud as a structural stress test for future detection methods and provides an evaluation checklist to address the methodological weaknesses identified.

sample.title: JEV vs. LLMs: A Comparative Analysis for Phishing Email Detection
sample.abstract: Phishing remains a major source of credential theft and fraudulent payments, and email security systems must classify large message volumes reliably, quickly, and at manageable cost. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer flexible text understanding, but their token-based generation increases response time and API cost, and the reliability of their confidence values requires measurement. Jev 1.13, a typed decision model from TypeSafe AI, instead returns a structured outcome with a confidence value. This paper compares Jev 1.13 with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, and Meta Llama 4 Maverick on a labelled dataset of 1500 emails, covering classification performance, decision latency, token consumption, API cost, and probability calibration. Jev achieves the highest accuracy (79.67%), precision (71.43%), recall (97.97%), and F1 score (82.62%). It also records the shortest batch time (173.88 seconds), the lowest token count (597,895), the lowest cost (USD 0.015103 per 1000 decisions), and the lowest Brier score (0.1698) and ECE (0.1594). These results suggest that Jev is a promising option for fast, structured, high-volume triage. LLMs retain the advantage of generating explanations, which we do not evaluate, and all four systems require further validation before standalone deployment.

sample.title: VRLLM: Turning LLMs into Powerful Tabular Classifiers
sample.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on text, but whether pretrained LLMs are effective for large-scale tabular classification remains unclear, as many previous works demonstrate that LLMs' tabular data classification performance falls behind tree-based models or neural architectures designed for tabular data. At Visa Research, we managed to fine-tune a pretrained Llama 3.2 1B LLM on billions of rows of labeled tabular data and make it outperform a wide array of tabular classifiers and even our competitive production deep learning model. For ease of reference, we refer to the model as the Visa Research LLM (VRLLM). In this paper, we share how we achieved this exciting result, covering data preparation, training recipe, ablation studies of design choices and deployment validation. We also benchmark frontier LLMs on the same task and analyze their prediction behavior across model families and generations. Our interpretability experiments suggest that VRLLM learns feature-specific predictive associations, while component ablations indicate that the earliest two FFN layers contribute to the emergence of linearly decodable task information. Our paper provides an engineering recipe and a focused empirical case study on adapting compact LLMs to industrial tabular prediction tasks.

sample.title: An Explainable Machine Learning Framework with Large Language Model Features for Predicting Monetary Redress in Bank Fraud and Scam Complaints
sample.abstract: Liability for scam losses is shifting towards banks, yet few interpretable tools can anticipate which fraud and scam complaints will end in redress. This study develops SCAM-XD, an explainable framework that predicts whether a complaint to the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) flagged as possible fraud or a scam closes with monetary relief reported by the company. From the CFPB narratives archive, the study builds a benchmark of these complaints, about half of which human coders confirm as fraud or scams. A large language model (LLM) codes each narrative for scam type, payment rail, authorisation, manipulation cues and signals of the bank's response, agreeing closely with human coding on scam type. These features are combined with structured fields, company identity and text representations in a stacking ensemble, explained with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and linked to a cost-sensitive triage layer. Tested on a later period, SCAM-XD improves significantly on strong baselines across seeds, including a reimplemented topic model approach. LLM features yield a compact, interpretable model that nearly matches a high-dimensional text baseline but do not significantly improve the full model. Company identity is the strongest driver of predicted redress, yet firm identity alone predicts far less well, and payment rail and bank response cues act in directions consistent with liability rules. Under assumed costs, thresholds selected on validation data substantially reduce modelled expected cost relative to standard thresholds, whereas model choice matters much less. Redress depends on both the firm and the facts that determine liability.

sample.title: The Economics of Instant Payments: A Structured, Evidence-Graded Review of Financial Inclusion, Welfare, and Macro-Financial Effects across Global Fast-Payment Systems
sample.abstract: Purpose: This article examines the economic consequences of instant payment systems (financial inclusion, welfare, growth and macro-financial stability) and seeks to separate the well-established effects from the projections and correlations that form the basis of much of the practitioner discussion. Methodology: This is a structured narrative review. The evidence is synthesized under an explicit four-tier scheme that gives primacy to peer-reviewed causal studies and central bank research over industry reports, separates out the observed from the forecasted, and places causal identification at the heart of the analysis. The review draws on 22 sources published between 2014 and 2026. The four systems under review are Brazil's Pix, India's UPI, the US FedNow and RTP and the EU's SEPA Instant. These are compared on design features. Findings: The best-evidenced finding is microeconomic: mobile-money access is estimated to have lifted around 2% of Kenyan households out of poverty and there are quasi-experimental findings on the impact of adoption in Mexico and India. The aggregate GDP and consumer savings data are all based on industry estimates and should be treated as indicative only. Differences in outcomes across the four systems are associated with system design (operator model, pricing, mandate and interoperability) rather than with the technology itself, although with four systems and no causal design this is a pattern, not an identified effect. The macro-financial risks are material, notably deposit-funding pressure and authorized-push-payment fraud (£450.7 million in the United Kingdom in 2024). Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: The paper offers a five-channel transmission framework, an evidence-graded synthesis that distinguishes causal effects from projections, and a design-feature comparison that explains cross-country heterogeneity. It directs researchers toward credible identification and policymakers toward public, low-cost, interoperable and well-supervised designs on which inclusive outcomes depend.

sample.title: Money laundering, terrorist financing, and smuggling: emerging threats to Pakistan’s national security
institutions: Shaheed Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto Institute of Science and Technology
sample.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the institutional and regulatory factors shaping the implementation of Pakistan’s anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT) framework, with specific attention to security risks allied with smuggling-related illicit financial flows. It develops a sequential-mechanism framework linking regulatory compliance, institutional weaknesses, interagency coordination and enforcement effectiveness to the potential intersection between smuggling, money laundering and terrorist financing. Design/methodology/approach This research uses legal document analysis as a risk-assessment method. It examines the legislative frameworks, policy instruments and official government reports to evaluate the effectiveness of Pakistan’s anti-money laundering (AML) and countering the financing of terrorism (CFT) regimes. Findings The analysis indicates that, although Pakistan has made improvements driven in part by Financial Action Task Force compliance requirements, significant deficiencies remain. These include weak institutional capacity, insufficient interagency coordination and inadequate oversight of high-risk sectors, particularly non-profit organizations and real estate. The study also underscores how emerging digital technologies create new vulnerabilities by enabling porous financial boundaries and facilitating illicit financial transactions. Originality/value By articulating the security implications of financial crime and mapping the systemic vulnerabilities within Pakistan’s AML/CFT architecture, this paper offers context-specific reforms aimed at strengthening intelligence capabilities, regulatory compliance and regional cooperation. This integrated perspective contributes to a deeper understanding of how illicit finance directly undermines national security.

sample.title: AI agents leave tracks: Why behavior remains one of the best ways to spot them
sample.abstract: Imagine two digital banking sessions beginning within the same minute.

sample.title: Ethical CV: Deep-Fake Detection Via Biological Signals
sample.abstract: Deepfake videos are becoming more common and are often used for harmful purposes like identity fraud, political manipulation, and spreading false or misleading content. While modern deepfake generators create videos that look very realistic, they still struggle to copy subtle human behaviors like natural blinking, accurate lip-sync, and small facial movements. Most current detection tools focus on surface-level visuals such as lighting or video quality, which may not be reliable as deepfakes become more advanced. Ethical CV introduces a smarter solution by analyzing natural biological signals in the face to detect whether a video is real or fake. It uses computer vision to track these signals and machine learning to check if they follow real human patterns. Early tests show this method is more accurate than relying on visual cues alone. Ethical CV is flexible, easy to understand, and useful in areas like media verification, digital forensics, and the safe, responsible use of AI in digital content. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance with 94.2% accuracy, 92.8% precision, and 95.1% recall on benchmark datasets.

sample.title: FRAMEWORK GAIA-FIS: GOVERNANÇA DE IA PARA MITIGAÇÃO DE FRAUDES POR DEEPFAKES DE ÁUDIO E IDENTIDADES SINTÉTICAS
sample.abstract: A proliferação da IA generativa criou um novo vetor de risco corporativo, deepfakes de áudio para fraudes financeiras. Paralelamente, o Brasil discute a regulação do setor por meio do PL nº 2.338/2023, que propõe deveres de governança. Este artigo apresenta o Framework GAIA-FIS, modelo prático de governança desenhado para organizações brasileiras. Adotou-se abordagem qualitativa, baseada em análise documental e mapeamento cruzado entre requisitos regulatórios e controles da ISO/IEC 42001:2024. Baseado no PL, na LGPD e na ISO/IEC 42001:2024, o framework propõe 20 controles operacionais estruturados em cinco dimensões e guiados pelo ciclo PDCA, com o propósito de reduzir a lacuna entre a conformidade legal e a defesa técnica contra identidades sintéticas. Por se tratar de uma proposta ainda não validada empiricamente, recomenda-se sua aplicação experimental em estudos futuros.

sample.title: Financial stability implications of AI adoption in the financial industry and the real economy
sample.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the financial industry as well as the broader economy, creating both opportunities and risks. Banks and asset managers, which represent key channels of financial intermediation in the euro area, are increasingly using AI for tasks such as credit scoring, fraud detection and portfolio management. While AI adoption can support innovation and enhance operational efficiency, it may also introduce new risks and amplify existing vulnerabilities, including a reliance on a small number of technology providers that creates concentration and third-party dependencies across the financial system. At the same time, financial institutions are also increasingly exposed to AI-driven developments in the real economy. A novel firm-level indicator suggests that a sizeable share of firms, concentrated mainly in the IT and financial sectors, is significantly exposed to AI-related opportunities and risks. Policies should focus on improving the quality of data that monitor the use of AI, strengthening the oversight of critical AI providers and adapting market safeguards and supervisory capabilities to emerging risks.

sample.title: Prevenção de Fraudes e Golpes Digitais em Meios de Pagamento Eletrônicos: mecanismos jurídico-regulatórios e proteção ao consumidor no Sistema Financeiro Nacional
sample.venue: Revista da Procuradoria-Geral do Banco Central
authors: Danniel Pedro Lima de Araújo Da Conceição
sample.abstract: Este artigo analisa o marco jurídico-regulatório para prevenção de fraudes e golpes digitais no Sistema Financeiro Nacional (SFN), com ênfase em meios de pagamento eletrônicos, especialmente o Pix. O objetivo é avaliar a eficácia dos mecanismos de governança e segurança cibernética do Banco Central do Brasil (BC) e do Conselho Monetário Nacional (CMN) na proteção do consumidor financeiro. A metodologia adota a análise normativa de resoluções recentes, como a Resolução Conjunta 6/2023 e as atualizações do Regulamento do Pix referentes ao Mecanismo Especial de Devolução (MED), aliada à jurisprudência do Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) e aos acórdãos do Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU). Os resultados revelam uma evolução regulatória focada no compartilhamento obrigatório de dados sobre fraudes e na responsabilidade objetiva dos prestadores de serviço por falhas de segurança ou engenharia social. Conclui-se pela necessidade de reforçar o monitoramento em tempo real e as tecnologias de detecção, transferindo o risco da fraude do consumidor vulnerável para as instituições, em consonância com a Lei 15.252, de 4 de novembro de 2025, e os princípios da cidadania financeira.

sample.title: From Batch to Instant: A Reference Architecture and Process Model for Modernizing National-Scale Disbursement Platforms with Real-Time, Multi-Rail Payments
sample.venue: International Journal of Computer Trends and Technology
sample.abstract: For a long time, large-scale disbursement of funds relied on overnight processing and checks. However, the emergence of instant payment systems like the FedNow Service from the Federal Reserve and the RTP network from The Clearing House, as well as push-to-card and digital wallet payment systems, allows for the funds to be delivered to the recipients in seconds [2][3]. Furthermore, recipients of these funds have demonstrated a strong preference for instant delivery when it is an available option [7]. However, the platforms that carry national disbursement volume were built for batch processing and cannot be taken out of service for rebuilding. This paper is a conceptual study. The aim of this study is to propose a reference architecture and a process model to enable the migration of a national-scale disbursement platform from 24-hour batch processing to near-instant multi-rail payouts while ensuring the operations of the existing platform are not interrupted. The proposed architecture introduces a layer for disbursement orchestration and rail routing that selects the fastest, least-cost eligible rail for each payout while ensuring that any fraud, anti-money-laundering, and sanctions controls are performed on each payout before it is sent. If a payment fails, the system automatically routes the payment through an alternative rail after confirming the failure of the original payment to avoid duplicate payments. A phased, reversible migration is proposed for the existing platform to the event-driven system. The proposed architecture and migration plan are evaluated using a comparison with existing literature and a scenario-based walkthrough against the proposed requirements for the platform. As this is a conceptual study, no experiments were conducted to evaluate the proposed architecture, migration plan, and requirements. The benefits of the proposed platform have been reported alongside a classification of the evidence supporting these benefits as either published data, practitioner observations, or assumptions and estimates, with empirical measurement left for future work.

sample.title: Leakage-aware federated-style simulation for fraud risk prediction in AI-enabled FinTech platforms
sample.abstract: AI-enabled FinTech platforms increasingly rely on automated fraud-risk prediction to secure high-volume digital payments, mobile-money transactions, and real-time financial services. However, fraud detection remains difficult because fraudulent transactions are rare, financial data are sensitive, and centralized machine-learning models may create privacy and data-governance risks. This study evaluates a leakage-aware and imbalance-aware federated-style simulation for fraud-risk prediction in AI-enabled FinTech platforms. The study does not implement FedAvg, cryptographic secure aggregation, differential privacy, or model-parameter exchange. Instead, the PaySim Synthetic Financial Dataset was partitioned into five simulated FinTech clients, local models were trained separately, and prediction-level aggregation was used to compare centralized and simulated decentralized learning settings. The experimental workflow included data-quality assessment, leakage-aware feature selection, feature engineering, class-imbalance analysis, centralized model development, threshold optimization, and federated-style model comparison. The results show that fraud cases represented only 0.0466% of all transactions and occurred only in CASH_OUT and TRANSFER operations. The best-balanced centralized model was the Improved Random Forest at a threshold of 0.33, achieving an F1-score of 0.3019. Federated Ensemble Aggregation achieved the highest PR-AUC of 0.2699 and a precision of 1.0000, but its recall remained low at 0.1429. The centralized Improved Random Forest retained the highest F1-score of 0.3019, indicating a stronger overall precision-recall balance. Global feature-importance analysis showed that transaction amount, log-transformed amount, temporal features, transaction type, and destination-account activity were the main fraud-risk indicators. These findings should be interpreted as evidence from simulated decentralized fraud-risk learning rather than a full secure federated learning implementation.

sample.title: The Dark Side of AI: Fraud, Deception, and the Erosion of Trust
sample.abstract: Fraud and deception are not new. They have existed for as long as human civilization. What AI changes is the scale, speed, and sophistication at which deception can be conducted. Scams that once required a team of people can now be executed by a single individual deploying automated agents. AI has lowered the barrier to entry for creative work, for business, for education, and for fraud. A deepfake is an AI-generated or manipulated audio, video, or image designed to convincingly imitate a real person. AI can generate invoices, contracts, résumés, certificates, and legal documents that look entirely authentic. Creating a fake degree certificate, a forged reference letter, or a convincing but fraudulent contract is no longer a specialist skill. Phishing has always relied on tricking people into clicking links or handing over credentials, but it has historically been detectable by poor grammar, generic greetings, and implausible scenarios.

sample.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
sample.abstract: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use "advanced cryptographic tools" to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

sample.title: Modeling the Future of Finance: Digital Transformation, Fintech Innovations, Market Adaptation, and Strategic Growth
sample.venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
sample.abstract: The financial industry is undergoing a profound transformation driven by rapid advancements in digital technologies, fintech innovations, and evolving market dynamics. This paper explores the critical role of digital transformation in reshaping financial services, emphasizing the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, big data analytics, and cloud computing to enhance efficiency, security, and customer experience. Fintech innovations have disrupted traditional banking models, enabling digital payments, decentralized finance (DeFi), roboadvisors, and open banking, fostering financial inclusion and accessibility. Market adaptation remains a crucial aspect of this evolution, as financial institutions must navigate regulatory challenges, cybersecurity threats, and shifting consumer expectations. This study examines the impact of digital disruption on traditional financial frameworks, highlighting the adoption of agile methodologies, risk management strategies, and regulatory compliance to ensure stability and resilience in a rapidly changing landscape. Additionally, the rise of embedded finance and digital currencies is reshaping transactional ecosystems, prompting financial institutions to innovate and collaborate with technology providers to sustain competitive advantage. Strategic growth in the digital finance era requires a data-driven approach, leveraging predictive analytics and machine learning to optimize investment decisions, enhance fraud detection, and personalize financial services. The paper presents a framework for financial organizations to embrace digital transformation by integrating emerging technologies with sustainable business models. Furthermore, it discusses the role of financial literacy and digital accessibility in fostering inclusive economic growth, ensuring that technological advancements benefit diverse populations. By synthesizing insights from case studies, market trends, and regulatory developments, this research provides a comprehensive outlook on the future of finance, highlighting opportunities for stakeholders to capitalize on technological advancements while mitigating associated risks. The study underscores the need for a collaborative approach among financial institutions, regulators, and technology firms to create a secure, efficient, and customer-centric financial ecosystem. The findings offer valuable implications for policymakers, industry leaders, and researchers seeking to understand and shape the trajectory of digital finance in the coming decades.

sample.title: MaRCo@BIS: AI-agentic econometric analysis for central bankers
sample.abstract: This paper introduces MaRCo@BIS, the MAcroeconometric Research Companion: a framework of plain-text workflow files, a verified dictionary of canonical model specifications and a tested reference library, read by an off-the-shelf agentic coding environment.

sample.title: Risk-Aware AI Deployment Architecture for Secure and Regulated Banking Environments
sample.abstract: With an increasing imperative for banks to use AI at scale and regulatory requirements becoming more sophisticated and faster-paced, most organizations treat core security, explainability, and regulatory aspects as post-deployment bolt-ons. Instead, we propose a new, integrated, risk-driven AI architecture where these concerns are integral from day one. The framework categorizes each AI use case into one of three risk tiers. Each risk tier incorporates mandated security via hardware protection with Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), comprehensive explainability via tools like SHAP, LIME, and explainable boosting models (EBMs), and an increasing level of calibrated human oversight, ranging from human-in-the-loop to human-in-command configurations. A successful year-long pilot at a U.S. regional bank (approximately $45 billion in assets) involving 47 production models validated our framework. Compared to before the pilot, the average AUC of fraud detection models increased from 0.74 to 0.81, the AML false-positive rate reduced from 12.4% to 7.6%, and the average regulatory audit review time fell by 38%. This document outlines the architecture and three specific case studies from the pilot-two: one used in real-time production and two used to review historical decisions, providing an end-to-end walkthrough. The key differentiating factor of this framework is treating regulatory compliance as a continuous operating component rather than a compliance checkpoint, which we refer to as living compliance .

sample.title: The Mediating Role of Digital Literacy Between Financial Literacy and Investment Scam Awareness
sample.venue: International Journal of Accounting and Business Finance
sample.abstract: This study analyses whether digital literacy mediates the relationship between financial literacy and investment scam awareness. Despite the rapid expansion of digital financial services, there remains limited knowledge of whether financial and digital literacy interact to shape resistance to online investment scams. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among undergraduates who were selected through stratified random sampling in Sri Lanka. Financial literacy is measured through budgeting skills, financial attitude, financial product literacy and risk awareness. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was applied to estimate the direct effects and mediating effects. Budgeting skills, product literacy and risk awareness enhance digital literacy, while financial attitude shows no meaningful effect. Digital literacy exhibits the strongest direct influence on investment scam awareness. Mediation analysis confirms that digital literacy transmits the effects of budgeting skills, product literacy and risk awareness to scam awareness, whereas financial attitude remains non-significant. The study conceptualizes digital literacy as a coping appraisal mechanism that enables individuals to operationalize financial knowledge in digital financial environments. Guided by Protection Motivation Theory, the study interprets financial literacy as supporting threat appraisal and digital literacy as supporting coping appraisal. The single institution, cross-sectional and self-reported design may restrict generalizability and causal inference. Future studies should use multi-site samples, longitudinal designs, fraud simulation experiments.

sample.title: Enhancing Forensic Accounting with Data Analytics: An Empirical Study of Financial Risk Mitigation and Insolvency Prediction
sample.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sample.abstract: In an increasingly complex and digitalized financial environment, the detection and prevention of corporate fraud and financial distress have become critical for investors, lenders, regulators, and corporate governance bodies. This study examines the integration of data analytics and forensic accounting to enhance fraud detection and insolvency prediction. Using a comprehensive case study of Bhushan Steel Limited (BSL), the research evaluates the effectiveness of the Altman Z-Score and Beneish M-Score models over a fifteen-year period (2012–13 to 2025–26). The findings indicate that the Altman Z-Score consistently identified financial distress and insolvency risk well before the company’s collapse, demonstrating strong predictive capability. In contrast, the Beneish M-Score detected earnings manipulation only during specific periods, reflecting limitations in identifying long-term structural deterioration. Statistical analysis further confirms the significance of both models in assessing financial reporting risks, although the Beneish framework exhibited greater variability. The study highlights the value of integrating traditional forensic accounting techniques with advanced data analytics and AI-driven systems to improve early warning mechanisms, strengthen corporate transparency, support informed decision-making, and enhance financial stability. The findings provide practical insights for regulators, financial institutions, auditors, and investors seeking proactive approaches to risk management and fraud prevention.

sample.title: AI-Driven Financial Fraud Auditing and Evidence Chain Construction in Smart Manufacturing
sample.venue: ICST Transactions on Scalable Information Systems
sample.abstract: INTRODUCTION: In smart manufacturing enterprises, procurement, production, warehousing, sales, and financial settlement data are distributed across multiple business systems. Financial fraud increasingly involves cross-entity collusion, nested business chains, and fragmented evidence, making it difficult for traditional sampling audits to simultaneously ensure accurate risk identification, efficient verification, and traceable evidence support. OBJECTIVES: To address fragmented cross-system associations among manufacturing audit data, difficulties in tracing multi-hop fraud propagation across business entities, and insufficient evidence support for model-generated risk alerts, this study develops an AI-driven financial fraud auditing framework tailored to smart manufacturing processes. The framework links fraud risk identification, dynamic audit-path optimization, and verifiable evidence-chain construction within a unified closed-loop procedure. METHODS: Multi-source heterogeneous audit samples are constructed through entity matching, temporal alignment, and data-quality filtering. Business process constraints are introduced to encode inconsistencies in transaction amounts, material quantities, event timing, and entity relationships. A heterogeneous graph neural network jointly identifies high-risk entities, anomalous transactions, and fraud categories while tracing cross-entity risk propagation paths. The audit process is further formulated as a sequential decision-making task, in which deep reinforcement learning dynamically selects verification actions according to risk information gain, execution cost, and evidence sufficiency. Original records, risk relationships, audit actions, and review statuses are subsequently organized into a structured and traceable evidence chain. RESULTS:Simulation experiments show that the proposed method achieves an F1 score of 92.7% and an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 98.4% for fraud detection, together with a 90.7% recall rate for risk propagation paths. Evidence completeness reaches 95.4%, while the average number of audit steps required to establish a complete evidence chain decreases to 6.9. Direct real-world testing was further conducted on three anonymized manufacturing enterprises containing 715,220 raw cross-system records and 3,660 independently audited business chains. With all trained parameters and decision thresholds fixed, the framework identified 271 of 307 confirmed anomalous chains and achieved a pooled Precision of 89.74%, Recall of 88.27%, F1 score of 89.00%, AUC of 0.956, and false alarm rate of 0.92%. Risk-propagation-path recall and evidence completeness reached 86.64% and 92.18%, respectively, while the average number of audit steps was 7.5. CONCLUSION: Integrating business-process-constrained heterogeneous graph reasoning, risk-feedback-driven audit decision-making, and structured evidence verification enables complex financial fraud to be identified, localized, and substantiated within a unified audit workflow. The proposed framework extends conventional fraud detection from isolated risk classification toward traceable cross-entity reasoning and evidence-supported audit decision-making in smart manufacturing environments.

sample.title: Temporal Graph Learning for Robust Detection of Coordinated Fraud in Dynamic Transaction Networks
sample.venue: International Journal of Advanced Engineering and Technology Research
sample.abstract: Coordinated fraud can produce repeated, synchronized transfers whose signatures are obscured by heterogeneous activity, missing edges, and evolving behavior. This paper studies a lightweight temporal graph learning strategy based on account-level transaction attributes, static neighborhood descriptors, and eight-bin temporal coordination statistics. Static and temporal feature variants are each trained with the same simulated edge-deletion augmentation to disentangle the effects of timing descriptors and robustness training. Experiments are conducted on a controlled, fully specified synthetic benchmark containing 4,800 accounts, approximately 15,000 transfers per run, and simulator-assigned coordinated actors; the benchmark is not a real-world labeled fraud dataset. Three independent runs use chronological, nonoverlapping train/validation/test snapshots. The edge-augmented static graph achieves test average precision 0.631, while the identically augmented temporal feature model reaches 0.602; their nonaugmented counterparts score 0.571 and 0.569, respectively. At 20% and 40% test-edge removal, augmented static-graph average precision is 0.518 and 0.389, respectively. A matched augmentation control, fixed-budget top-100 precision, and timestamp shuffling separate the roles of training robustness and within-snapshot timing. The study provides an efficient, transparent protocol for evaluating coordinated-pattern detection in evolving transaction networks.

sample.title: Know Your Agent (KYA): Why KYC Wasn’t Built for AI Agents
sample.abstract: For decades, Know Your Customer (KYC) rules have rested on one premise: a business opening an account can establish that a real, identifiable person stands behind it. The rules started with banks. The same judgment now opens a sportsbook wallet, a crypto exchange account, a buy now, pay later credit line and a marketplace seller […] The post Know Your Agent (KYA): Why KYC Wasn’t Built for AI Agents appeared first on SEON .

sample.title: Generative AI in Financial Systems and Banking Forensics
sample.abstract: The constantly rising technology adoption in the financial sectors has shown more dynamic patterns in their fraud activities, making them increasingly complex. Despite the presence of class imbalance in fraud detection scenarios in the real world, increasing label latency, the dynamics of fraud attack patterns, and the rise of sensitive data in financial data sets act as barriers for applying rule-based machine learning techniques in financial products for precise fraud detection. Generative Artificial Intelligence refers to a revolution in the analysis of financial fraud because it encompasses all the critical processes involved in legitimate as well as fraudulent financial operations. The use of representation learning and simulation of transactions achieved by generative models enables the prior detection of financial fraud. The use of generative AI is applicable in various financial security systems such as transaction risk evaluation, identification of payment fraud, analysis of anti-money laundering (AML), Know Your Customer (KYC) automation, identification of synthetic identities, and evolutionary patterns of financial fraud identification. The current chapter offers an in-depth analysis of the application of generative AI in financial systems and banking forensics. The use of generative techniques for behavioral simulations, aggressive fraud simulations, fraud analysis and simulations through graphs and time-series analysis, and finally, design and implementation issues and regulations in integrating generative AI in financial systems. The above topics and considerations put together create a comprehensive framework through which one can apply and understand the application of generative AI in the financial and banking system for fraud analysis and detection.

sample.title: A Multi-Dimension EML Feature Framework and Multi-Model-Based Email Anomaly Detection System
institutions: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
sample.abstract: Detecting business email compromise (BEC), account takeover (ATO), and insider threats that use legitimate accounts and business language requires analyzing the sender’s role and prior conversations alongside a message’s technical attributes. However, because data combining corporate email with human resources information is subject to restrictions regarding access to personal and proprietary business information, it is difficult to study organizational roles and communication relationships simultaneously. We propose a multi-dimensional UBA feature framework that integrates raw EML files, MTA logs, and role and authority information from ERP, together with a synthetic email corpus of a fictional company, NexaSoft. Based on an organization of 126 employees and 117 normal business scenarios, we define 23 feature-based and 11 contextual anomaly types and build a dataset of 124,355 emails (76,850 normal, 47,505 anomalous), organized into feature-based and context-based datasets. Linking each message to organizational roles and reply relationships allows normal work and anomalous requests to be represented in the same organizational and conversational environment. The detection method comprises a rule layer for explicit security conditions, an XGBoost layer for structural and statistical anomalies, and a multi-view layer for context-dependent anomalies, in which models M1–M4 analyze message semantics, behavior and time, organizational role and policy, and past conversation. On their assigned classes, M1, M2, and M3 achieve Macro-F1 of 0.9863, 0.9752, and 0.9110 under scenario-separated evaluation, and M4 achieves a mean Macro-F1 of 0.9213 over three seeds. Removing prior conversation lowers M4’s Macro-F1 by 4.34 pp, confirming its contribution. The dataset and detection framework thus enable the study and evaluation of both technical and context-dependent email anomalies, grounded in organizational roles and conversation flow, in one business environment.

sample.title: Geometry enhanced depth map super-resolution with multi-modal feature fusion
A Set-Theoretic Tuple Model with Level-Consistent Normalization and Non-Compensatory Aggregation for Assessing the Cyber Resilience of Critical Infrastructure
institutions: State University of Information and Communication Technologies
State Scientific Institution "Institute of Information, Security and Law of the National Academy of Legal Sciences of Ukraine"
sample.abstract: Cyber-resilience engineering frameworks organize protective activity into goals, objectives and basic actions but give no formal rules for turning heterogeneous security measurements into auditable scores. Building on earlier set-theoretic data and metric models of such a framework, this paper develops a set-theoretic tuple model for assessing the cyber resilience of critical infrastructure and analyzes, with proofs, the evaluation rules on which those models relied. The hierarchy of the Cyber Resiliency Engineering Framework is encoded as an indexed family of sets with an injective identifier map; admissible threat-scenario projections form a finite distributive lattice; and each basic action carries a tuple of metrics. A clipped affine normalization agrees with a five-level class table if and only if the gaps between class boundaries are proportional to those between score breakpoints, and the two-threshold rule of the earlier models is consistent with no table; an anchored piecewise-linear normalization is consistent by construction. A capped knockout operator, which keeps a missing critical capability from being offset by other metrics, retains veto, idempotency and continuity in the normalized scores, whereas neither the hard gate nor power discounting has all three. In an illustrative bank phishing scenario, 9 of 38 observed metrics receive a linear score outside their tabulated level, and the threat-intelligence action moves from high (0.903) to above average (0.856). A parameter study shows how the cap threshold, the weights and the choice of core metrics affect the verdicts. Constructed degraded states activate the cap, the operator is compared with the geometric and harmonic means and the minimum, and a randomized check of the formal rules over 100,000 synthetic states shows that the effects are not peculiar to the example; it does not validate the policy parameters. The model is a formal scoring method that turns heterogeneous security evidence into reproducible, auditable scores; its rules are mathematically valid, but it has not been validated against expert judgment or field data, and no operational or predictive validity under an adversary is claimed.
